[{:db/id 17592186563743 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "014d7fc8-5099-5882-8aa1-ded2fbbcf5aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(t)$ and $g(t)$ only" :db/id 17592186562941} {:answer/id #uuid "1662f69d-0d6b-5863-8f09-5d9d05419260" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi )$" :db/id 17592186562992} {:answer/id #uuid "5fdede5d-fa26-5289-a238-94143dcae14e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$f(t)$ and $h(t)$ only" :db/id 17592186563165} {:answer/id #uuid "9706168f-6882-59ce-be20-eefcba9f53d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$g(t)$ and $h(t)$ only" :db/id 17592186563284} {:answer/id #uuid "dab073b4-14ff-58ad-bfaa-7282357cb131" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi )$" :db/id 17592186563424}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186562992} :answer-field/id #uuid "24c4782e-d988-5b6a-b328-68cc3dd0adb4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d69b9419-ecda-5adb-b076-9a4d08de1698" :question/math-academy-id "q-32701" :question/problem "Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨{\sin }^{2}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨t\sqrt{t},\,1-{t}^{2},\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi ).$ 

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi ,2\pi )$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval. 

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\sin }^{2}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$ to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we have that $g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,2,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${h}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $h(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is: 

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi ).$"} {:db/id 17592186563746 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05ed7714-762b-563c-aa6e-395fc6bb299a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186562950} {:answer/id #uuid "12226c0d-85bd-508b-82d8-13bf97d8f83b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186562981} {:answer/id #uuid "3bd14c1c-2112-52ab-bcdc-5d7b174123b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=-\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186563079} {:answer/id #uuid "55af48ee-55a1-5c40-847d-5742b568cea0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186563140} {:answer/id #uuid "f8844c5c-08d4-51a1-8c11-9ac8c49c3885" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x=\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186563501}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186562950} :answer-field/id #uuid "707a53ec-3f89-531c-a47b-914f51a9c97c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563571}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "da0e0865-56b2-565d-ac33-deaee1268cf4" :question/math-academy-id "q-84903" :question/problem "Find the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=(7-5x)(x+1).$" :question/worked-solution "From the equation $y=(7-5x)(x+1),$ we find that the roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=\frac{7}{5}$ and ${x}_{2}=-1.$ 

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7}{5}-1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7}{5}-\frac{5}{5})}{2} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{1}{5}.$"} {:db/id 17592186563760 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c8383c9-5a00-5106-8ade-ebcb1afc1644" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186562966} {:answer/id #uuid "2ea52a0e-e6a5-522f-8a2f-e28cb7fa9518" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186563050} {:answer/id #uuid "48b88652-e6ed-5cdf-94e0-9c52630df3e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186563105} {:answer/id #uuid "68b0f87b-d56a-5e56-bcb2-6c135e0e44a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186563187} {:answer/id #uuid "804a3d7f-93d1-5460-9e8a-4cea93ac58d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186563227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563050} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f6b8a55-8b0f-5157-98ff-b7ec894bdaee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563567}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f7872fd6-9c54-5e48-b08b-71d8ca0a2063" :question/math-academy-id "q-83552" :question/problem "Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186563763 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "57ea209f-e155-526a-94ca-0d966c493e42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i+\frac{1}{4}\,j" :db/id 17592186563141} {:answer/id #uuid "96c6d7cb-49e7-5e45-b566-508c8a442dec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4\,i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186563281} {:answer/id #uuid "9f5e6c1e-a123-5805-9a48-ff55d4732a4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j" :db/id 17592186563304} {:answer/id #uuid "b3791795-25ea-52db-9a06-ea2ad48e2ced" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j" :db/id 17592186563341} {:answer/id #uuid "d18ea431-dd2b-59ac-94dc-2a47eca46a91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j" :db/id 17592186563406}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563281} :answer-field/id #uuid "fe69802c-24d6-5c9a-b43c-e07a25e5de2d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563641}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ffacb628-f280-51e0-9811-c0f525cc08ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-83591" :question/problem "In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4})?$" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡y+4x-\frac{1}{x})i-x{\sec }^{2}⁡y\text{ }j \\ -∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+4\cdot 1-\frac{1}{1})i-1\cdot {\sec }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $-4\,i-2\,j.$"} {:db/id 17592186563824 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e1edb3c-53e2-59fb-8b25-bd49ec07d7ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9 r^{3} (3 \sin^{2}{(\theta )} - 2)" :db/id 17592186563818} {:answer/id #uuid "179e0ce9-20d2-5083-94bb-403ba2113db7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 9 r^{3} \sin^{2}{(\theta )}" :db/id 17592186563820} {:answer/id #uuid "367d7cc1-3324-54fc-9fb9-97d117004d5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9 r^{2} (\sin^{2}{(\theta )} - 2)" :db/id 17592186563830} {:answer/id #uuid "802b78f8-6827-5cd8-9458-b108ba1aa055" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 18 r^{3} \cos^{2}{(\theta )}" :db/id 17592186563842} {:answer/id #uuid "e66f5319-c723-5e2c-94aa-56c9c8ccafda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9 r^{3} (\sin^{2}{(\theta )} - 2)" :db/id 17592186563856}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563856} :answer-field/id #uuid "ba192ad9-824f-5b2a-9948-ce270cf9499b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "21cd5573-a0e4-5bef-86ec-1c6e167cab52" :question/problem "Given that $$
\displaystyle {∮}_C F\cdot dr=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{6}\boxed{}\,dr\,d\theta,
$$ where $F(x,y)=⟨3{y}^{3}+{e}^{x},\,\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-6{x}^{3}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=36$ oriented counterclockwise, what expression belongs in the blank after applying Green’s theorem and changing to polar coordinates, simplified pointwise before integration?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(3{y}^{3}+{e}^{x})\,dx+(\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-6{x}^{3})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/47/47ee81cb3603c75c8a83dca2df1153733902576892fa6eed3df4bccd329655ee.png)

Since $P(x,y)=3{y}^{3}+{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-6{x}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=9{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-18{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(3{y}^{3}+{e}^{x})\,dx+(\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}+10}-6{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\ & ={∬}_{D}(-18{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,drd\theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-18{x}^{2}-9{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-18\cdot (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-9\cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}(-18{r}^{2}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -9{r}^{2}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={∬}_{Δ}(-18{r}^{3}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -9{r}^{3}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta \\ & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}-18{r}^{3}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -9{r}^{3}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186563828 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25ec3af8-1efb-5bac-9653-b4bbeb227b26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3 r^{3} (\cos^{2}{(\theta )} - 3)" :db/id 17592186563825} {:answer/id #uuid "4ef44ce3-1fed-5c9e-bfcd-9fa6a3cf53c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 6 r^{3} \cos^{2}{(\theta )}" :db/id 17592186563836} {:answer/id #uuid "618036f5-1521-5d86-bd10-2233ad57f06b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3 r^{2} (\cos^{2}{(\theta )} - 3)" :db/id 17592186563838} {:answer/id #uuid "90d63d22-f3b5-5dc8-bace-ac4440bf2edb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3 r^{3} (5 \sin^{2}{(\theta )} - 2)" :db/id 17592186563843} {:answer/id #uuid "9dfc6627-6984-5941-a167-46191993853d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "- 9 r^{3} \sin^{2}{(\theta )}" :db/id 17592186563847}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563825} :answer-field/id #uuid "9dbf35a0-0cac-5fb0-af95-6fe98a827932" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563846}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2ec57f20-b633-5781-9a09-b50d332a0f91" :question/problem "Given that $$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨3,7⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,7)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨3,7⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ ({7}^{2}-{3}^{2})-({1}^{2}-{0}^{2}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-2x,2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}39 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =⟨-2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,6⟩ \\ 39 & =-6{c}_{1}+12{c}_{2} \\ 13 & =-2{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{7-1} & =\frac{x-0}{3-0} \\ \frac{y-1}{6} & =\frac{x}{3} \\ y-1 & =2x \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $-2{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}=13,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+4(2{c}_{1}+1) & =13 \\ -2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{1}+4 & =13 \\ 6{c}_{1} & =9 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=2{c}_{1}+1=4.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{3}{2},4).$"} {:db/id 17592186564506 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "12262de4-ff35-5b6d-902b-cc063519daf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186563994} {:answer/id #uuid "26e486e8-edca-5347-8954-f90b314bfea9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186564026} {:answer/id #uuid "3108d9ea-bf52-50bb-b021-c32e5e1cac89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186564052} {:answer/id #uuid "9a4848d1-6bdb-54f4-845a-a67e55c75c3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186564207} {:answer/id #uuid "f422fa0c-c176-5bb8-b7d5-4e0f06f500ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186564363}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564207} :answer-field/id #uuid "1df7676f-854b-544e-891a-356915ca7afe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186564383}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "90239ba3-7e56-5134-995c-b697d9dca4dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-37587" :question/problem "The function 
$f(x,y)$
has the second derivative

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y & \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y & -\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{bmatrix}
$$

and has a stationary point at $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$ If $H$ denotes the Hessian determinant of $f,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $H(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})<0$

II. $$
\displaystyle \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})>0
$$

III. The point $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ is a local maximum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

Evaluating the second derivative at $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we obtain   

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the determinant of ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get

$$
H(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})=\det ({f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}))=(-1)^{2}-{0}^{2}=1>0.
$$

- Statement II is false. We have $$
\displaystyle \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})={({f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}))}_{11}=-1<0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $H(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})>0$ and $$
\displaystyle \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})<0,
$$ the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ is a local maximum by the second partial derivative test.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186564511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ca77a3e-9085-58ef-87e4-a39c3ee58fbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186564188} {:answer/id #uuid "a69cfe99-5dda-5c7f-a8ae-e9e88f862d43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186564223} {:answer/id #uuid "c4a63f4b-3cca-51c6-b369-5d4f828546a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186564272} {:answer/id #uuid "dbef1e38-02bf-5cd7-beba-116a24ac4bd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186564317} {:answer/id #uuid "e866b3d9-12d2-51c5-a482-af43a7c89490" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186564336}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564223} :answer-field/id #uuid "893376bc-f857-5c82-9b7f-472d1ddbccda" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186564418}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9c34765f-7311-53ab-be9b-191b42487450" :question/math-academy-id "q-158585" :question/problem "Evaluate $z={2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}$ at the point $(2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(2,2),$ we substitute $x=2$ and $y=2$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{|}_{(2,2)} & =({2}^{-x}+\frac{1}{y}){|}_{(2,2)} \\  & ={2}^{-2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186564515 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ce47d28-eaa1-546c-8183-2127b628176c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨{e}^{2},0,2⟩\cdot ⟨x+\frac{\pi }{4},\,y+4,\,z+1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186564042} {:answer/id #uuid "364d2199-0b35-5058-91d2-00830dfeac8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2{e}^{4},0,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{4},\,y-4,\,z-1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186564058} {:answer/id #uuid "424acf8b-08ac-5611-8aa3-de65c4fec28f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2e,0,4⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{4},\,y-4,\,z-1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186564080} {:answer/id #uuid "bb62c03c-bf38-5191-8248-65e025952de8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-{e}^{4},1,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{4},\,y-4,\,z-1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186564256} {:answer/id #uuid "d9cbbaea-b40c-59ab-894a-2ac16a7ce025" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨{e}^{4},-2,2⟩\cdot ⟨x+\frac{\pi }{4},\,y+4,\,z+1⟩=0" :db/id 17592186564313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564058} :answer-field/id #uuid "6cd0d23f-0d58-5865-9c0a-7562b441a711" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186564408}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a6978155-572b-505c-b00f-8a94900d562b" :question/math-academy-id "q-102702" :question/problem "Given the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{z}^{2}$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes  through the point where $(x,y,z)=(\frac{\pi }{4},4,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z)=k$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be expressed as

$$
∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩=0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})=(\frac{\pi }{4},4,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =-2{e}^{y}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\text{ }i+{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\text{ }j+2zk \\ ∇\,f(\frac{\pi }{4},4,1) & =-2{e}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\text{ }i+{e}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\text{ }j+2(1)k \\  & =-2{e}^{4}\,i+0\,j+2k \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{4},0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0},\,z-{z}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(\frac{\pi }{4},4,1)\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{4},\,y-4,\,z-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨-2{e}^{4},0,2⟩\cdot ⟨x-\frac{\pi }{4},\,y-4,\,z-1⟩ & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186564537 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00b86450-d396-50c2-b792-96eb2e069dee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-w,-z)" :db/id 17592186563969} {:answer/id #uuid "1707b2e5-7f13-581b-928d-cb954858885d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2w,2z)" :db/id 17592186563999} {:answer/id #uuid "2295ae60-1e26-5128-8f27-466b06ffd6c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2w,3z)" :db/id 17592186564018} {:answer/id #uuid "2c117928-80a8-595c-9b86-d8c72d7f0afb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2w,-2z)" :db/id 17592186564039} {:answer/id #uuid "c0661565-ff3d-5e5e-b035-22e247858f0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-w,2z)" :db/id 17592186564264}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563999} :answer-field/id #uuid "87c637ca-477b-51e8-ad73-42e7989eff3f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186564417}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f548e29c-4fb0-5de0-8aa0-2659faa5a2eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-73720" :question/problem "Find the midpoint of the line segment with endpoints $(-w,7z)$ and $(5w,-3z).$" :question/worked-solution "Let $({x}_{m},{y}_{m})$ be the midpoint between $\underbrace{(-w,7z)}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{,}\,{y}_{1})}$ and $\underbrace{(5w,-3z)}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{,}\,{y}_{2})}.$

We use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{m},{y}_{m}) & =(\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2},\frac{{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{-w+5w}{2},\frac{7z+(-3z)}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{-w+5w}{2},\frac{7z-3z}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{4w}{2},\frac{4z}{2}) \\  & =(2w,2z).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "03557524-3809-52d4-9d68-9faf937bdb58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564600} {:db/id 17592186564601 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03557524-3809-52d4-9d68-9faf937bdb58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564600} {:answer/id #uuid "224f63a5-963c-5451-b6e8-7fba150db1a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564602} {:answer/id #uuid "343fd6ee-2f12-525f-b827-6036ba3e52e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186564609} {:answer/id #uuid "9c8cec09-fbba-518e-ad05-89fcd612bc74" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564626} {:answer/id #uuid "d98c2129-2808-5ee4-8422-3f6a6eeb389d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564646}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564600} :answer-field/id #uuid "d22be944-ac35-5b9d-84ab-bd2397fe1885" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186564642}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "09e5259b-47e9-5e22-b6a8-c7e9106ef293" :question/problem "Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${120}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$" :question/worked-solution "We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$"} {:answer/id #uuid "224f63a5-963c-5451-b6e8-7fba150db1a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186564602} {:answer/id #uuid "2442c3e4-6efc-5e15-89f6-7d2d57190032" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{15}{2})" :db/id 17592186564604} {:db/id 17592186564606 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29381743-bc0a-58b7-b7c6-16932dd9f9e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186564607}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564607} :answer-field/id #uuid "66f7196b-f145-51aa-93ef-8dcbc705481c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186564616} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "248e1098-29d9-543b-83d4-0b32e84165eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186564605}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186564605} :answer-field/id #uuid "d519eb60-a305-58da-aa54-032b41b18629" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186564643}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "26aee229-9b71-5508-be41-0115539b71ac" :question/problem "If the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $1,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${210}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$

{{field-2}}$).$" :question/worked-solution "We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=1,\,\theta ={315}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡({315}^{∘}) \\  & =1\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $-3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{-3}{{x}^{8}} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }[-3\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{8}}] \\  & =-3\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}\right)=0,
$$

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

$$
-3\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{8}}=-3\cdot 0=0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186565434 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "162b92da-df23-5c30-ad49-2fd32f33a03e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186564972} {:answer/id #uuid "295bfcf1-2a63-541e-8767-7a6693f4baa2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3}{4},\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186565006} {:answer/id #uuid "724aaf30-aac6-5e20-acb1-5fa47f134fe4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1)" :db/id 17592186565113} {:answer/id #uuid "8053c7ab-909b-5f33-9ce9-0d798cb23006" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},2)" :db/id 17592186565136} {:answer/id #uuid "ebb4def9-72b8-5730-ab1a-af5ca0f9d64a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},1)" :db/id 17592186565289}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565136} :answer-field/id #uuid "59557dca-7f7b-53f1-95d6-4b59fe6e4251" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186565351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5c3d7252-78a8-50a4-b514-2643c3b47ad3" :question/math-academy-id "q-106075" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,3)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,3⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ ({1}^{2}+3)-({0}^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =2{c}_{1}+2 \\ 1 & =2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{3-1} & =\frac{x-0}{1-0} \\ \frac{y-1}{2} & =x \\ y & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{1}{2},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1=2.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{2},2).$"} {:db/id 17592186565448 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c9f894b-0695-5fb5-a2fc-03e32b1ccede" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)" :db/id 17592186565009} {:answer/id #uuid "61321b40-2ea0-5afa-9cb1-4cc94c8b9dae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)" :db/id 17592186565088} {:answer/id #uuid "9c669607-1843-5584-8f41-4389bb11e66b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)" :db/id 17592186565176} {:answer/id #uuid "b380e63b-0a3b-5d84-8474-0490488b54a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)" :db/id 17592186565206} {:answer/id #uuid "eec60117-16db-52c1-b4e7-87394fffcc2e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)" :db/id 17592186565298}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565088} :answer-field/id #uuid "2235b94a-23b2-515a-9cb2-13dc47980c69" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186565336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9876167b-d3d3-5f4c-9305-b455d21b66dc" :question/math-academy-id "q-342816" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-3y={u}_{\pi /4}(t)\cdot \cos \,(4t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=1,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /4}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$
Y(s)=\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{s\,{e}^{-\pi s/4}}{({s}^{2}+16)(s-3)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t)={e}^{3t}+\frac{1}{25}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot g(t).
$$

Find the function $g(t).$ 

Hint: You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the initial value problem, we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s).$

To find the inverse transform, we first ignore the exponential term ${e}^{-\pi s/4}$ (which corresponds to a time shift) and focus on the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+16)(s-3)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s-3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+16),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+16)(s-3)}=\frac{A}{s-3}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+16}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s=A({s}^{2}+16)+(Bs+C)(s-3).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=3,$ we have

$$
3=A({3}^{2}+16)+0\,⟹\,25A=3\,⟹\,A=\frac{3}{25}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=-\frac{3}{25}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
0=16A-3C\,⟹\,0=16\,\left(\frac{3}{25}\right)-3C\,⟹\,C=\frac{16}{25}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{25}(\frac{3}{s-3}-3\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16}+4\cdot \frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{25}(3\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\}-3\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16}\}+4\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{4}{{s}^{2}+16}\}) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}(3{e}^{3t}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/4}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \frac{1}{25}[3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4}))+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\cos \,(4\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4}))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$ and $\sin \,(4\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4}))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot \frac{1}{25}(3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{25}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})(3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $$
\displaystyle y(t)={e}^{3t}+\frac{1}{25}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot g(t),
$$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=3{e}^{3(t-\pi /4)}+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186565466 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "072c003f-940f-5827-9c69-c6534a1061e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186564952} {:answer/id #uuid "25a59e37-3156-5f96-a6d3-a085278a86ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186564997} {:answer/id #uuid "638d7ca2-b9ee-56e3-ad94-7e22ab34a1e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186565092} {:answer/id #uuid "ac923911-04d7-59bb-9992-7a8446c5e934" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186565194} {:answer/id #uuid "c5a09306-4232-5e19-a749-d592df6f358b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)" :db/id 17592186565236}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565092} :answer-field/id #uuid "0d53ce85-93a3-5040-89c6-3357d95d5db8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186565332}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d1348d32-c72c-5639-a597-5810a3541a7f" :question/math-academy-id "q-342800" :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+2y={u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot \cos \,(3t-\pi )\,,\,y(0)=-1,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /3}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})$ is the unit step function.

You're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$
Y(s)=-\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{s\,{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{({s}^{2}+9)(s+2)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t)=-{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{13}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot g(t).
$$

Find the function $g(t).$ 

Hint: You may make use of the following results:

$$
L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

We focus on the term with the exponential ${e}^{-\pi s/3}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:

$$
F(s)=\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+9)(s+2)}.
$$

We'll solve this in three steps.

**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition

Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+2)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $({s}^{2}+9),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\frac{s}{({s}^{2}+9)(s+2)}=\frac{A}{s+2}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+9}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s=A({s}^{2}+9)+(Bs+C)(s+2).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A,B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-2,$ we have

$$
-2=A((-2)^{2}+9)+0\,⟹\,13A=-2\,⟹\,A=-\frac{2}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of ${s}^{2},$ we have

$$
0=A+B\,⟹\,B=-A=\frac{2}{13}.
$$

- Comparing the constant terms, we have

$$
0=9A+2C\,⟹\,0=9\,\left(-\frac{2}{13}\right)+2C\,⟹\,C=\frac{9}{13}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{13}(-\frac{2}{s+2}+\frac{2s+9}{{s}^{2}+9})=\frac{1}{13}(-2\cdot \frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}+3\cdot \frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9}).
$$

**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function

We find the inverse transform $f(t)={L}^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{1}{13}(-2\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+2}\}+2\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}\}+3\cdot {L}^{-1}\{\frac{3}{{s}^{2}+9}\}) \\  & =\frac{1}{13}(-2{e}^{-2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property

Finally, we address the ${e}^{-\pi s/3}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
{e}^{-as}\cdot F(s)=L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a)\}.
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform gives

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}=u(t-a)\cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\frac{\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})f\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \frac{1}{13}[-2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3}))+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3}))].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(t-\pi /3))=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(t-\pi /3))=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot \frac{1}{13}(-2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{13}\,u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})(2{e}^{-(t-\pi /2)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $$
\displaystyle y(t)=-{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{13}u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot g(t),
$$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=2{e}^{-2(t-\pi /3)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186565467 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f716f286-0901-500a-b1e6-20a7dee63999" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3+4e" :db/id 17592186565313}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565313} :answer-field/id #uuid "89f12e8d-bf93-5637-a264-6851084e5f96" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186565364}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d2ff517e-a169-5a1c-9487-46b4246b351b" :question/math-academy-id "q-340023" :question/problem "Given the function $y=-3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+4{e}^{x},$ the slope of the tangent line at $x=1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0ea54cb1-a0d4-5539-a164-15702dc537d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-105795" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (F-3G)$ at the point $(1,0,9)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=(2\sqrt{z}+x)\,i+xy\,j+{y}^{2}\,k,\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}y\,k.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-3G) & =∇\times F+∇\times (-3G) \\  & =∇\times F-3∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 2\sqrt{z}+x & xy & {y}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\sqrt{z}+x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{z}+x)]k \\  & =(2y-0)i-(0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}})j+(y-0)k \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-3G) & =∇\times F-3∇\times G \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k-3[3{x}^{2}y\,k] \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k-9{x}^{2}y\,k \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y(1-9{x}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(1,0,9),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-3G))(1,0,9) & =2(0)\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}}\,j+0(1-9(1)^{2})\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186566214 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ccaddae-969a-5bb6-97a9-8d0e0b772e0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,\frac{3}{2})\cup (\frac{3}{2},\infty )" :db/id 17592186565699} {:answer/id #uuid "1a94b6e6-c74e-520f-ae8d-73a46e554999" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,\frac{1}{2})\cup (\frac{1}{2},\infty )" :db/id 17592186565724} {:answer/id #uuid "509c8237-e2bb-5759-8728-da4096bca8f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,4)\cup (4,\infty )" :db/id 17592186565806} {:answer/id #uuid "98712a50-8a01-56bf-b370-98559bfe5794" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,-2)\cup (-2,\infty )" :db/id 17592186565921} {:answer/id #uuid "b6071168-7def-5769-b7ee-41381140092c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\infty ,-\frac{3}{2})\cup (-\frac{3}{2},\infty )" :db/id 17592186565975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565724} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1cc2dc1-18fb-52fa-8e67-8e8e0b36e205" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566183}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "29510dc5-be54-5010-a9b8-7e994b64e473" :question/math-academy-id "q-40012" :question/problem "What is the domain of the function $f(x)=-\frac{3}{4x-2}?$" :question/worked-solution "A reciprocal function is defined for all values of $x$ except for those that make the denominator zero. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values of $x$ that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-2 & =0 \\ 4x & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{4} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is $$
\displaystyle x\in (-\infty ,\frac{1}{2})\cup (\frac{1}{2},\infty ).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186566221 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8553596b-4bed-5f28-bf3d-359109448203" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,0,\frac{2}{e}⟩" :db/id 17592186565887} {:answer/id #uuid "c876445d-364d-54c2-a964-eda7f78c0d80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨0,2e,1⟩" :db/id 17592186566002} {:answer/id #uuid "cb2b2a5b-e478-5762-9565-7d86b996e74f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{e},0,2e⟩" :db/id 17592186566007} {:answer/id #uuid "e39f0bf0-41ab-5680-8a0a-a65746d7ad80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{1}{e},0,\frac{2}{e}⟩" :db/id 17592186566048} {:answer/id #uuid "ef621264-33c3-594b-bcb1-888fe58a6145" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2e,1,0⟩" :db/id 17592186566071}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565887} :answer-field/id #uuid "7200c5c6-834c-582d-bb4f-488640d68497" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566150}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "38f95650-79fd-557c-9c72-45e47bd9ea35" :question/math-academy-id "q-131475" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x{e}^{y},yz,0⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{-y}.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨-y,0,-x{e}^{y}⟩,\,∇f=⟨{e}^{-y},-x{e}^{-y},0⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,1,2).$" :question/worked-solution "We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ {e}^{-y} & -x{e}^{-y} & 0 \\ x{e}^{y} & yz & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[(-x{e}^{-y})(0)-(yz)(0)]i-[({e}^{-y})(0)-(x{e}^{y})(0)]j+[({e}^{-y})(yz)-(x{e}^{y})(-x{e}^{-y})]k \\  & =0\,i+0j+(yz{e}^{-y}+{x}^{2})k \\  & =⟨0,0,yz{e}^{-y}+{x}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =(x{e}^{-y})⟨-y,0,-x{e}^{y}⟩+⟨0,0,yz{e}^{-y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-xy{e}^{-y},0,-{x}^{2}⟩+⟨0,0,yz{e}^{-y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-xy{e}^{-y},0,yz{e}^{-y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
∇\times (f\,F)(0,1,2)=⟨0,0,\frac{2}{e}⟩.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186566224 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "504fe88b-8989-50fd-9bf6-4fb3a0874f14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-j+k" :db/id 17592186565805} {:answer/id #uuid "65367f18-ef71-5d52-84f0-4d352c7adcb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5\,i+5\,j" :db/id 17592186565836} {:answer/id #uuid "953d0060-629d-5930-8b1a-dc079696c8e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186565919} {:answer/id #uuid "cb311272-e389-523f-83ba-df596e274f53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\,i-j+5\,k" :db/id 17592186566008} {:answer/id #uuid "de460cf2-dd72-57b6-89cf-2648f5feed59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-k" :db/id 17592186566039}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565836} :answer-field/id #uuid "743b8050-afb0-5239-be1f-b571663c2f9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566151}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3c0d5e56-2169-54d3-9966-1a109d2d5523" :question/math-academy-id "q-105796" :question/problem "Calculate $∇\times (F+G)$ at the point $(0,-1,1)$ for the vector fields $F$ and $G,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+3z\,j-2y\,\text{k},\,(∇\times G)(x,y,z)=(6z-1)\,j.
$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & 3z & -2y\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(3z)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(3z)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)]k \\  & =(-2-3)i-(0-0)j+(0-0)k \\  & =-5\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F+G) & =∇\times F+∇\times G \\  & =-5\,i+(6z-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(0,-1,1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F+G))(0,-1,1) & =-5\,i+(6(1)-1)\,j \\  & =-5\,i+5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186566227 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e2a5228-4d34-5c57-8a6c-a3feb27ed440" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{4}-{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565702} {:answer/id #uuid "2e001848-6114-55d4-898d-e807366debec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "60-{(y-18)}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565748} {:answer/id #uuid "4803ab05-0b65-5cb4-92e9-f03eef1b730f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}-{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565792} {:answer/id #uuid "4e4aefa9-79b2-5f3f-9f24-fa82ea18cebc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{165}{4}-{(y+\frac{9}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565800} {:answer/id #uuid "564dbae7-bea0-5bb4-b219-b6f52f82ad54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}+{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565816}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565702} :answer-field/id #uuid "416ac210-0c5c-5b57-b96d-e01801ddf600" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566132}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "52455c8c-f427-542e-9cf2-e8b407fdf74f" :question/math-academy-id "q-140407" :question/problem "Rewrite $-{y}^{2}+9y-21$ by completing the square." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1$. So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-({y}^{2}-9y+21)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{y}^{2}-9y+21
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{9}{2}y+21
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}^{2}$, writing the constant term $21$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{9}{2}y+{\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}^{2}}-{\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}^{2}+21
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)}^{2}+21
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{2}+9y-21 & =-({(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}-{(y-\frac{9}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}

{{field-3}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $10$. So, we take out a factor of $10$ from the entire expression:

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$

$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{10}x+\frac{7}{100}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{2}$, writing the constant term $\frac{7}{100}$ last:

$$
\underbrace{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{10}x+{\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{2}}-\,{\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{2}+\frac{7}{100}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+\frac{1}{10})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)}^{2}+\frac{7}{100}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x+\frac{1}{10})}^{2}+\frac{3}{50}.

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k.$ Then, since we know that the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{1}{4},$ we will set our result equal to $\frac{1}{4}.$ 

From the equation $y=(2x+k)(x-3k),$ we find that the roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{k}{2}$ and ${x}_{2}=3k.$ 

To find the axis of symmetry, we take the average of the roots, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{k}{2}+3k)}{2} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{6k-k}{2}\right)}{2} \\  & =\frac{5k}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We know that the axis of symmetry is $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5k}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 5k & =1 \\ k & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186566273 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d9be715-36a9-5f87-aaff-b73f3c392482" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565726} {:answer/id #uuid "64fb7564-0e54-5edc-bf06-22fc601176e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565835} {:answer/id #uuid "7625faaf-7a06-5f8d-9f7a-5f31afa9fee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565862} {:answer/id #uuid "82e0bdf4-a937-5979-9022-49f3096a8334" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186565884} {:answer/id #uuid "d5496e58-5442-54c8-8ae7-8fd4a6dda1d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186566022}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565884} :answer-field/id #uuid "bb17ec4b-63ee-5206-af27-3498015a3fd6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566177}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f7c6f3ba-6533-5a1f-b464-492440ca8f6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-163179" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=y,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Given that the center of mass is at $(1,2),$ find the moment of inertia about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =x{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(x-1)^{2}y+{y}^{3}-4{y}^{2}+4y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}(x-1)^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{9}{2}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{9}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}(x-1)^{3}+\frac{9}{4}x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{9}{2}-(-\frac{3}{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{15}{2}+{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}\cdot 9 \\  & =\frac{15}{2}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186567046 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "37dd99bc-3607-581f-978c-a71b67914c2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[5]{{x}^{9}}-2{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{3{x}^{3}}+C" :db/id 17592186566477} {:answer/id #uuid "9126a86d-bcfd-5fec-9571-5503eba42ee5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{9}}}{9}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{2}{3{x}^{3}}+C" :db/id 17592186566648} {:answer/id #uuid "a5d265ad-a1a6-58b0-b6d6-e96a59278366" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{9}}}-\frac{2}{x}-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}+C" :db/id 17592186566688} {:answer/id #uuid "dafdca6c-9141-5612-9f79-f5c98e819afc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\sqrt[5]{{x}^{4}}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{6}{{x}^{4}}+C" :db/id 17592186566803} {:answer/id #uuid "f64dcd14-9eac-5db3-bba6-758aa5bc23bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{4}}}{4}-\frac{1}{2x}-\frac{2}{3{x}^{6}}+C" :db/id 17592186566857}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566648} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1056adf-eded-5bde-8128-44705a2baad4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566981}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "676d4494-4f46-573f-a890-2a8daa607201" :question/math-academy-id "q-113850" :question/problem "Find the antiderivative of 
$\sqrt[5]{{x}^{4}}-x+\frac{2}{{x}^{4}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$

First, we use the constant multiple rule and the product rule:

$$"} {:db/id 17592186567052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1df86f71-4e8c-5223-a2c3-114b3c3a90ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186566425} {:answer/id #uuid "23ed9481-6f88-5b6b-806c-7902c0dee17a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{4}" :db/id 17592186566439} {:answer/id #uuid "755654b4-0e0c-54a7-a879-4314f25dc630" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186566584} {:answer/id #uuid "79a314e6-0668-5c44-b3d1-02a3cf9ad5c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186566595} {:answer/id #uuid "7b9ccd66-db58-59f7-af47-1c86f73f9c4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186566599}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566439} :answer-field/id #uuid "789cacb9-1990-5456-9318-5cf3591eaa13" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566934}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "738ade6c-0972-56b4-b1bb-9f8fdeb237e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-159661" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants.

$$

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y))+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (0+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$ 

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186567061 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e78b876-2391-5925-9f6b-e1686b55096a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186566489}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566489} :answer-field/id #uuid "5961090d-3a51-57b9-a935-949cdac567c9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186566916}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8ea911ef-18d1-54db-a83b-3b4bb372d13e" :question/math-academy-id "q-353117" :question/problem "![](images/ee/eec15c94d63cab750a0dc15525d800452a1a1dbdd3e948dff8ef8d6cf0e2abc7.png)

Find the area $A$ of the shaded region that lies between the polar curves $r=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us two solutions for $\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ]:$

$$
\theta =-\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{3}
$$

To determine which is the inner function and which is the outer, let's draw an arrow from the origin that passes through the shaded region.

![](images/9b/9bcc7175d07a6d9bb4c3fa202f3ad711effa962e3c9a798b3869f9601d4214c3.png)

The arrow

- *enters* the region through the inner function $r=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

To find the area, we use the formula

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where

$\,$ ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3},\,$ and $\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}((\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-\frac{\pi }{3})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{3}\right)+\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{3})-(-\sqrt{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\sqrt{3}-\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186567065 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ddab15d-a213-59cd-9fa7-21cc781db0f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186566391} {:answer/id #uuid "6e681722-68eb-5e1b-be66-9761b2526ae5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186566570} {:answer/id #uuid "6f68471e-bf27-5ded-b086-2a567f880f0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4+\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186566574} {:answer/id #uuid "84309097-603c-5779-9ab8-18a0c7d5d182" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2-\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186566614} {:answer/id #uuid "fe5c2371-01f6-548a-ab82-c607c80df138" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4+\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186566873}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566391} :answer-field/id #uuid "9bb14c76-0569-5f28-a8c5-d938b0472df9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566951}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9e654085-a432-5396-af7c-98196ef1aed1" :question/math-academy-id "q-126408" :question/problem "![](images/ea/ea8b9532d6b2b9318f77155a585d46dd18cb168c455318bd5abe72c4a11a4500.png)

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Consider the rightmost petal, oriented along the $x$-axis. First, we find the values of $\theta $ for which the two curves intersect:

Using the chain rule, we have

$$

$$

Then, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$

Therefore, 

$$

\displaystyle \int \frac{{x}^{5}+7}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{5}+7}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{3}+\frac{7}{{x}^{2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+\int 7{x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+7\int {x}^{-2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\left(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\right)+7\left(\frac{{x}^{-1}}{-1}\right)+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{7}{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186567093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "253445fe-fff1-58b7-9019-3e38491dac58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186566442} {:answer/id #uuid "2ddd0cfc-1ccf-5d4e-857f-c5a638f03f52" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186566455} {:answer/id #uuid "72a3ae63-0575-5426-a7c0-15120c576ff4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186566577} {:answer/id #uuid "87430684-ea2a-5175-8c38-072537596c8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186566619} {:answer/id #uuid "a5a6a36f-25e4-5d5d-aa20-c816606c275d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186566686}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566686} :answer-field/id #uuid "2e6bb6c0-dbeb-5577-8434-7c53a76a2f69" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186566896}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dfe77a47-89cf-58c9-a7e4-db0e7d6a133d" :question/math-academy-id "q-159662" :question/problem "For the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}).$" :question/worked-solution "We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differenciation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (2x+{y}^{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186567105 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "064a104c-4e51-5489-b7b3-01bd2228b1ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "27" :db/id 17592186566373} {:answer/id #uuid "1d642645-7c2a-5ab7-8f58-4f03edba3213" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186566423} {:answer/id #uuid "457523d5-a938-5ee1-a080-7acf69cac9c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36" :db/id 17592186566500} {:answer/id #uuid "6077bd80-b2f2-516a-9522-53d1d4881f71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186566547} {:answer/id #uuid "7b153448-8d81-5ab9-b5f8-58997bf3f8b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186566597}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186566547} :answer-field/id #uuid "fd4f35ba-dc99-55f4-89c9-fd9fa4a3c49f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186567004}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f1c4174f-ebe1-5065-81d1-0761f7cc8648" :question/math-academy-id "q-72907" :question/problem "Let $R=[0,6]\times [1,2]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
{x}_{i-1}-{y}_{j}\le \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le {x}_{i}-{y}_{j-1}
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & \le \frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} \\  & \le U(f,P).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 18-9\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 9\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}

Therefore, we conclude that
