\displaystyle {∬}_{D}x(1-y)\,dA,
$$ where $$
\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,y\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region $$
\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,y\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x(1-y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{\int }_{y}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}x(1-y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{\int }_{y}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}x(1-y)\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y)[{\int }_{y}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}x\,dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y){[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{y}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y)(\frac{1-{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y)(1-2{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y-2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}(1-y-2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\,dy & =\frac{1}{2}{[y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}+\frac{1}{8}-0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}-\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186583651 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26d1bdb4-7677-576f-8e12-6038e97b1b18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186583228} {:answer/id #uuid "54ef80e4-7f0c-50ea-b1d1-ed134df4a7af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186583287} {:answer/id #uuid "70fe9066-ed8a-5267-8790-abb20006433f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡4" :db/id 17592186583319} {:answer/id #uuid "96d57427-0466-5cca-8d01-f1f3a359e07f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2+\operatorname{ln}⁡4" :db/id 17592186583369} {:answer/id #uuid "b76b8451-9003-5203-8ea2-df548a2ea327" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2" :db/id 17592186583408}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186583287} :answer-field/id #uuid "1d8d6007-e26e-5fb7-89c7-1c3502618418" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186583512}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e7debd15-2d28-5242-b13a-9ade99910127" :question/math-academy-id "q-81775" :question/problem "Calculate $$

where $$

\displaystyle D=\{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{1}{4}\le x\le \frac{1}{2},\,x\le y\le 1-x\}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{x}\,dA & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}{\int }_{x}^{1-x}\frac{2y}{x}\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}{\int }_{x}^{1-x}\frac{2y}{x}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{x}^{1-x}2y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{1}{x}[{y}^{2}]_{x}^{1-x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{1}{x}((1-x)^{2}-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{1}{x}(1-2x)dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}(\frac{1}{x}-2)dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}(\frac{1}{x}-2)dx & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2x]_{1/4}^{1/2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-1-(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186584334 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "48599e91-2523-5ec1-b3c3-fe8c7aebb792" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/id 17592186583887} {:answer/id #uuid "6570f0f0-bc07-596b-8b85-a399ac2106f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)" :db/id 17592186583933} {:answer/id #uuid "73e2b769-4990-5a1b-9c7c-984f53990423" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{3}" :db/id 17592186583967} {:answer/id #uuid "87556450-3ec8-5770-b547-7c519b42b64a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}" :db/id 17592186584002} {:answer/id #uuid "aa8954ca-3bd2-5b0f-93f9-b31de7e328e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The integral diverges" :db/id 17592186584064}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584002} :answer-field/id #uuid "370fbc0d-e96a-5247-af7f-334a46e2961e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584252}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0d300418-0c26-5a33-9c02-5a619acbc02c" :question/math-academy-id "q-152234" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the following result:

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$"} {:db/id 17592186584339 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0230aa11-bd80-5d8e-9db1-38b9d3749d67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The integral diverges" :db/id 17592186583776} {:answer/id #uuid "284b43b1-666e-5e44-8fb1-29b52c0adbad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186583842} {:answer/id #uuid "76192bac-a30a-575e-bf2f-d92a8d3ad64a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{-1}" :db/id 17592186583970} {:answer/id #uuid "a2ed8220-8ca8-5f0f-a7f4-51d0f25580f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e" :db/id 17592186584043} {:answer/id #uuid "a87e429f-d6e3-5233-9004-82e1d166d247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186584058}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186583970} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4d94635-cba4-5c31-8e43-d676667fb98d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584314}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1c9a9fee-618c-5e7e-ac98-7a9bc0a025a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-6296" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the following result:

$$

$$

Calculate $a$ such that the average rate of  change over $[a,6]$ is equal to $3.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's calculate the average rate of change of $f(x)$ over the interval $[a,6]$:

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Given a normal random variable $Y∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(Y\ge y)=P(Z\ge \frac{y-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =0$ and $\sigma =5.$

First, we transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 4.1) & =P(Z\ge \frac{4.1-0}{5}) \\  & =P\,(Z\ge \frac{4.1}{5}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.82)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](images/e5/e52cf18a535093c62068e0de8b4319dce833a5637b80ffb15a4c738efbdeebce.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.82) & =1-P(Z<0.82) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.82) \\  & =1-Φ(0.82)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(0.82)=0.7939.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.82) & =1-0.7939 \\  & =0.2061.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(Y\ge 4.1)=0.2061.

\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}x([2\sqrt{x}]-[x])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}x(2\sqrt{x}-x)\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}(2{x}^{3/2}-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {(\frac{4}{5}{x}^{5/2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{128}{5}-\frac{64}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{128\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585032 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c256b77-5f08-5887-b333-8877afee714c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186584576} {:answer/id #uuid "3446d6fc-f0cf-5cb3-8466-2006e3899f1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186584594} {:answer/id #uuid "8b76d2d7-4f2f-5f46-ad11-336a281018ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186584722} {:answer/id #uuid "99f75b5e-7f13-52e2-81a6-78712d74881f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186584745} {:answer/id #uuid "fef596ed-6ccd-5749-83e5-a409df40956a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186584916}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584916} :answer-field/id #uuid "f40b7cd4-5dc8-5163-acf4-62d9c5073958" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186585019}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "0a9fd3bd-e2f3-55f3-aa45-e573890e8c45" :question/math-academy-id "q-84098" :question/problem "Compute $\text{E}[\frac{1}{2}X]$ if $\text{E}[X]=6.$" :question/worked-solution "For any constant $a$ and any random variable $X,$ we have

Assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "The domain of $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of all values where $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\ne 0,$ and is given by the expression

$$

$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne {60}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘},$ where $n$ is an integer."} {:db/id 17592186585035 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d114bb7-f29b-5265-b5a3-16913970e0b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-6}}" :db/id 17592186584544} {:answer/id #uuid "542512b6-1a1f-50c6-ab13-cd6b4b958400" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-36}}" :db/id 17592186584639} {:answer/id #uuid "88333962-2128-5776-a6e3-e08d1acfc721" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-6}}" :db/id 17592186584715} {:answer/id #uuid "e501426e-58ce-5ad8-bc65-8dcaf2123e04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-36}}" :db/id 17592186584869} {:answer/id #uuid "f98c7ddf-a2b4-5ce2-b0c0-f9117dbbbfd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-36}}" :db/id 17592186584897}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584897} :answer-field/id #uuid "0bc2dcdb-f1ea-5c93-84e2-428c6c571991" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584926}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "174e333f-17d0-5184-915a-45f74e7f6d8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-95497" :question/problem "If $y=12\operatorname{arcosh}⁡\left(\frac{x}{6}\right),$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12\operatorname{arcosh}⁡\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)) \\  & =12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)) \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)}^{2}-1}}\cdot {\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)}^{′} \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-1}}\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-36}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585036 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07ca1e6c-a9db-594b-9016-8d2f4f95e494" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186584520} {:answer/id #uuid "2e6885e2-6c79-56ac-a707-f154c368c4c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186584582} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e4803a-3193-5a61-ad59-41fa6d8162b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186584760} {:answer/id #uuid "c76dfb14-ed87-5c28-aa7c-c3d97f8ae0d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186584821} {:answer/id #uuid "e259caa1-7c25-584a-8413-f8b7a68494ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186584865}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584520} :answer-field/id #uuid "9f02793e-5a9a-51f8-ade8-5864438f715e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "17f7ba10-4976-547e-9411-f559e227b76c" :question/math-academy-id "q-87241" :question/problem "Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}k{e}^{10x},\, & x<0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1
$$

In our case, for the function $f(x)=k{e}^{10x}$ on the interval $-\infty <x<0,$ the second condition states that

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{10x}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}k{e}^{10x}\,\text{d}x &={[\frac{k}{10}{e}^{10x}]}_{-\infty }^{0}=\frac{k}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

$$
\frac{k}{10}=1\,⟹\,k=10.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585037 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "76e509b2-0ac4-5187-b65e-54ae242fc329" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={240}^{∘}+n\cdot {540}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186584677} {:answer/id #uuid "b02891b5-cdca-54f9-83a6-7d5ae9d1e464" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={240}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186584778} {:answer/id #uuid "bcb0f441-edcf-5696-995c-104a9b192394" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={180}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186584801} {:answer/id #uuid "d356a64b-5487-506f-b3aa-93975f173303" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={390}^{∘}+n\cdot {540}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186584836} {:answer/id #uuid "e3a73498-b369-57ba-a3f6-fd9c1a4a0bbe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x={390}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}" :db/id 17592186584867}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584836} :answer-field/id #uuid "be61a511-11c3-543b-b96d-e8af60df15a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584994}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "18550e90-a777-5381-a26f-8dce221d2c39" :question/math-academy-id "q-117605" :question/problem "Which expression gives all of the zeros of $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3}-{40}^{∘})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer." :question/worked-solution "First, let's start by defining a new variable $X$ as

$$
X=\frac{x}{3}-{40}^{∘}.
$$

So, we need to calculate the zeros of 

$$
y=\operatorname{cos}⁡X.
$$

The zeros of this function are given by the following expression:

$$
X={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the zeros of our original function, we rewrite $X$ in terms of the original variable $x$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ \frac{x}{3}-{40}^{∘} & ={90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ \frac{x}{3} & ={130}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ x & ={390}^{∘}+n\cdot {540}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the zeros are $x={390}^{∘}+n\cdot {540}^{∘},$ where $n$ is any integer."} {:db/id 17592186585046 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24e53e88-cd52-59f8-80ce-4dc396c845ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3264" :db/id 17592186584554} {:answer/id #uuid "37a9b56d-2760-5f2e-a5a3-44f11c7c3df8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3228" :db/id 17592186584598} {:answer/id #uuid "7560d60f-ef3d-5228-b547-759275027467" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2877" :db/id 17592186584672} {:answer/id #uuid "a130a3b3-730b-5a66-bef5-907cb5011585" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3192" :db/id 17592186584751} {:answer/id #uuid "d4826a63-645a-5576-b2a3-2a85f48b41b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2514" :db/id 17592186584840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584751} :answer-field/id #uuid "2e927b66-a2e6-5a05-b316-31a474700baf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584939}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "39113b6f-b5fc-50b6-9a42-202dfacac91e" :question/math-academy-id "q-131540" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X∼N(-4,{1}^{2}),$ compute $P(X<-4.47).$

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.6\,$ | $\,0.2578\,$ | $\,0.2546\,$ | $\,0.2514\,$ |
| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.2912\,$ | $\,0.2877\,$ | $\,0.2843\,$ |
| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3264\,$ | $\,0.3228\,$ | $\,0.3192\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(X<x)=P(Z<\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =-4$ and $\sigma =1.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<-4.47) & =P(Z<\frac{-4.47-(-4)}{1}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.47) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.47) \\  & =Φ(-0.47)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](images/b7/b7855674356d8fad68f144d19bacd47d1818b3bb05a8d466bb6aec645e769bf3.png)

According to the table, we have

$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(X<-4.47)=0.3192.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585055 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fde90de-155f-51cc-98ee-73261c16d39a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-\frac{16}{3},3)$ and $(\frac{16}{3},-5)$" :db/id 17592186584528} {:answer/id #uuid "25ddf7a0-82ac-5954-8f3a-ba6d421a3a5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,-1)" :db/id 17592186584558} {:answer/id #uuid "3ba393ca-d82e-5764-bfcd-8098426ee420" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-18,5)$ and $(18,-7)$" :db/id 17592186584602} {:answer/id #uuid "40d5d3a4-2ae3-5ee6-9123-152ce19c0179" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(-\frac{2}{3},1)$ and $(\frac{2}{3},-3)$" :db/id 17592186584615} {:answer/id #uuid "a1a92e7b-2f5d-5501-a517-253f58e816fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{3},-3)" :db/id 17592186584753}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584615} :answer-field/id #uuid "035c833c-422f-5fc3-8846-056e44bbd02a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584919}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "44d45946-d5ae-5ded-ba5e-267014bb4886" :question/math-academy-id "q-126899" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3},2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨-1,-1⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{t}^{2},2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨-1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨-1,-1⟩\cdot ⟨-2{t}^{2},2⟩ & =0 \\ (-1)(-2{t}^{2})+(-1)(2) & =0 \\ 2{t}^{2}-2 & =0 \\ 2(t+1)(t-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $t=\pm 1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨-\frac{2(-1)^{3}}{3},2(-1)-1⟩=⟨\frac{2}{3},-3⟩, \\ r(1) & =⟨-\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3},2(1)-1⟩=⟨-\frac{2}{3},1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨-1,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $(-\frac{2}{3},1)$ and $(\frac{2}{3},-3).$"} {:db/id 17592186585061 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d1ee0da-3b49-5238-861c-38b5df7e5f09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186584526} {:answer/id #uuid "1ac5cda3-ee1d-5685-a3ec-cbc3c6783db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186584540} {:answer/id #uuid "1b301d54-d06d-501b-ae37-4fdcc3c997aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186584543} {:answer/id #uuid "51233e56-4314-5007-b78e-87b901ff837c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186584635} {:answer/id #uuid "88ec41d4-6635-5ea1-a44e-cb72ab2e90f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186584717}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584635} :answer-field/id #uuid "d247ad79-c623-5870-9092-680522af21b4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186585002}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4f66cc83-baee-51f5-8daa-d191a7f966f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-65311" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x?$

Compute $P(0\le Y<10\,|\,X=4)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le Y<10\,|\,X=4) & =\frac{P((0\le Y<10),X=4)}{P(X=4)} \\  & =\frac{P(X=4,(0\le Y<10))}{P(X=4)} \\  & =\frac{P(X=4,Y=0)+P(X=4,Y=5)}{P(X=4)} \\  & =\frac{f(4,0)+f(4,5)}{{f}_{X}(4)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(4) & =f(4,0)+f(4,5)+f(4,10) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}+0+\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(4,0)=\frac{3}{16}$ and $f(4,5)=0.$ 

Finally, substituting our values into our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le Y<10\,|\,X=4) & =\frac{f(4,0)+f(4,5)}{{f}_{X}(4)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{16}+0)}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{3}{16}\right)}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585075 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "728ecdef-2296-5cc6-a60c-9cf83ef133d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186584664} {:answer/id #uuid "9905ae2e-e4ef-5d53-946f-586296033fd0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-10" :db/id 17592186584743} {:answer/id #uuid "a895485d-8d39-5f19-9bc9-0a7ea84c7dc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186584769} {:answer/id #uuid "c2e9786f-645b-5f0f-b775-87f233e252b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186584814} {:answer/id #uuid "e0db6a79-3905-52e9-b2ee-ef50bd910af8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-20" :db/id 17592186584863}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584863} :answer-field/id #uuid "60562cd8-f02c-5e40-bd23-948289b98218" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584961}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7f5ee041-2b7c-5ed1-82d7-9183ba46e498" :question/math-academy-id "q-109298" :question/problem "A random variable $X$ has the probability distribution given below.

Calculate $\text{E}[-\frac{3}{2}X-5].$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's find $\text{E}[X].$ 

The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot \frac{1}{4}+5\cdot \frac{1}{8}+10\cdot \frac{1}{4}+15\cdot \frac{1}{8}+20\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[-\frac{3}{2}X-5] & =-\frac{3}{2}\text{E}[X]-5 \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot 10-5 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585081 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a6e93553-7cf4-5b33-827e-eadc4cd68dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1661" :db/id 17592186584766}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584766} :answer-field/id #uuid "b6f0911a-1cc1-5c54-a553-af78f3c5f5ff" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186584988}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "87bcce97-5287-5a8d-a497-dccd691ee1a9" :question/math-academy-id "q-336466" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(a<X<b)=P(\frac{a-\mu }{\sigma }<Z<\frac{b-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =6$ and $\sigma =3.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(7.26<X<8.85) & =P(\frac{7.26-6}{3}<Z<\frac{8.85-6}{3}) \\  & =P(0.42<Z<0.95).\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](images/39/39f9ac74ed4f39708f882116edb554b15051ea820e4b5ea8a38e5451ed706251.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.42<Z<0.95) & =P(Z<0.95)-P(Z\le 0.42) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.95)-P(Z\le 0.42) \\  & =Φ(0.95)-Φ(0.42).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.95) & =0.8289 \\ Φ(0.42) & =0.6628\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.42<Z<0.95) & =Φ(0.95)-Φ(0.42) \\  & =0.8289-0.6628 \\  & =0.1661.\end{aligned}
$$

f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}},\, & x\le -3, \\ 0,\, & x>-3.\end{aligned}\right.

Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius $1.5,$ as shown above. Find the maximum possible area of the triangle." :question/worked-solution "Let's call $l$ the length of one leg. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the area of the triangle is given by

$$
A(l)=\frac{1}{2}l\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}\,.
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $3$, the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<3.$

We want to maximize $A(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}-\frac{{l}^{2}}{2\sqrt{9-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ 9-{l}^{2}-{l}^{2} & =0 \\ {l}^{2} & =\frac{9}{2} \\ l & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ | $(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2},3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ |  | $2.5$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Finally, the maximum possible area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{9-{\left(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585086 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8b6a9466-6622-514c-b6d0-9353aa6390fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\pi" :db/id 17592186584721} {:answer/id #uuid "b84bb223-a911-52df-bb66-6e56e30dcfc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186584790} {:answer/id #uuid "d2f02822-944d-5c42-8c5a-05494a86e69b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186584835} {:answer/id #uuid "f63f8278-a9cc-578a-abc4-c70e702ae708" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi" :db/id 17592186584894} {:answer/id #uuid "fc9a942e-0694-5da8-8b7d-d8418c237a44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186584906}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584790} :answer-field/id #uuid "f2cf652d-23bc-5dc2-a268-3fff8a57145c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186585017}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "8d6cc8b4-8e21-5e37-8b4a-c2763b4cd71e" :question/math-academy-id "q-81563" :question/problem "Calculate the period of the function $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡(8x+\frac{\pi }{4})$" :question/worked-solution "Given a function of the form $y=A\operatorname{csc}⁡(Bx+C)+D,$ the period is $\frac{2\pi }{B}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{1/6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{1/6+1}}{(\frac{1}{6}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{7/6}}{\left(\frac{7}{6}\right)}+C \\  & =\frac{6{x}^{7/6}}{7}+C.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{13\pi }{4}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

$$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We apply the sum, constant multiple, and power rules as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{x}+1) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{(\frac{1}{2}-1)} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186585103 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b65c8cf-4c70-5896-a357-95b325d5ff31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,3]\cup [5,\infty )" :db/id 17592186584573} {:answer/id #uuid "7cc4faca-3693-53fc-81d2-9219974dfb21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-5]\cup [-3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186584696} {:answer/id #uuid "7f65c921-1bb8-5f83-838b-202cecbcbc69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-5]\cup [3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186584701} {:answer/id #uuid "94c44f1f-62c3-59e6-8602-8c82597aa3c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,0]\cup [5,\infty )" :db/id 17592186584738} {:answer/id #uuid "e2143825-68b1-52ed-afff-3410550d1918" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "f(x)\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [0,\infty )" :db/id 17592186584864}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186584573} :answer-field/id #uuid "22cdfe9f-7af6-5273-b3d3-8a72041e4322" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186584933}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d23ba213-aeb3-53b8-b777-ecd714efa3fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-117768" :question/problem "Find the range of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})+4.$" :question/worked-solution "The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $-1$ and adding $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})+4\ge 1+4 \\  & f(x)\ge 5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $-1$ and adding $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{3})+4\le -1+4 \\  & f(x)\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$

$$
P(Y\ge y)=P(Z\ge \frac{y-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

First, we transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 17.76) & =P(Z\ge \frac{17.76-9}{12}) \\  & =P\,(Z\ge \frac{8.76}{12}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.73)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.73) & =1-P(Z<0.73) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.73) \\  & =1-Φ(0.73)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we know that

$$
Φ(0.73)=0.7673.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z\ge 0.73) & =1-0.7673 \\  & =0.2327.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$

| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "First, we express the given probability as

*Hint: Note that the interval $-1<X<7$ is symmetric about the mean $\mu =3.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the given interval is symmetric about the mean:

$$
P(-1<X<7)=P(3-4<X<3+4)
$$

So, we find the cumulative probability using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1<X<7) & =0.5346 \\ 2P(3<X<7) & =0.5346 \\ P(3<X<7) & =0.2673 \\ P(X<7)-P(X<3) & =0.2673 \\ P(X<7)-0.5 & =0.2673 \\ P(X<7) & =0.7673 \\ P(X\le 7) & =0.7673\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 7) & =0.7673 \\ P(Z\le \frac{7-3}{\sigma }) & =0.7673 \\ Φ\left(\frac{4}{\sigma }\right) & =0.7673 \\ \frac{4}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.7673)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.73)=0.7673\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(0.7673)=0.73.
$$

Therefore, we have

Given that the above predicate is defined over the universal set $R,$ which of the following statements are true?

II. The truth set of $P(x)$ is $R.$

III. $∃x\in R,\,P(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The *existential quantification* of a predicate $P(x),$ defined over the universal set $U,$ transforms this predicate into a statement that we write as

$$
∃x\in U,\,P(x).
$$

This statement is true if the predicate $P(x)$ is true for a single element $x\in U,$ i.e. if the truth set ${T}_{P}$ of the predicate is not empty:

$$
{T}_{P}\ne ∅
$$

First, notice that:

- the truth set of "$x<2$" is the set $(-\infty ,2),$ and

- the truth set of "$2x>3$" is the set $(\frac{3}{2},\infty ).$

Since $A⇒B≡¬A∨B,$ the truth set of our predicate is 

$$
{T}_{P}=\overset{―}{(-\infty ,2)}\cup (\frac{3}{2},\infty )=[2,\infty )\cup (\frac{3}{2},\infty )=(\frac{3}{2},\infty ).
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the given statements.

- Statement I is false. The truth set is *not* empty.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, ${T}_{P}=(\frac{3}{2},\infty ).$

- Statement III is true. Since ${T}_{P}$ is *not* empty, the statement $∃x\in R,\,P(x)$ is true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186585749 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4834fe93-2dd3-59c2-9e0c-8e2e1bd8ab71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186585308} {:answer/id #uuid "4ce0dffd-2fc2-50b6-998a-8000bea2ff7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186585313} {:answer/id #uuid "92eea147-d98a-54c5-b38d-970588b6ec57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186585436} {:answer/id #uuid "ae190add-99df-5b1a-b5fc-544128ec9398" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi" :db/id 17592186585479} {:answer/id #uuid "c012f9c2-8419-5118-ac33-af9c463f8804" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi" :db/id 17592186585504}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186585436} :answer-field/id #uuid "1111a75a-fd40-5e51-b2f1-fcf37f20e6ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186585598}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4b9f3956-68a2-519a-8ef5-14d82fb1067f" :question/math-academy-id "q-117655" :question/problem "Calculate the period of the function $$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(3,-\frac{17}{2})$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-3)^{2}+{(y+\frac{17}{2})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+9+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{289}{4} \\  & ={x}^{2}-6x+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{325}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-6x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}+17y+\frac{325}{4} \\  & ={y}^{2}+18y+\frac{325}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y+18 & =0 \\ 2y & =-18 \\ y & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=-9$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=-9.$"} {:answer/id #uuid "26759a0e-ed59-5e2d-ae4e-95a79b36614c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k\in (-\infty ,\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186586740} {:answer/id #uuid "5c8d0286-2dba-5a35-83ca-4a847651e3a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "k\in (\frac{1}{2},\infty )" :db/id 17592186586837} {:answer/id #uuid "c3627dd2-c043-5254-a264-cdadfdb1fe47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186587026} {:db/id 17592186587299 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0319149c-faad-52f1-9ad3-aa7836beef04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{38}" :db/id 17592186586673} {:answer/id #uuid "2660777a-6b3b-5b3f-aab9-b8eddfe02994" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{46}" :db/id 17592186586739} {:answer/id #uuid "4b5e767e-7284-5218-a730-4a9b2cfe7f1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186586807} {:answer/id #uuid "daf98ade-ba83-58e1-98ad-53d18b7801e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{35}" :db/id 17592186587071} {:answer/id #uuid "e98d87ec-ecca-5908-ba61-b3ee24232a05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{7}" :db/id 17592186587107}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186586807} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed0e6d57-2958-5b0d-b807-9a1ae8652a1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186587269}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "383600e4-79b3-56ec-8133-5401a0897721" :question/math-academy-id "q-78156" :question/problem "Calculate $\lim_{s\to 1}||f(s)||$, if $$
\displaystyle f(s)=⟨\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡{s}^{2}}{s-1},\frac{6s-\operatorname{sin}⁡(s-1)}{3s-2},\frac{{s}^{3}+4s-2}{{s}^{2}+s-1}⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 1}f(s) & =⟨\lim_{s\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡{s}^{2}}{s-1},\,\lim_{s\to 1}\frac{6s-\operatorname{sin}⁡(s-1)}{3s-2},\,\lim_{s\to 1}\frac{{s}^{3}+4s-2}{{s}^{2}+s-1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the limits one-by-one.

- The first component can be found using L'Hopital's Rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{t\to 1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡{s}^{2}}{s-1} & =\lim_{t\to 1}\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡s}{s-1} \\  & =\lim_{t\to 1}\frac{(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s)^{′}}{(s-1)^{′}} \\  & =\lim_{t\to 1}\frac{\left(\frac{2}{s}\right)}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 1}\frac{6s-\operatorname{sin}⁡(s-1)}{3s-2} & =\frac{6(1)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1-1)}{3(1)-2} \\  & =\frac{6-0}{1} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

- For the third component, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 1}\frac{{s}^{3}+4s-2}{{s}^{2}+s-1} & =\frac{(1)^{3}+4(1)-2}{(1)^{2}+(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{1} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lim_{s\to 1}f(s)=⟨2,\,6,\,3⟩.$

Finally, the limit of $‖f(s)‖$ as $s$ approaches $1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{s\to 1}‖f(s)‖ & =‖\lim_{s\to 1}f(s)‖ \\  & =‖⟨2,\,6,\,3⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+36+9} \\  & =\sqrt{49} \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186587301 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "126c56aa-8758-539c-b552-fdf3f416cf5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "123.45" :db/id 17592186586695} {:answer/id #uuid "319e6782-021b-5036-b0b3-6e0d46b9ab4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "112.59" :db/id 17592186586760} {:answer/id #uuid "738e13a2-2196-5c74-bb27-99b7cce975c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "121.37" :db/id 17592186586875} {:answer/id #uuid "7beec582-9936-5679-817a-21fd993d4648" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "115.37" :db/id 17592186586892} {:answer/id #uuid "cfc178b0-47d2-5491-a0fd-6a7b112ba4a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "109.66" :db/id 17592186587049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186587049} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c872a96-9eca-5b26-999a-9edb06954c96" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186587197}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3c3a9fd9-add3-5f7e-b93b-ea7810207c34" :question/math-academy-id "q-95136" :question/problem "The systolic blood pressure of a group of people is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $12\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Additionally, $90\%$ of the people have a systolic blood pressure between $0.82\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and $1.18\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Find the mean systolic blood pressure of this group, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{12}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.82\mu <X<1.18\mu )=0.9.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.82\mu <X<1.18\mu ) & =0.9 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.18\mu ) & =0.9 \\ P(\mu <X<1.18\mu ) & =0.45 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.18\mu ) & =0.5+0.45 \\ P(X<1.18\mu ) & =0.95\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.18\mu ) & =0.95 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.18\mu }{12}) & =0.95 \\ Φ\left(\frac{0.18\mu }{12}\right) & =0.95 \\ \frac{0.18\mu }{12} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.95)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.95)≈1.6449.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.18\mu }{12} & =1.6449 \\ 0.18\mu  & =19.7388 \\ \mu  & =\frac{19.7388}{0.18} \\  & ≈109.66.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186587303 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "325e0b9b-e44e-596e-8063-e9b6aa9a7664" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23.5\%" :db/id 17592186586763} {:answer/id #uuid "38209872-6741-5379-9a33-e36894b48a1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "28.8\%" :db/id 17592186586774} {:answer/id #uuid "66d6484d-34f5-5bfb-97a9-3989783ca51a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25.3\%" :db/id 17592186586854} {:answer/id #uuid "b5b4d913-1222-517f-bb47-3c61e2354ac4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "19.80\%" :db/id 17592186586996} {:answer/id #uuid "b86fe268-938a-5141-88c2-6b99b344d329" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16.81\%" :db/id 17592186587000}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186586774} :answer-field/id #uuid "af9f399d-b447-595e-bb7e-e89923ca4c99" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186587239}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3eae1263-f400-536b-bb78-8cc3f0362312" :question/math-academy-id "q-95131" :question/problem "The systolic blood pressure of a group of people is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $14\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Additionally, $60\%$ of the people have a systolic blood pressure between $0.9\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and $1.1\mu \,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Find the percentage of people with a systolic blood pressure lower than $110\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$

| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3264\,$ | $\,0.3228\,$ | $\,0.3192\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the systolic blood pressure of a randomly selected person. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{14}^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<110).$ But first, we need to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu )=0.6.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.9\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.6 \\ P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.3 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.1\mu ) & =0.5+0.3 \\ P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.1\mu ) & =0.8 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.1\mu }{14}) & =0.8 \\ Φ\left(\frac{0.1\mu }{14}\right) & =0.8 \\ \frac{0.1\mu }{14} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.8)\end{aligned}

$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X<110)$ as follows:

$$

Therefore, approximately $28.8\%$ of the people have a systolic blood pressure lower than $110\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$"} {:db/id 17592186587304 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2202f6fe-b53b-5a2d-a1db-2533ed538332" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}x^{\frac{5}{4}}" :db/id 17592186586733}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186586733} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d10d539-8c5e-514d-8877-3d19db95faab" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186587183}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3efb6512-0e32-57d7-9bcc-102471dd5cbb" :question/math-academy-id "q-167541" :question/problem "The antiderivative of $\sqrt[4]{x}$ equals{{field-1}} $+\,\text{ }C$" :question/worked-solution "Since $\sqrt[4]{x}={x}^{1/4}$, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{1/4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{1/4+1}}{(\frac{1}{4}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/4}}{\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)}+C \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check our answer by differentiating: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5}+C) &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\ &= \frac{4}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4})+0 \\ &= \frac{4}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{4}{x}^{5/4-1} \\ &= {x}^{1/4}\hspace{1em}{\color{green}✓}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186587315 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04238ee2-aa8f-5ea4-afc4-8c53cd4b44ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,-2,-2\sqrt{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186586675} {:answer/id #uuid "33b6e5bf-bbfc-54b2-84a2-7c955dd1bda7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,-1,2⟩" :db/id 17592186586767} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1be478-d414-5a22-9d34-1ffbf6c4df41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2,-3,2-\sqrt{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186586891} {:answer/id #uuid "82e0db46-1173-5b6d-8fb7-9651267fe612" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-1,-2,2-2\sqrt{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186586907} {:answer/id #uuid "c3627dd2-c043-5254-a264-cdadfdb1fe47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨1,\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186587026}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186586907} :answer-field/id #uuid "56c504a5-cb4f-5fb7-8c3e-508a3cfa7736" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186587194}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5a47d32b-8e4c-52a9-ad00-e5d92ad70a75" :question/math-academy-id "q-130289" :question/problem "Find $\lim_{t\to 0}[f(t)-2g(t)]$ given that
$f(t)$ and $g(t)$ are defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{t}^{2}-1,\,\frac{4+t}{2-{t}^{2}}⟩, \\ g(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\sqrt{t}+\sqrt{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the limit of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{t\to 0}f(t) & =⟨\lim_{t\to 0}\,(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\lim_{t\to 0}\,({t}^{2}-1),\,\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{4+t}{2-{t}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨1+\operatorname{sin}⁡0,{0}^{2}-1,\frac{4+0}{2-{0}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\ \lim_{t\to 0}g(t) & =⟨\lim_{t\to 0}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{2},\,\lim_{t\to 0}\,(\sqrt{t}+\sqrt{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{0}+\sqrt{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use properties of limits to calculate the final result:

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{2x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-2t/3}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-2x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$

$$

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)},
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=(k-1)x+5 \\ y &=\frac{2}{x}+3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and simplifying, we get a quadratic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(k-1)x+5 & =\frac{2}{x}+3 \\ (k-1)x+2 & =\frac{2}{x} \\ (k-1){x}^{2}+2x & =2 \\ (k-1){x}^{2}+2x-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since  $k\ne 1$,  by using the quadratic formula, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{{2}^{2}-4(k-1)(-2)}}{2(k-1)} \\  & =\frac{-2\pm \sqrt{8k-4}}{2(k-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the line *not* to intersect the hyperbola, the quadratic formula above must *not* give any real solutions.

So, the expression inside the square root must be negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}8k-4 & <0 \\ 8k & <4 \\ k & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k\in (-\infty ,\frac{1}{2}).$"} {:answer/id #uuid "0ce771c3-c5b4-50c8-af1b-fd23377d9cc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "2740eb12-7415-5c22-a779-12b0980aa32b" :question/math-academy-id "q-52530" :question/problem "Rewrite $2{z}^{2}+3z-1$ by completing the square." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, we take out a factor of $2$ from the entire expression:

$$
2({z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z-\frac{1}{2})
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot z-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2},$ writing the constant term $\frac{1}{2}$ last:

$$
{{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot z+{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}}_{⏟}-{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{17}{16}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression::

$$
\begin{aligned}2({z}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}z-\frac{1}{2}) & =2({(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{17}{16}) \\  & =2{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{17}{16} \\  & =2{(z+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{17}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186588194 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27319df5-a74b-51ff-91a0-efef312143e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi }{2}$" :db/id 17592186587619} {:answer/id #uuid "4db3379d-b40f-5367-89f3-b9a1819d53a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi }{2}$" :db/id 17592186587698} {:answer/id #uuid "5841452a-fbf5-5a22-8d9f-5184043a31b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$0$ and $\pi$" :db/id 17592186587715} {:answer/id #uuid "5faf3924-fc67-578f-9190-207e408e3c9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\frac{\pi }{2}$ only" :db/id 17592186587724} {:answer/id #uuid "be848024-fcef-5bc7-b49e-d58ff9e7b161" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\pi$ only" :db/id 17592186587908}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186587908} :answer-field/id #uuid "acbe2710-7062-57b4-bf97-b2dad7eff4b6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186588133}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3215364b-8b73-5bb3-8206-9369e50bdeb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143017" :question/problem "Compute the values of $$
\displaystyle \theta \in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{2}]
$$ for which the polar curve $r=5$ has vertical tangents, given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$" :question/worked-solution "We have a vertical tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the vertical tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\theta ) & =0 \\ \theta  & =\pi n\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only one belongs to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=\pi .
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether our candidate has ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solution into ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${y}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=\pi ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\pi ) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =5(-1) \\  & =-5 \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=\pi$ is a valid solution.

So, our curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =\pi .$

$$
-4({x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{2})
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{2}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2},$ writing the constant term $\frac{1}{2}$ last:

$$
{{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}}_{⏟}-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4({x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{2}) & =-4({(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =-4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-4)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\  & =-4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186588196 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7da1aee5-3932-528a-9e0b-86a651c6c102" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi}{4}" :db/id 17592186587791}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186587791} :answer-field/id #uuid "10c7e795-0185-5a7e-acba-242d880217a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186588048} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6a69cc7d-7728-5ea6-a08f-e901d6dcbc12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi}{4}" :db/id 17592186587749}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186587749} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa92b11b-5001-5ef5-be98-12d2870c2098" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186588171}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3ecca038-75c0-5e56-a4b2-b98e6d347a4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-363393" :question/problem "Compute the values of $\theta \in [0,\pi )$ for which the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta$ has a horizontal tangent, given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

In **ascending order**, the polar curve has horizontal tangents at

${\theta }_{1}=$

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We have a horizontal tangent when

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.
$$

To find the horizontal tangents, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${x}^{′}(\theta ).$ 

We're given that

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the values of $\theta$ where ${y}^{′}(\theta )=0.$

By writing down and solving the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\theta  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ \theta  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. However, among the solutions above, only two belong to the required domain, namely

$$
{\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4},\,{\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.
$$

**Step 3**: Check to see whether any candidates have ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0.$ 

We substitute our candidate solutions into ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and check that ${x}^{′}(\theta )\ne 0.$ If ${x}^{′}(\theta )=0,$ further investigation is necessary.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =-\sqrt{2} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is a valid solution.

- Substituting ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right) & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =\sqrt{2} \\  & \ne 0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}$ is a valid solution.

Therefore, in ascending order, our curve has horizontal tangents at ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$

\displaystyle {\log }_{5}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}{\log }_{5}⁡(8{x}^{3})=3.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the logarithms share the same base.

First, we apply the power rule to the *second* term to make the coefficient in front of each logarithm the same:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\log }_{5}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}{\log }_{5}⁡(8{x}^{3}) & =3 \\ {\log }_{5}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)+{\log }_{5}⁡((8{x}^{3})^{1/3}) & =3 \\ {\log }_{5}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)+{\log }_{5}⁡(2x) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we combine the logarithms using the product rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\log }_{5}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 2x) & =3 \\ {\log }_{5}⁡({x}^{3}) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing this equation in its equivalent exponential form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{{\log }_{5}⁡({x}^{3})} & ={5}^{3} \\ {x}^{3} & =125\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation for $x$ using the usual methods.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{125} \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=5$ back into the original equation, we get

$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & =-3(1)(1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =-3x+\frac{3\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186588243 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7bf90b4a-f6c1-55f9-ad2b-85a225345a5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}-\sqrt{\frac{2-x}{2}}" :db/id 17592186587788}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186587788} :answer-field/id #uuid "63d33fcf-824a-55b1-8cad-63ab454bc9fe" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186588090}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b08a198d-6d80-57ca-ae8b-47a0ea232935" :question/math-academy-id "q-222065" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=-2{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+2$ for $x\le \frac{1}{3}.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To find the inverse of a function, we follow these steps:

**Step 1:** Replace $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=-2{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+2
$$

**Step 2:** Swap $x$ and $y:$

$$
x=-2{(y-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+2
$$

**Step 3:** Solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2{(y-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+2 \\ x-2 & =-2{(y-\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\ \frac{2-x}{2} & ={(y-\frac{1}{3})}^{2} \\ -\sqrt{\frac{2-x}{2}} & =y-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}-\sqrt{\frac{2-x}{2}} & =y\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we take the negative square root because if $x\le \frac{1}{3}$ is the domain of $f,$ then the range of the inverse is ${f}^{-1}\le \frac{1}{3}.$

**Step 4:** Replace $y$ with ${f}^{-1}(x):$

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{3}-\sqrt{\frac{2-x}{2}}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "b18468e0-9f81-562f-8526-e520564c0491" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-\frac{70}{41},-\frac{35}{41},\frac{270}{41}⟩" :db/id 17592186588723} {:answer/id #uuid "ba76aebb-59d1-528d-9b46-57f600d41e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{35}{41},-\frac{35}{41},\frac{35}{41}⟩" :db/id 17592186588745} {:answer/id #uuid "cca78dfc-4dc0-559a-8393-29d8d5eaa8b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{70}{41},-\frac{210}{41},\frac{35}{41}⟩" :db/id 17592186588775} {:answer/id #uuid "f369c825-abf9-56bb-89f8-2c43ceea3faf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{210}{41},-\frac{70}{41},\frac{35}{41}⟩" :db/id 17592186588847} {:db/id 17592186589037 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e309397-2ae0-59c6-beb7-cd8f2054152e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186588377} {:answer/id #uuid "5c33f6ad-a97b-54e7-8f7b-7d6f8dc0064c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186588528} {:answer/id #uuid "62d0d54b-89f5-5069-9a28-61f1b1dd3720" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186588547} {:answer/id #uuid "660ba7f7-1282-5388-b660-f90d0ece4aa5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186588558} {:answer/id #uuid "b4b1540a-7f05-5da7-8b18-9a447252615a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186588730}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186588558} :answer-field/id #uuid "fc95ef28-8dd6-52fe-9446-885d34cbfad1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186589023}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2217399f-848d-5f24-8c2e-4b27a8fe86e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-149671" :question/problem "Find $\text{E}[\frac{13X}{1-X}],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{12}{13}(1-x)^{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
r(x)=\frac{13x}{1-x}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\frac{13X}{1-X}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}\frac{13x}{1-x}\cdot \frac{12}{13}(1-x)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}12x(1-x)\text{d}x \\  & =12{\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}(x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =12{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{-1/2}^{1/2} \\  & =12[(\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{24})-(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{24})] \\  & =12\left(-\frac{1}{12}\right) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186589043 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "49ff0186-f4ce-51de-8276-93b89c48fa4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186588495} {:answer/id #uuid "6db02914-e35b-5d29-b60a-d30fe7ce0a90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186588579} {:answer/id #uuid "9fb6a80c-6bc5-5d7a-b9ce-625aa765b129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{55\pi }{42}" :db/id 17592186588687} {:answer/id #uuid "a78015a7-9e9b-51c0-a8d1-bde2512a95dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{67\pi }{42}" :db/id 17592186588704} {:answer/id #uuid "dc6389b1-d67e-54fe-b818-b919d64af40c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186588812}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186588687} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac728fc-3d15-54af-8dc3-6504642ce91a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186588929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2c11ce06-c970-57cf-bc52-2f9a93a36ad9" :question/math-academy-id "q-85578" :question/problem "![](images/67/67490fe1008a6c590389080456845a413928193ceced3248e924e476496b8f1b.png)

The region enclosed by the curves $y=\sqrt{x}$ and $y={x}^{3}$ for $x\in [0,1]$ is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the line $y=2.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid." :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw our vertical arrow through the given region. The arrow should be pointing away from the axis of rotation.

![](images/84/846c6c56587f9f60aedf3952250c03f03e2a92ee90f067d1379ced74108b4296.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x},$ and

- *leaves* through the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

Now, we can find the volume of our solid as the difference between the volumes of the solids generated by the outer and inner curves.

- **Step I.** Figure out the volume generated by the outer curve $y={x}^{3}.$

![](images/6c/6c53fcb7d12f2aefb6e899c42441d048e93a43ce548812816b8882b76135f858.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{outer}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-({x}^{3})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step II.** Figure out the volume generated by the inner curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$

![](images/0e/0eab7ed4e195fa626db187071964bb14959678d5a04333d8760f5182ea93ed1d.png)

The corresponding volume is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{inner}} & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper})-(\text{lower})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-(\sqrt{x})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step III.** Find the difference.

Finally, we can write the volume of the original solid as

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={V}_{\text{outer}}-{V}_{\text{inner}} \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-{x}^{3}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[2-\sqrt{x}]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}((2-{x}^{3})^{2}-(2-\sqrt{x})^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{6}-4{x}^{3}-x+4\sqrt{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{7}\,{x}^{7}-{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\,{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,{x}^{3/2})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{1}{7}\,(1)^{7}-{1}^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\,(1)^{2}+\frac{8}{3}\,(1)^{3/2})-(0)] \\  & =\pi \left(\frac{55}{42}\right) \\  & =\frac{55\pi }{42}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186589052 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "47021d65-5401-5fef-8a77-6ebe9baba972" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.023" :db/id 17592186588491} {:answer/id #uuid "68b68adc-9ed0-59da-a7e7-8ca484136339" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.017" :db/id 17592186588566} {:answer/id #uuid "82c4894d-c1b3-5405-9171-b473876c4e75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.027" :db/id 17592186588622} {:answer/id #uuid "997e3a73-d636-5266-a53f-ed5dfba11fd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.033" :db/id 17592186588671} {:answer/id #uuid "dbf2cbab-7fcf-5639-a581-26e8a57b53e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.042" :db/id 17592186588809}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186588491} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d58c283-2585-5821-b528-c541d7158b93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186588906}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "50e71934-28ae-506f-82e4-c2be88812c3c" :question/math-academy-id "q-132280" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼B(165,0.6),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=90).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=165$ and $p=0.6.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =165\cdot 0.6 \\  & =99 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =165\cdot (1-0.6) \\  & =66 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(165)(0.6)=99
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(165)(0.6)(1-0.6)=39.6.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(99,39.6).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=90).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=90)≈P(89.5\le Y\le 90.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(89.5\le Y\le 90.5) & =P(\frac{89.5-99}{\sqrt{39.6}}\le Z\le \frac{90.5-99}{\sqrt{39.6}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.51\le Z\le -1.35) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.35)-P(Z<-1.51) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.35)-P(Z\le -1.51) \\  & =Φ(-1.35)-Φ(-1.51) \\  & =0.0885-0.0655 \\  & =0.023\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=90)≈0.023.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0227.$"} {:db/id 17592186589059 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "77bd579e-68df-5e73-b401-390f3e274d08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{31}{5}" :db/id 17592186588599} {:answer/id #uuid "7b12650d-9f49-55e8-9f30-dcde8a3d6869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{4}" :db/id 17592186588606} {:answer/id #uuid "c27e3ca0-3014-5b8d-84eb-a7732203ec20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186588758} {:answer/id #uuid "c67bc4c9-f621-5e25-979b-7a61b73e0e8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186588768} {:answer/id #uuid "f5f57af5-e35d-516e-860e-ff88135de2a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186588852}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186588599} :answer-field/id #uuid "e05963d3-2be7-5db0-935d-0d4392b49788" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186589013}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5c32a1f2-06cf-5ba7-aefa-b2ee1f2bff8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-152892" :question/problem "A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function
