where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{y}^{1}\frac{3(x+2y)}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{y}^{1}(x+2y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+2xy]}_{x=y}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+2y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\frac{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0\le y\le x\le 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{3(x+2y)}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{3(1+4y-5{y}^{2})}{4}\right)} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2(x+2y)}{1+4y-5{y}^{2}}, & \,0\le y\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+{e}^{y}}{e}, & \,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{3e+1}{6e},\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{3}{2e},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2821,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2870,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \left(\frac{2x+{e}^{y}}{e}\right)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{e}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{x}^{2}y+xy{e}^{y})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{e}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y{e}^{y}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{e}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{1}{2}y{e}^{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{e}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y{e}^{y}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{e}{2}-\frac{e}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{6e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{5}{6e}-\left(\frac{3e+1}{6e}\right)\left(\frac{3}{2e}\right) \\  & =\frac{e-3}{12{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{\left(\frac{e-3}{12{e}^{2}}\right)}{(0.2821)\cdot (0.2870)} \\  & ≈-0.04,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186594227 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2376757d-a62d-51e9-ac20-65b410312a29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dd240541-da69-5f1e-b10e-57cf984c2241" :question/math-academy-id "q-182662" :question/problem "Prove that $$

$$ using mathematical induction.

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove that our statement is true for the base case $n=\,${{field-1}}.

For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}} &={{field-2}}\end{aligned}
$$

which equals the right-hand side. Thus, our statement is {{field-3}} for $n=1.$

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=$ {{field-4}}, we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}={{field-5}}.
$$

**Inductive Step**: To prove $P(k+1),$ we write

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}})+{{field-6}}.
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}})+\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}} & ={{field-7}} \\  & ={{field-8}},\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=1-\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}
$$ is true for all {{field-9}}." :question/worked-solution "The principle of induction states the following: Suppose we have a sequence of mathematical statements $P(1),P(2),P(3),…,$ where

- $P(1)$ is true, and

- $P(k)⇒P(k+1)$ for every $k\in N.$

Then, $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in N.$

In this case, the general statement $P(n)$ we're required to prove is the following:

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=1-\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}
$$

We start by proving the so-called base case, $P(1).$ To do this, we substitute $n=1$ into both the left-hand side and right-hand side and show that they're equal:

We proceed using induction on $n.$

**Base Case**: We first prove our statement is true for the base case $n=1.$
For the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}} &=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and for the right-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{2}^{1}} &=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, our statement is true for $n=1.$

Next, we state our inductive hypothesis. Here, we assume that the given statement is true for some $n=k\ge 1.$ 

Due to the base case, we already *know* that the statement is true for *some* value of $k,$ namely $k=1,$ so this assumption is valid.

**Inductive Hypothesis**: We assume that for some $n=k\ge 1,$ we have

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k}}.
$$

We must show that $P(k)⇒P(k+1).$ Let's start by writing down $P(k+1).$ This is the first part of the so-called **inductive step**, so let's write that, too.

**Inductive Step**: We're required to prove that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}}.\,\,(∗)
$$

The idea is to rewrite the left-hand side of $(∗)$ *using the inductive hypothesis* and apply algebraic techniques to show that this equals the right-hand side.

When proving sums of finite series using induction, the key to unlocking the proof is to write the last term on its own, as follows: 

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}{a}_{i}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{a}_{i})+{a}_{k+1}
$$

Let's apply this technique in this case:

We write

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}})+\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}}.
$$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({\sum }_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}})+\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}} & =1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k}}(1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k}}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{2}^{k+1}},\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

Since we've shown that the left-hand side of $(∗)$ equals the right-hand side, our proof is complete. So let's write down our conclusion. 

Therefore, by the principle of induction, $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}=1-\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}
$$ is true for all $n\ge 1.$"} {:db/id 17592186594228 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "763787eb-8f29-5444-b6f8-b99d862d1698" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{64}{3}" :db/id 17592186593652}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186593652} :answer-field/id #uuid "e5cc2777-96ed-5ab4-ba6e-a41460086dc9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186594125}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "de6ea974-0ebd-5e85-8d18-9e5dd70695c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-346622" :question/problem "![](images/50/500b67a9964191ebbc4fea9ba50870f691b68c9ecdd7e663762a47531d099e6a.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

$A=$ 
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{x}^{2}+8 & =-{x}^{2} \\ -2{x}^{2}+8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-2$ to $x=2.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](images/33/336a1503663239debacda06ca200e47151493ffbc94c3b797afb274c3355db97.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-{x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-3{x}^{2}+8.$

We can now set up the integration with our $x$ values (Top-Bottom):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}[(-3{x}^{2}+8)-(-{x}^{2})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(-2{x}^{2}+8)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(8-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the integrand is an even function. Therefore, we can find the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(8-2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{(8x-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2((8\cdot 2-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {2}^{3})-0) \\  & =2((16-\frac{16}{3})-(0)) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{32}{3} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594229 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "155ba72f-3d7d-58c5-993f-1188c36455e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186593429} {:answer/id #uuid "30e28dec-fa23-5b7f-9951-fee0e5844de3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186593492} {:answer/id #uuid "3920bbbd-260b-58f8-936a-7e75927e44a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186593506} {:answer/id #uuid "7b592af0-5c74-5889-89a9-b3b159179d4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186593668} {:answer/id #uuid "bb54513e-d2d5-58b8-9412-15eed13734e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186593824}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186593668} :answer-field/id #uuid "5efc2d6a-f8ad-5667-a1ec-f91f444b3514" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594045}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "df202318-e036-5725-91a7-7b2e2e6925e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-143624" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

Find $P(X<Y\,|\,X=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}2x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2x{[{e}^{y}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =2x(2-1) \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}2x, & \,0\le x\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x<1,0<y<\operatorname{ln}⁡2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{2x{e}^{y}}{2x} \\  & ={e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{y}, & \,0\le y\le \operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<Y\,|\,X=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)) & =P(\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)<Y\,|\,X=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)) \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3/2)}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{3}{2}\right))\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3/2)}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[{e}^{y}]}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3/2)}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =2-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594230 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4d57b1cf-d3b7-5da1-89c4-f9501f1a7cb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186593566} {:answer/id #uuid "98a6ad83-ecbb-5f68-ba08-bb51e4628c46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186593747} {:answer/id #uuid "d28660bc-6d6f-5816-b552-7f46d7d94a5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186593881} {:answer/id #uuid "db55f3cd-f4b8-522b-8930-8d57f33c98d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186593900} {:answer/id #uuid "f5c2e299-0228-5280-a864-9361955e6168" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186593960}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186593747} :answer-field/id #uuid "64d03211-62fe-50b0-9936-aa855c4f425f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594051}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e2b4a8e1-c944-5e20-92a2-94a43bdb1ad4" :question/math-academy-id "q-3282" :question/problem "Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=-{x}^{2}-2$ and $y=-x-2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a sketch:

![](images/af/af2b16006d5616854a3fb4e5f116c84375ee78f633ab8f313045b3d6feed922b.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-2 & =-x-2 \\ x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(1-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, we draw our vertical arrow.

![](images/bf/bf320ce6791c3f776961fee7fe3b7714895a3f5e38d8d721fd653ee816eb8997.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-{x}^{2}-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(-{x}^{2}-2)-(-x-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-(0-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594232 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19d95be1-9570-5a00-a102-d264aff4e1f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.16" :db/id 17592186593437} {:answer/id #uuid "49bac261-ae12-51ff-8c42-c331e9bce4e3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.08" :db/id 17592186593557} {:answer/id #uuid "4e357132-43b8-5ae7-994c-39c13a13ac57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.18" :db/id 17592186593569} {:answer/id #uuid "82ac5fe2-3210-5b78-abfa-235c935b281e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.05" :db/id 17592186593689} {:answer/id #uuid "d6eaf161-1e68-52ab-b429-22846c9e03fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.12" :db/id 17592186593886}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186593557} :answer-field/id #uuid "e21b54d5-b641-576f-92cf-bde2d4c9f57c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594122}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e8e3e751-672b-5965-af1d-da39efcbadf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-148334" :question/problem "$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{xy+2}{4}, & \,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{12},\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{2},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.5713,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2887,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{xy+2}{4}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+2xy)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{2}-(-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}-\left(\frac{1}{12}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{72}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{\left(\frac{1}{72}\right)}{(0.5713)\cdot (0.2887)} \\  & ≈0.08,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186594666 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15bedf42-500c-5d31-98ef-11aabeb84ecb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186594352} {:answer/id #uuid "163cb5b9-258a-55ec-a48d-1740a57fe3d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186594355} {:answer/id #uuid "34982957-8991-5ada-afbf-4bb14c1fc6aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186594390} {:answer/id #uuid "3850e612-5788-50a9-aeca-761190a8adc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186594392} {:answer/id #uuid "7b65c4c6-a765-5968-9445-a882c1b19c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186594450}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594352} :answer-field/id #uuid "243999a8-f876-5beb-a8d9-97210f156149" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594601}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "06cd2c17-5f93-59e3-9ff6-6f3aecce2789" :question/math-academy-id "q-163718" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(kx+6)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=19\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f7/f7468aaa11c79f4306b67a558f09cbf5d8a6a480b726e883ecb373d7e5660e37.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(kx+6)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=kx+6.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=kx+6.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (kx+6)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=3\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(3)^{2} & =\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+6(0)+C \\ C & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=19\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(19)^{2} & =\frac{k(8)^{2}}{2}+6(8)+\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{361}{2} & =32k+48+\frac{9}{2} \\ 32k & =128 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594668 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14d4efc6-1069-5ea5-842f-8aaa08f4905e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi" :db/id 17592186594350} {:answer/id #uuid "8b675762-96e4-5e45-acf0-873b4018a5ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186594466} {:answer/id #uuid "b317f905-88f2-5087-bb2a-9f1719e2d250" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi" :db/id 17592186594508} {:answer/id #uuid "ea55f8fb-e8fd-5801-a571-a15b6b722358" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186594564} {:answer/id #uuid "f6e3c304-5647-510a-9b1f-410ce164475b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\pi" :db/id 17592186594583}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594350} :answer-field/id #uuid "5fbecdde-2e50-536d-babb-3eba966fe9ad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0dddc257-8e4b-5d9e-b703-54f233755f53" :question/math-academy-id "q-270035" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x+3}}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+3 & =-({x}^{2}-2x)+3 \\  & =-(({x}^{2}-2x+1)-1)+3 \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-1)+3 \\  & =-(x-1)^{2}+1+3 \\  & =4-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x+3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4-(x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4(1-(x-1)^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}/{2}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\frac{x-1}{2}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-1}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $1-\sqrt{3}$ | $1+\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \\  & =3(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{3}-\left(-\frac{\pi }{3}\right)) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594672 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03a2eeba-f28e-536b-b290-066300996d55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186594328} {:answer/id #uuid "0b7d8e35-bcbc-52c3-9780-4732e1864288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186594340} {:answer/id #uuid "0d656c57-fe6b-5eed-ad68-465993932c90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186594342} {:answer/id #uuid "1a264f60-73e9-5141-9087-5cfd2afe6c8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186594359} {:answer/id #uuid "ff414909-e846-589d-9b38-9a7fe70d3155" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186594591}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594342} :answer-field/id #uuid "404ff207-fd2a-5284-8365-d866034ea19e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594611}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1e79b675-9899-5259-931d-6dbe4181e60e" :question/math-academy-id "q-19535" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-4x+5}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+5 \\  & =({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})-4+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{{x}^{2}-4x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{(x-2)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1+(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x-2).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x-2.
$$

 
Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-4x+5}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{1+(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594676 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "413a002a-8100-58c9-bdac-c2440be8faf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/id 17592186594399} {:answer/id #uuid "5f17eb07-5929-57f0-aac6-50630f205ee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186594420} {:answer/id #uuid "60ba7ab8-7455-56ab-99a2-a8ffe6a17c8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡2t" :db/id 17592186594423} {:answer/id #uuid "ad6a611c-4af8-5747-affb-fff4cfb6491f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+4" :db/id 17592186594500} {:answer/id #uuid "f95b3be6-8e85-577e-9a77-93080195c8de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186594585}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594585} :answer-field/id #uuid "97d8e07d-45e3-5b07-a1ed-e9752aae1672" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594634}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "35457bb4-6eb5-506c-9c51-27a24ab5dc36" :question/math-academy-id "q-97598" :question/problem "The velocity $v$ of a particle $P$ at time $t$ is given by $v(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.$ Find the tangential component of acceleration at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The tangential component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{T}=\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||}.
$$

First, we need to compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $v\cdot a$ and $||v||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot a & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+0-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\  & =0, \\ ||v|| & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡t+{\cos }^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate tangential component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{T} & =\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$

Then, we compute $v\cdot a$ and $||v||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot a & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,2t,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,2,\,0⟩ \\  & =4t \\ ||v|| & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the tangential component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{T} & =\frac{v\cdot a}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{4t}{2\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594689 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "000715b4-4e9b-5f55-9ffe-d5a03979374a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}" :db/id 17592186594321} {:answer/id #uuid "25db432e-c6ac-5c1f-b3c7-4442d46b6f87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}" :db/id 17592186594371} {:answer/id #uuid "2c387be7-dc4a-560a-b58a-e173ad73b288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}" :db/id 17592186594382} {:answer/id #uuid "b2f41758-ee67-52ba-8694-0d05ce583199" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}" :db/id 17592186594507} {:answer/id #uuid "c8da94e9-1cff-534b-99dd-98f97d59185d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2{t}^{2}+1}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}" :db/id 17592186594531}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594382} :answer-field/id #uuid "4581a264-14ca-5c5e-b725-2a89cf3b9afc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6bf098fc-85c7-58f3-8383-c1caaa211b73" :question/math-academy-id "q-97609" :question/problem "The velocity $v$ of a particle $P$ at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)=⟨0,\,t,\,2{t}^{2}⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}.

First, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $v\times a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\times a & =⟨0,\,t,\,2{t}^{2}⟩\times ⟨0,\,1,\,4t⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & t & 2{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 4t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}t & 2{t}^{2} \\ 1 & 4t\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2{t}^{2} \\ 0 & 4t\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}0 & t \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2},0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $||v||$ and $||v\times a||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|| & =\sqrt{{(0)}^{2}+{(t)}^{2}+{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}, \\  & =t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}, \\ ||v\times a|| & =\sqrt{{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =2{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{2{t}^{2}}{t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\frac{2t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}.\end{aligned}

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}7({x}^{2}-4x+\frac{18}{7}) &= 7((x-2)^{2}-\frac{10}{7}) \\ &= 7(x-2)^{2}-10\end{aligned}
$$

When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(2x-\frac{1}{2})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest." :question/worked-solution "![](images/60/6046ef89f9abcc78be695d69df64471fb9c68645473c946e7f3212be27e2c6fb.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x-\frac{1}{2})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(1)+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =0 \\ x & =0\,m,\,\frac{1}{2}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594709 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "205ab221-682a-51be-a0ba-f61f8323ffb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi" :db/id 17592186594365} {:answer/id #uuid "243baa4c-bf11-5c48-ada7-bff57f3a07d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi" :db/id 17592186594369} {:answer/id #uuid "4c5c7053-4118-5861-aa31-7afcc22d8274" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\pi" :db/id 17592186594405} {:answer/id #uuid "5f8b106f-0eb3-5c53-8273-4f22e0eb0e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186594421} {:answer/id #uuid "eaa25260-c2fc-560b-ae7e-3be5546febd5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186594565}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594405} :answer-field/id #uuid "762f38fc-6bc2-5470-9574-50be6bafa6c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594626}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "adafea93-529f-54c5-8424-4a2b9bb98a17" :question/math-academy-id "q-270402" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\sqrt{2}-5}^{-3}\frac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+10x+24}}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+10x+24 & ={x}^{2}+10x+({5}^{2}-{5}^{2})+24 \\  & =({x}^{2}+10x+25)-25+24 \\  & =(x+5)^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
{\int }_{\sqrt{2}-5}^{-3}\frac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+10x+24}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{\sqrt{2}-5}^{-3}\frac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{(x+5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec} \,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+5.$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+5.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $\sqrt{2}-5$ | $-3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\sqrt{2}$ | $2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{2}-5}^{-3}\frac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+10x+24}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}-5}^{-3}\frac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{(x+5)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{2}\frac{60}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =60\operatorname{arcsec} u\,{|}_{\sqrt{2}}^{2} \\  & =60(\operatorname{arcsec} (2)-\operatorname{arcsec} (\sqrt{2})) \\  & =60(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =5\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594711 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0485e8d0-a745-5f4a-b09f-9737ad49c56e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{t+1}" :db/id 17592186594331} {:answer/id #uuid "264e13af-97ae-55dd-8289-e0383bf64f3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{2t}}" :db/id 17592186594373} {:answer/id #uuid "6b5631a0-edf7-5221-bb33-f425edc19c28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{t+1}" :db/id 17592186594431} {:answer/id #uuid "c9abd531-1a5e-5993-8e8a-4187ee480a69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{(t+1)\sqrt{2t}}" :db/id 17592186594533} {:answer/id #uuid "e2e0e542-bd18-5dd9-a4b9-ae8116808bdb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}" :db/id 17592186594557}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594557} :answer-field/id #uuid "3680e0fe-3e48-5354-949b-d2de364c059f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594610}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bed5f6a1-cd6e-5de8-8764-b26c3222a9a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-97611" :question/problem "The velocity $v$ of a particle $P$ at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)=⟨t,\,1,\,\sqrt{2t}⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$
{a}_{N}=\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||}.
$$

First, we compute the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $v\times a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v\times a & =⟨t,\,1,\,\sqrt{2t}⟩\times ⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ t & 1 & \sqrt{2t} \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}1 & \sqrt{2t} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}t & \sqrt{2t} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}t & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}},\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{2},-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $||v||$ and $||v\times a||:$

$$
\begin{aligned}||v|| & =\sqrt{{(t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}+2t+1}, \\  & =\sqrt{(t+1)^{2}} \\  & =t+1, \\ ||v\times a|| & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{2}\right)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{t}{2}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{t}^{2}+2t+1}{2t}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{(t+1)^{2}}{2t}} \\  & =\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the normal component of the acceleration, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =\frac{||v\times a||}{||v||} \\  & =\frac{\left(\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{2t}}\right)}{t+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594712 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "be13d1c4-9722-5dac-995e-663749d5b3dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186594519}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594519} :answer-field/id #uuid "473dd54d-1c1f-5af4-97ff-2f6c09d536ba" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186594613}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c7e7cd1c-1892-56d3-9d86-82cd2a91c9cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-351587" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We break up the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the second of these integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36x}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=2+3{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=6x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{36x}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{6}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{3}{{u}^{2}}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36x}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{36x}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }({-\frac{3}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{2}}|}_{0}^{a}\,) \\  & =\lim_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{3}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{2}}+\frac{3}{(2+0)^{2}}) \\  & =-0+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{36|x|}{{(2+3{x}^{2})}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186594716 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "002a5abe-2feb-5869-a269-6a01eb2e0339" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t(t+16)}}" :db/id 17592186594323} {:answer/id #uuid "aa993937-7369-53c3-94a3-297dcd25611f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{t+1}{\sqrt{t+16}}" :db/id 17592186594494} {:answer/id #uuid "bb022cbe-0966-590b-aaa6-d0049a965270" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{t(t+16)}}" :db/id 17592186594516} {:answer/id #uuid "d4a43e08-f7ae-59d4-bb36-87ab6f9cc1d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{t(t+4)}}" :db/id 17592186594545} {:answer/id #uuid "f9ca3d17-aaba-5c32-9bd1-664683912cc0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{\sqrt{t+4}}" :db/id 17592186594587}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594516} :answer-field/id #uuid "009097c8-12c8-50ab-b9ed-4c6c719ed771" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186594593}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "dc6fd842-fe55-508e-aada-2552005bd218" :question/math-academy-id "q-97613" :question/problem "The position $r$ of a particle $P$ at time $t>0$ is given by $r(t)=⟨\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}},\,4t,\,-7⟩.$ Find the normal component of the acceleration of $P$ at time $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The normal component of acceleration is given by

$$

$$

where $y\in [0,2].$

$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186595956 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0328fa56-6dc7-5a0d-a620-487fcd4a5f85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186594831} {:answer/id #uuid "2f8b97b1-418a-51ce-97ff-26abae6632b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186594974} {:answer/id #uuid "31eb95cc-bec1-5cdc-b4e3-63ed14ac135b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{23}{2}" :db/id 17592186594980} {:answer/id #uuid "6f4c3ec1-1584-5ce5-8c26-567662c5b608" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{19}{2}" :db/id 17592186595191} {:answer/id #uuid "dad12ae8-0046-5c82-80bb-14c6abf1e049" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{25}{2}" :db/id 17592186595554}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594980} :answer-field/id #uuid "98247a3d-d7b0-50a9-be13-f3fba5af01c1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186595816}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7a7d26a1-5910-53f8-991b-b91af1493d53" :question/math-academy-id "q-85723" :question/problem "Using the trapezoidal rule with the partition

we conclude that $⟨1,-4⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(16,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186595962 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08911307-498e-557d-b69f-4c4a6f366299" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186594845} {:answer/id #uuid "7434c3a2-d090-54c9-93bb-ac56038eccc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186595204} {:answer/id #uuid "8bcbbcb1-4f96-5529-81f1-009860e973c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186595291} {:answer/id #uuid "981c7d7f-752a-5f9e-8826-61c574abd52f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186595349} {:answer/id #uuid "bd68ecf2-51d1-5121-88f9-adc4454785ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186595463}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186595204} :answer-field/id #uuid "63b1a33b-ccee-5108-91bf-b5da0f45bda8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186595777}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8043a273-a319-5370-970a-271d28c684d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-143585" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 3, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{3}{2},$ find $\text{E}[2Y-4X].$" :question/worked-solution "We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[{x}^{2}y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =3{x}^{2}-0 \\  & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3(\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[2Y-4X] & =2\,\text{E}[Y]+(-4)\,\text{E}[X] \\  & =2\,\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)-4\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186595965 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02255f96-c42e-578e-870b-69261aa70626" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements is true" :db/id 17592186594826} {:answer/id #uuid "34fafad2-ce97-573c-80a7-f2d04ffcdef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186594989} {:answer/id #uuid "402ea738-302d-5168-943e-cad9a0496ac7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186595024} {:answer/id #uuid "96c72117-5d39-5c9e-8f0c-8df2fa7bba89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186595343} {:answer/id #uuid "f8730e27-4bfa-52b8-8dfc-6113e4acf205" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186595653}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186594826} :answer-field/id #uuid "a5e7d411-235f-5db3-8199-89400f7730ae" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186595838}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "90221e5f-e86e-53c2-ae31-0642a68abcc4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143388" :question/problem "The joint probability density function for the continuous random variables  $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2},\, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{X}(x)=\frac{3}{2}x+1$ for $y\in [0,1]$

II. $f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent" :question/worked-solution "Two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability density functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the marginal density function for $X,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[xy+\frac{{y}^{3}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

 
where $x\in [0,1].$

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=4,$ $b=7,$ and $c=9.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(7,4)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7 & = & 4\cdot 1 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 4 & = & 3\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =7-4\cdot 1 \\ 1 & =4-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4-3 \\  & =4-(7-4) \\  & =4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1) & =1 \\ 4\cdot 2\cdot 9+7\cdot (-1)\cdot 9 & =9 \\ 4\cdot 18+7\cdot (-9) & =9,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(18,-9)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(18+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-9-\frac{a}{d}t)=(18+7t,\,-9-4t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=18+7t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=18+7\cdot (-2)=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186596630 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2a4f14f4-2961-5de0-bbd5-b707f099d227" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4-3t,\,-1+7t)" :db/id 17592186596147} {:answer/id #uuid "38bff961-6acc-5feb-a263-15d90eb4be53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1+7t,\,-4-3t)" :db/id 17592186596173} {:answer/id #uuid "a04b7049-aa05-57ec-9a32-b5a66f92b885" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4+7t,\,1+3t)" :db/id 17592186596332} {:answer/id #uuid "b2372766-5566-5178-9d56-e9d0cb60e30c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4+7t,\,-1-3t)" :db/id 17592186596364} {:answer/id #uuid "e227af2b-0f16-516f-a7e6-1872488820da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1+7t,\,4-3t)" :db/id 17592186596443}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596364} :answer-field/id #uuid "2fe7828e-520f-5f36-8a1c-188bd97ae386" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186596521}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0faa73a9-441f-53be-94fe-c5df5f2bad0f" :question/math-academy-id "q-93803" :question/problem "Given that $(x,y)=(4,-1)$ is a solution of the Diophantine equation $3x+7y=5,$ which of the following gives the general solution to the equation? 

*Hint: Assume that $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$*" :question/worked-solution "First, recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d\,|\,c,$ where $d=\text{gcd}(a,b).$ Moreover, if $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ is a solution to the equation, then the general solution is given by

$$
({x}_{0}+\frac{b}{d}t,\,{y}_{0}-\frac{a}{d}t),\,t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…
$$

Here, we have $a=3,$ $b=7,$ $c=5,$ and

$$
d=\text{gcd}(3,7)=1.
$$

 

Since $(4,-1)$ is a solution of $3x+7y=5,$ the general solution must be

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\frac{7}{1}t,\,-1-\frac{3}{1}t) & =(4+7t,\,-1-3t),\end{aligned}
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$"} {:db/id 17592186596633 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "36a64f4d-cfe5-5c75-9f6b-00b5ecb2e42c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "25" :db/id 17592186596168}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596168} :answer-field/id #uuid "80b89f71-3055-559f-a5d8-baf9f348bf3f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186596555}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1c078e29-f3c7-58f3-b586-861487b886b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-315933" :question/problem "![](images/f1/f17ce467f5bff34f0c04326d1a23ca8621f459571be8c98a745174a3d5587337.png)

Consider all possible circular sectors $MON$ with perimeter $P=100$ units. Determine the radius $r$ of the circular sector with the largest possible area. Do not round the answer.

$r=$
{{field-1}} units" :question/worked-solution "First,  let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta$ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $100$ units, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
100=2r+r\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{100-2r}{r}=\frac{100}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{100}{r}-2) \\  & =50r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=50-2r.
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 50-2r & =0 \\ -2r & =-50 \\ r & =\frac{(-50)}{(-2)} \\ r & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=25$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(25)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(25)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=25$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$"} {:db/id 17592186596634 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "201eb658-3ad1-5ea8-8cc8-fa568f2d5db0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186596128} {:answer/id #uuid "26f17310-0edb-542f-916a-8c57da6aec73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186596140} {:answer/id #uuid "8085731e-64f5-5a67-a628-aa2d60ad8f6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186596284} {:answer/id #uuid "9a391520-7d49-5800-bbea-aacce057f946" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186596322} {:answer/id #uuid "ef7b530f-5600-5b8d-a048-83ae369570a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186596461}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596128} :answer-field/id #uuid "c9588bb5-0c01-5ed6-9e22-37dd66972473" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186596594}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1e52f529-60e9-51eb-91ee-90ffeab28c47" :question/math-academy-id "q-48810" :question/problem "Given that $r=-2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta$ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that$\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3$ at the point where $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},$ find $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$" :question/worked-solution "Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(-2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (2{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=3$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot 2{\csc }^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 3 & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (2{\csc }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)) \\ 3 & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (2\cdot 4) \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186596637 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9ec7e5f6-9981-5cc4-bb8a-602cd53b0054" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4.08" :db/id 17592186596328}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596328} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1aeef83-2b6a-54f6-859a-fd3983f89cc4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186596609}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "26a24488-f2a7-5cba-b390-bc6f9aa0a1ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-342059" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the given interval is symmetric about the mean:

$$

So, we find the cumulative probability using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X<5) & =0.3758 \\ 2P(3<X<5) & =0.3758 \\ P(3<X<5) & =0.1879 \\ P(X<5)-P(X<3) & =0.1879 \\ P(X<5)-0.5 & =0.1879 \\ P(X<5) & =0.6879 \\ P(X\le 5) & =0.6879\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 5) & =0.6879 \\ P(Z\le \frac{5-3}{\sigma }) & =0.6879 \\ Φ\left(\frac{2}{\sigma }\right) & =0.6879 \\ \frac{2}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.6879)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.49)=0.6879\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(0.6879)=0.49.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sigma } & =0.49 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{2}{0.49} \\ \sigma  & ≈4.08\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186596639 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a05486e8-dbd1-582f-8aa3-ed6c0b7c745c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186596333}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596333} :answer-field/id #uuid "124878d3-32be-5de0-a602-acffbe31b445" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186596501}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "28d4018d-5112-5682-81ff-aad93ccb004c" :question/math-academy-id "q-342032" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. III. The probability of getting $32$ odd numbers on $80$ rolls of a $6$-sided die." :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if

$$

The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-5,-2].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,0]\,.$ The corresponding region is a quarter circle. In part 1, we found the area of the circle as $A=4\pi .$ So we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{4}A \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4\pi  \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,\frac{5}{2}]\,.$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [\frac{5}{2},5]\,.$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, we obtain

What is the largest possible area $A$ of the circular sectors?" :question/worked-solution "First,  let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta$ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $1$ unit, so we also have the constraint condition

$$
1=2r+r\theta .
$$

Now, by making $\theta$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{1-2r}{r}=\frac{1}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{1}{r}-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=\frac{1}{2}-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}-2r & =0 \\ r & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we confirm that $r=\frac{1}{4}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=\frac{1}{4}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

Therefore, the circular sector of the largest area will have a radius of $\frac{1}{4}$, and the area is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)-{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}

$\text{cm}$" :question/worked-solution "First,  let $r$ be the radius of the circular sector and let $\theta$ be the angle (in radians) subtended by it. We want to maximize the area

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\theta .
$$

We know that the perimeter is fixed at $40\,\text{cm},$ so we also have the constraint condition

$$
40=2r+\theta r.
$$

Now, by making $\theta$ the subject of the constraint equation, we find that 

$$
\theta =\frac{40-2r}{r}=\frac{40}{r}-2.
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $A,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A(r) & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}(\frac{40}{r}-2) \\  & =20r-{r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $A,$ so we need to differentiate $A$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{A}^{′}(r)=20-2r.
$$

Setting ${A}^{′}(r)=0$ and solving for $r$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ 20-2r & =0 \\ -2r & =-20 \\ r & =\frac{(-20)}{(-2)} \\ r & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we confirm that $r=10$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative gives

$$
{A}^{″}(r)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(10)=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(10)$ is negative, we conclude that $r=10$ is indeed a maximum of $A(r).$

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=3,$ $b=11,$ and $c=7.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(3,11)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}11 & = & 3\cdot 3 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 3 & = & 2\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =11-9 \\ 1 & =3-2\cdot 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3-2\cdot 1 \\  & =3-(11-9) \\  & =3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1) & =1 \\ 3\cdot 4\cdot 7+11\cdot (-1)\cdot 7 & =7 \\ 3\cdot 28+11\cdot (-7) & =7,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(28,-7)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(28+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-7-\frac{a}{d}t)=(28+11t,\,-7-3t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=28+11t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=28+11\cdot (-2)=6.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186596684 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d315f58e-2f3c-560f-9f1f-77c594742661" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186596413}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596413} :answer-field/id #uuid "d61f42b3-d6ef-58c4-a94a-44eacfecef19" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186596604}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9979f237-ee91-5238-852f-85e56821efe9" :question/math-academy-id "q-342717" :question/problem "Given that $r=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta$ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $$

I. $f:R\to (0,\infty )$ defined by $f(x)={2}^{2x}$

II. $g:Q\to [0,\infty )$ defined by $g(x)=|x|$

III. $h:R\to R$ defined by $h(x)={x}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $f:X\to Y$ is an *into* function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element $y$ in $Y$ such that it has no preimage in $X:$ 

$f:X\to Y$ is an into function if $∃\,y\in Y$ such that $∀\,x\in X,$ we have $f(x)\ne y.$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- I is a *not* an into function. Given $y\in (0,\infty ),$ we can choose $x=\frac{1}{2}{\log }_{2}⁡y\in R.$ Then $f(x)=f(\frac{1}{2}{\log }_{2}⁡y)={2}^{2\cdot (1/2{\log }_{2}⁡y)}=y.$

- II is an into function. Let's take $\pi \in [0,\infty ).$ There is no number $x\in R$ such that $g(x)=|x|=\pi .$ The only numbers $x$ that satisfy $g(x)=\pi$ are $x=\pm \pi \notin Q.$

- III is an into function. Let's take $-1\in R.$ There is no number $x\in R$ such that $h(x)={x}^{2}=-1.$ In fact, ${x}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186596721 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ed33379-581c-52f0-9c68-71db43a87877" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.652" :db/id 17592186596126} {:answer/id #uuid "412f7a21-838e-5e1d-9c4d-679ab3b73a11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.658" :db/id 17592186596180} {:answer/id #uuid "b8d69d51-75c1-5b78-b36b-480a9f3cfda6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.661" :db/id 17592186596375} {:answer/id #uuid "d1303863-3a0f-5673-8d1d-da33511d9075" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.647" :db/id 17592186596408} {:answer/id #uuid "eaebb62b-9ab4-5ced-a11f-e6b3f8ba0fee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.640" :db/id 17592186596454}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186596180} :answer-field/id #uuid "b635de3e-28b0-5dd2-b1ec-d2321f32af9b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186596585}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f83f881a-350e-522d-9065-97acb85f3320" :question/math-academy-id "q-95811" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼B(90,0.47),$ use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(40\le X<50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=90$ and $p=0.47.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =90\cdot 0.47 \\  & =42.3 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =90\cdot (1-0.47) \\  & =47.7 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(90)(0.47)=42.3
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(90)(0.47)(1-0.47)=22.419.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(42.3,22.419).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(40\le X<50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(40\le X<50)=P(40\le X\le 49)≈P(39.5\le Y\le 49.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(39.5\le Y\le 49.5) & =P(\frac{39.5-42.3}{\sqrt{22.419}}\le Z\le \frac{49.5-42.3}{\sqrt{22.419}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.59\le Z\le 1.52) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.52)-P(Z<-0.59) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.52)-P(Z\le -0.59) \\  & =Φ(1.52)-Φ(-0.59) \\  & =0.9357-0.2776 \\  & =0.6581\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(40\le X<50)≈0.658.
$$
