$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/x}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le \frac{1}{x}\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{0}^{1/x}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/a0/a0511ac8febd79f7f061b2c62d995d540778cee2697ea1063b0a708aa7e99c60.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,{y}^{2}\le x\le 4\}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x={y}^{2}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt{x}
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/b4/b4440e26c1b1805c47632f66806a096a61cbfe2d2ebd93a7f7de3daef8b65efb.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{1/x}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}{\int }_{0}^{1/x}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x[{\int }_{0}^{1/x}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x[\sqrt{z}]_{0}^{1/x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{x}}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{x}}[y]_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{4} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(4).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186603057 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0994fa7b-0cfc-550e-8939-1590b16106f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(2)=⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡2,5⟩" :db/id 17592186602580} {:answer/id #uuid "2639d9ae-e9ed-5429-85af-d3236abf5259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(2)=⟨-3\operatorname{ln}⁡2,5⟩" :db/id 17592186602611} {:answer/id #uuid "55afb591-2c0d-5bbc-a694-796ff282f1a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(2)=⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡2,5⟩" :db/id 17592186602665} {:answer/id #uuid "c782714f-02e3-5a21-9317-634ee36284a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(2)=⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186602799} {:answer/id #uuid "da3831d5-3efb-592b-90ce-6931af387917" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v(2)=⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡2,-2⟩" :db/id 17592186602831}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602580} :answer-field/id #uuid "58d08f18-c4e4-5f2d-ab2c-2757ebbfb775" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186602911}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "992ae7f7-bb75-5135-9444-8d03cdff6a63" :question/math-academy-id "q-122091" :question/problem "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨5+6t,\,12{t}^{2}⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨7-6t,\,9-12{t}^{2}⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨2,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=2\,\text{s}.$ Do not round the answer.

$\text{m/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨5+6t,\,12{t}^{2}⟩+⟨7-6t,\,9-12{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨12,\,9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot ⟨12,\,9⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,\frac{9}{4}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3,\,\frac{9}{4}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{9}{4}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3t,\,\frac{9}{4}t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨2,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2,\,-1⟩ & =⟨3(0),\,\frac{9}{4}(0)⟩+C \\ ⟨2,\,-1⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨2,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨3t,\,\frac{9}{4}t⟩+⟨2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+2,\,\frac{9}{4}t-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨3(2)+2,\,\frac{9}{4}(2)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,\frac{7}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=2$ equals the magnitude of $v(2).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{305}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of $P$ when $t=2\,\text{s}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{305}}{2}\,\text{m/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186603068 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23a4745c-f4d5-5423-8815-d3166784fd06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7795" :db/id 17592186602609} {:answer/id #uuid "4f08de0b-b070-55e7-b11d-796d309234ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8051" :db/id 17592186602655} {:answer/id #uuid "6ab35dad-9e76-58e8-9bc1-56cdfa72c695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7570" :db/id 17592186602683} {:answer/id #uuid "8aca128a-e192-57fb-9343-caecd6214940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7250" :db/id 17592186602720} {:answer/id #uuid "936ae1a6-c9cc-5387-acd8-2fd8253b01c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8301" :db/id 17592186602733}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602609} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec67cbac-f309-57db-ae09-9f56e2e2bdb1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186602979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "b12e550d-4e84-5838-8bf0-fa3203351fef" :question/math-academy-id "q-159806" :question/problem "Let $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}]^{T}$ be a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $Σ$ given by

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{k}]^{T}$ is a multivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y={c}^{T}X={\sum }_{i=1}^{k}{c}_{i}{X}_{i}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable, where $c$ is any $k\times 1$ column vector, and  

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu , \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, since we wish to know the distribution of $Y=-{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}+2{X}_{3},$ we have 

$$
c=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, for the mean of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={c}^{T}\mu  \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =0+9+4 \\  & =13,\end{aligned}
$$

and for the variance of $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & ={c}^{T}Σc \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 14 \\ 15\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-5+42+30 \\  & =67.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
Y∼N(13,67).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(-3\le Y\le 20).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-3\le Y\le 20) & =P(\frac{-3-13}{\sqrt{67}}\le Z\le \frac{20-13}{\sqrt{67}}) \\  & =P(-1.95\le Z\le 0.86)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.95\le Z\le 0.86) & =P(Z\le 0.86)-P(Z<-1.95) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.86)-P(Z\le -1.95) \\  & =Φ(0.86)-Φ(-1.95).\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.86) & =0.8051 \\ Φ(-1.95) & =0.0256\end{aligned}
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.95\le Z\le 0.86) &=0.8051-0.0256=0.7795.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(-3\le Y\le 20)=0.7795.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186603069 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0234bb78-4595-5a2f-bce3-fb9f44381d99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v=⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-3,-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-1⟩" :db/id 17592186602569} {:answer/id #uuid "08cbda19-1226-57e9-b52b-47c5904ef063" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v=⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-3}{2},-\frac{{t}^{3}+1}{3}+2t⟩" :db/id 17592186602578} {:answer/id #uuid "5a5ef5db-b309-53f7-a8f5-9aa41d4846bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v=⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-1}{2},-\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+2t-1⟩" :db/id 17592186602669} {:answer/id #uuid "a18c7b97-d955-5a53-a630-4819e33d1795" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v=⟨\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{2},-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+1⟩" :db/id 17592186602753} {:answer/id #uuid "c2462297-1331-53b4-9fef-833a3b06a6fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "v=⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-1,-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+2t-1⟩" :db/id 17592186602789}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602669} :answer-field/id #uuid "46e11900-53ed-540a-a099-8bd23f11bb69" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186602902}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b42affb2-8753-5f67-bac4-a9747c357467" :question/math-academy-id "q-7203" :question/problem "The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

where ${F}_{1},$ ${F}_{2},$ and ${F}_{3}$ are measured in newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨-1,\,4⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{5}{2}\,\text{s}.$ Do not round the answer.

$\text{m/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2}+{F}_{3} \\  & =⟨6{e}^{t},\,9\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨12-6{e}^{t}+\frac{3}{t+1},\,-20-9\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩+⟨-\frac{3}{t+1},\,2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨12,\,-18⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot ⟨12,\,-18⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,\,-3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\,\int (-3)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-3t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨-1,\,4⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-1,\,4⟩ & =⟨2(0),\,-3(0)⟩+C \\ ⟨-1,\,4⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨-1,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨2t,\,-3t⟩+⟨-1,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-1,\,-3t+4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=\frac{5}{2},$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v\,\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) & =⟨2\cdot \frac{5}{2}-1,\,-3\cdot \frac{5}{2}+4⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,-\frac{7}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{5}{2}$ equals the magnitude of $v\,\left(\frac{5}{2}\right).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v\,\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{7}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{113}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{5}{2}\,\text{s}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{113}}{2}\,\text{m/s}.$"} {:db/id 17592186603077 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39a3dbc1-6414-5c90-a88d-56b315d5ffaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "72" :db/id 17592186602635} {:answer/id #uuid "6b4e0568-b726-5419-a340-951140bcf6d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "168" :db/id 17592186602684} {:answer/id #uuid "846da60f-a571-5045-a07f-638e8666beef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "218" :db/id 17592186602708} {:answer/id #uuid "c24a1631-a895-52c6-becf-4e7e4048c712" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "126" :db/id 17592186602790} {:answer/id #uuid "f6581a18-0a4f-575a-96a1-c912ea69f11d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{163}{617}" :db/id 17592186602859}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602635} :answer-field/id #uuid "8dfe7879-fc68-5fad-b707-390c861df16f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186602940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "c5e0cf04-9068-5eee-ab1f-b19d115da85a" :question/math-academy-id "q-3139" :question/problem "Calculate the area of the finite region bounded by the curves $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-2$ and $y=x+6.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's draw a sketch of the two functions.

![](images/29/29475d9d3180a9be4268981ee68e4104d0e13b126891ecae6003df606a4b8427.png)

*(Note: Figure not drawn to scale)*

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we equate the two functions and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-2 & =x+6 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-x-8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x-32 & =0 \\ (x+4)(x-8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=-4$ to $x=8.$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](images/be/bee2dff5d1357f67b448f0bbe29a78dc9fd297c65ad324200b5abc906ecebbc6.png)

The vertical line 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=x+6.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-4}^{8}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{8}[\,(x+6)-(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-2)\,]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-4}^{8}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(-\frac{1}{12}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+8x\text{ })|}_{-4}^{8} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{12}\cdot {8}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot {8}^{2}+8\cdot 8\text{ }]-[-\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-4)^{3}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-4)^{2}+8\cdot (-4)\text{ }] \\  & =(-\frac{128}{3}+32+64)-(\frac{16}{3}+8-32) \\  & =\frac{160}{3}-\left(-\frac{56}{3}\right) \\  & =72\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186603078 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "cccd4d9f-8093-535b-9601-cdd9f2c2c77f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "192" :db/id 17592186602811}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602811} :answer-field/id #uuid "d035fe7f-91e3-5aef-aaca-7e3695d6f774" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186602966} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9a4ea3bc-d919-5004-9003-da4f10ac5d6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186602741}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602741} :answer-field/id #uuid "f63d7153-7315-5b8f-b2da-a5d1ecf358f1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186602987}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c664f0d3-e342-5b2c-a69a-92fe85646f0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-352830" :question/problem "The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is given by

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{t}^{3/2}+{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sqrt{t}+2{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨12\sqrt{t}+2t,\,\frac{3}{2\sqrt{t}}+6{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12\sqrt{t}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{t}}+6{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{\sqrt{t}}+2,\,-\frac{3}{4{t}^{3/2}}+12t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =4\cdot ⟨\frac{6}{\sqrt{t}}+2,\,-\frac{3}{4{t}^{3/2}}+12t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{24}{\sqrt{t}}+8,\,-\frac{3}{{t}^{3/2}}+48t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5x-3}{2{x}^{3}+7} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5x}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{7}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(2+\frac{7}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{5}{{x}^{2}},$ $\frac{3}{{x}^{3}},$ and $\frac{7}{{x}^{3}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(2+\frac{7}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & \to \frac{0-0}{2+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186603084 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "89cc569d-b654-57eb-972c-9a38ebf66841" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5511" :db/id 17592186602717} {:answer/id #uuid "8eb3441f-b2ee-515a-ae2e-da4f7580182c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5821" :db/id 17592186602728} {:answer/id #uuid "d1bd966b-f91f-5bff-b23a-03b6d0618753" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5432" :db/id 17592186602816} {:answer/id #uuid "d9d92449-e43c-5afe-b110-47e2a79417c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5244" :db/id 17592186602830} {:answer/id #uuid "fac69929-0ba6-52e3-bf23-e44c953716be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5686" :db/id 17592186602869}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186602869} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3107c67-93ed-5983-a6e7-99e6dfbeaf84" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186602985}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f5725729-baf7-5cb3-bb25-5d68eb99c802" :question/math-academy-id "q-159779" :question/problem "Let $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ be a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $Σ$ given by

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X=[{X}_{1},{X}_{2}]^{T}$ is a bivariate normal random vector with mean vector $\mu$ and covariance matrix $Σ,$ given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu =\begin{bmatrix}{\mu }_{1} \\ {\mu }_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,Σ=\begin{bmatrix}{\sigma }_{1}^{2} & {\sigma }_{12} \\ {\sigma }_{21} & {\sigma }_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

then the random variable $Y,$ defined as

$$
Y=a{X}_{1}+b{X}_{2}
$$

is a normally distributed random variable for all values of $a$ and $b,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}E[Y] & =a{\mu }_{1}+b{\mu }_{2}, \\ \operatorname{Var} [Y] & ={a}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{b}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+2ab{\sigma }_{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have ${\mu }_{1}=1$ and ${\mu }_{2}=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[4{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}] \\  & =4\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}] \\  & =4\cdot {\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2} \\  & =4\cdot 1+(-1) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we have ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}=3,{\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ and ${\sigma }_{12}={\sigma }_{21}=-5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var} [Y] & =\operatorname{Var} [4{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}] \\  & ={4}^{2}(3)+{1}^{2}(9)+2(4)(1)(-5) \\  & =48+9-40 \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
Y∼N(3,17).
$$

Now, we need to compute $P(-5<Y<4).$ First, transform $Y$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-5<Y<4) & =P(\frac{-5-3}{\sqrt{17}}<Z<\frac{4-3}{\sqrt{17}}) \\  & =P(-1.94<Z<0.24)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.94<Z<0.24) & =P(Z<0.24)-P(Z\le -1.94) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.24)-P(Z\le -1.94) \\  & =Φ(0.24)-Φ(-1.94)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.94) & =0.0262 \\ Φ(0.24) & =0.5948\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.94<Z<0.24) & =Φ(0.24)-Φ(-1.94) \\  & =0.5948-0.0262 \\  & =0.5686.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(-5<Y<4)=0.5686.
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "20cf5bc3-cd4f-5de5-9e93-648009d7ab19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(\frac{x}{5}+2)" :db/id 17592186603328} {:answer/id #uuid Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=1]$ given that $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{Y|1}=2.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=x] & =\text{E}[(Y-{\mu }_{Y|x})^{2}\,|\,X=x] \\  & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}\,|\,X=x]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)]-{\mu }_{Y|x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ let's first find the marginal distribution for $X,$ corresponding to the row totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{3}{8}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x$ is

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding row total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x:$

| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $1$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $X=2$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y\,|\,X=1] & =[{\sum }_{y}{y}^{2}\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)]-{\mu }_{Y|1}^{2} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}]-{2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{9}{2}-4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604009 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e9954f6-c7ff-5b3d-8b0d-e0b2138afa03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{e^{2}+1}{2\ln(4)}" :db/id 17592186603576}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603576} :answer-field/id #uuid "f136e5e7-71b4-5a83-a935-90292d874cdb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603987}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1fa8ded2-a679-5843-82b8-454cd4b8e0ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-351044" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}{\log }_{4}⁡(2x+1)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}{\log }_{4}⁡(2x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={\log }_{4}⁡(2x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{2}{(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}{\log }_{4}⁡(2x+1)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}-{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & ={\log }_{4}⁡(2x+1)\,(x){|}_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}-{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}x\left(\frac{2}{(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{\log }_{4}⁡(2\cdot \frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}+1)\,\left(\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\right)-{\log }_{4}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)\,(0)]-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}\frac{2x}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}{\log }_{4}⁡({e}^{2})-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\int }_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2}(1-\frac{1}{2x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{[x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)]}_{0}^{({e}^{2}-1)/2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}(\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604017 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "61c84852-cb29-57a7-81e0-d7824abb54c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "49{x}^{2}-4=0" :db/id 17592186603468} {:answer/id #uuid "af3104e5-84b4-534a-a762-124a5b4c8906" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "49{x}^{2}+49=0" :db/id 17592186603647} {:answer/id #uuid "ba6b61a7-a1e0-56ee-be24-056ae881fc9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "49{x}^{2}+7=0" :db/id 17592186603676} {:answer/id #uuid "bdeec8be-3c74-57e0-9a11-9f08ba3cc543" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "49{x}^{2}+4=0" :db/id 17592186603683} {:answer/id #uuid "ce788dd2-5719-5c9d-9be8-c1069e2eb4e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "49{x}^{2}-7=0" :db/id 17592186603718}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603683} :answer-field/id #uuid "978d0f80-bbde-5c42-9df8-8d388c1f0e7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603924}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "34cedba2-6777-5f31-b931-f944c48ec485" :question/math-academy-id "q-8187" :question/problem "A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=\frac{2\text{i}}{7}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $49$, find the equation." :question/worked-solution "Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=\frac{2\text{i}}{7}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=-\frac{2\text{i}}{7}$ must also be a root.  Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\frac{2\text{i}}{7})(x+\frac{2\text{i}}{7})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{\left(\frac{2\text{i}}{7}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{4}{49}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{4}{49} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{2\text{i}}{7},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $49.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $49.$ This gives

\displaystyle \int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x.

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=3{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)\cdot ({x}^{3})-\int \frac{{x}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C \\  & ={x}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{3})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

1\. Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis

3\. Stretch it by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

1\. Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $5.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=5f(x).
$$

2\. Translating the graph of $y=5f(x)$ by $1$ unit to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x+1).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=5f(x+1).
$$

3\. Stretching the graph of $y=5f(x+1)$ by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{x}{2}.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=5f(\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+1)=5f(\frac{x}{2}+1).
$$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=5f(\frac{x}{2}+1).$"} {:db/id 17592186604032 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1820095f-60b7-5eac-b322-e6f0dbe0f9ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186603309} {:answer/id #uuid "202fda53-a226-55ad-a14e-376e667b865c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186603327} {:answer/id #uuid "5881e0bf-dce3-58f7-8cac-e3156f25b2c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186603440} {:answer/id #uuid "edd250f5-0136-592a-b122-835c4535143b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186603780} {:answer/id #uuid "ef071b53-a6ab-53a0-a16f-bdab406a6974" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186603783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603309} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a5639cb-ccfc-586b-9404-78aa8da6694a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603915}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "64d7c357-a2fa-5e33-8280-0844acf5bf34" :question/math-academy-id "q-3291" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x)=4x-{x}^{2}$ on the interval $[0,4].$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}\,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4-0}\,{\int }_{0}^{4}(4x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{4}(2{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(2\cdot {4}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {4}^{3})-(2\cdot {0}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {0}^{3})] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(32-\frac{64}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{32}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604035 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3aacebb9-3633-54ea-af39-bd631b9b4a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186603388} {:answer/id #uuid "5cb51142-55c6-5ab6-945a-e4bcac1789f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2})" :db/id 17592186603455} {:answer/id #uuid "793cab6b-d60c-51bb-bc07-9e76536448b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{5}{2},\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2})" :db/id 17592186603518} {:answer/id #uuid "8de8cbec-fb13-5919-a1f8-a4e5dbb178fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186603574} {:answer/id #uuid "b4b7bccc-f563-5698-b59d-624f9875ebba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-5\sqrt{2},-5\sqrt{2})" :db/id 17592186603657}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603388} :answer-field/id #uuid "9ac6b221-8661-5dcf-aa7d-9013f4a7262c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "704bcb07-f5a9-504f-b384-7134e574b668" :question/math-academy-id "q-86625" :question/problem "![](images/23/2345e527962c82c89c2689f17ee061ce2a6691ec58b21fff1890bed106ad5b5a.png)

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(5,\pi )$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{\pi }{3},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$" :question/worked-solution "First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(5,\pi ),$ we must have $r=5.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $5,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $5.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta$-coordinate of $A$ is $\pi ,$ the $\theta$-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\pi +\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(5,\frac{4\pi }{3})$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{4\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =5\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-\frac{5}{2},-\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186604039 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c65e6bc2-3761-5b12-ae83-3388ce6c968b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186603704}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603704} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f1fcb85-43bc-52f1-93f8-bcb8dfa6391d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603884} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "94d931df-160a-58ef-a618-ff5f0af3e76d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186603592}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603592} :answer-field/id #uuid "89016ea6-b384-552b-b73a-e2c3915350d8" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603912} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "85eff289-6b9f-5850-870c-14dcc50a03c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186603555}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603555} :answer-field/id #uuid "9732bba1-839a-5f2c-90bd-dac79b6343fa" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603923}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "76b087be-44e8-561b-b10c-dc8dd2a5a929" :question/math-academy-id "q-346931" :question/problem "Express $\frac{4x+4}{{x}^{2}(3x-2)}$ as a sum of partial fractions.

| $\frac{4x+4}{{x}^{2}(3x-2)}\,=-$ | {{field-1}} | $-$ | {{field-2}} | $+$ | {{field-3}} |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $x$ |  | ${x}^{2}$ |  | $3x-2$ |" :question/worked-solution "Our task is to find $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ such that

$$
\frac{4x+4}{{x}^{2}(3x-2)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{C}{3x-2}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by ${x}^{2}(3x-2)$ gives

$$
4x+4=Ax(3x-2)+B(3x-2)+C{x}^{2}.
$$

Letting $x=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)+4 & =A(0)(3(0)-2)+B(3(0)-2)+C(0)^{2} \\ 4 & =B(-2) \\ B & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Letting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+4 & =A\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)(3\cdot \frac{2}{3}-2)+B(3\cdot \frac{2}{3}-2)+C{\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)}^{2} \\ \frac{20}{3} & =C\left(\frac{4}{9}\right) \\ C & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, letting $x=1$ and using our values for $B$ and $C$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(1)+4 & =A(1)(3\cdot 1-2)+(-2)(3\cdot 1-2)+15(1)^{2} \\ 8 & =A+13 \\ A & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4x+4}{{x}^{2}(3x-2)}=-\,\frac{5}{x}-\,\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{15}{3x-2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604040 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6dbd6fb8-a608-5ad8-af39-5977277ec152" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16x^2-8x-1" :db/id 17592186603498}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603498} :answer-field/id #uuid "39a564ab-f844-583f-b0c6-d77971811273" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603858}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "77df9bac-1d12-5960-982e-e36e09c1804f" :question/math-academy-id "q-275107" :question/problem "The quadratic polynomial $P(x)$ has the double root ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{4},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=-16.$ Find $P(x).$

$P(x)=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since our quadratic polynomial has the double root ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{4},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=-16,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(x-{x}_{1})^{2} & =(-16){(x-\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right))}^{2} \\  & =-16{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-16{(x+\frac{1}{4})}^{2} & =-16({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =-16{x}^{2}-8x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-16{x}^{2}-8x-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186604048 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fe2997a-1d76-5ecd-a83c-f33b44b509d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186603290}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603290} :answer-field/id #uuid "52b882ba-7bfd-5d78-b1e9-611bf71f5e44" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603875} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a4e7434-68dd-5b06-814b-b625fce37ac5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186603386}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603386} :answer-field/id #uuid "86322074-c6c5-53af-b991-669e654761fd" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603910}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "88ed896e-de35-51be-8b01-2f69db5ceea4" :question/math-academy-id "q-275951" :question/problem "The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(\sqrt{2},\theta )$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $(2,\theta -\frac{\pi }{4}).$ Determine the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-1,1).$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{-1}\right)| \\  & =|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =|-\frac{\pi }{4}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $A$ lies in the second quadrant, we have $\theta =\pi -{\theta }_{R}=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
(2,\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4})=(2,\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(0,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186604050 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "212bb511-94cf-517e-8c96-ba0949dbd528" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 7\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186603329} {:answer/id #uuid "3c4e2956-0adc-5c53-af7f-852b2c487f6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -3 \\ -3 & 11\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186603393} {:answer/id #uuid "435d9fe5-0e11-50a0-9a75-7a33a80b89d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186603410} {:answer/id #uuid "7b6681f6-ec96-541d-be6f-207951bc7eb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}16 & 0 \\ 0 & 16\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186603524} {:answer/id #uuid "f5633845-e12b-58f5-a075-5a575a857a4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}11 & 1 \\ 1 & 11\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186603793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603793} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca0790ab-3e5a-5301-b758-d4d7d246c005" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603963}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8bc45430-5302-5257-b100-4fa937047053" :question/math-academy-id "q-159412" :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y,\, & 1\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{19}{12},$  $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{5}{12},$ and $\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]=\frac{1}{4},$ find the covariance matrix for $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "For two random variables $X$ and $Y,$ the covariance matrix $Σ$ is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Recall that the variance of a random variable $X$ is determined by the formula

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2},
$$

and the covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

First, we find $\text{Var}[X].$
We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]$ using the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}y)\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{15}{4}-\frac{7}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{15}{4}y-\frac{7}{6}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{31}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{31}{12}-{\left(\frac{19}{12}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we compute $\text{Var}[Y].$ Using the given results, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-\text{E}[Y]^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-{\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{11}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's find $\text{Cov}[X,Y].$ By the rule of the lazy statistician, we find $\text{E}[XY]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}xy\cdot f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}xy(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}({x}^{2}y-x{y}^{2})\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{7}{3}y-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{7}{6}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-\left(\frac{19}{12}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{5}{12}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{144}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the covariance matrix is given by

$$
Σ=\begin{bmatrix}\text{Var}[X] & \text{Cov}[X,Y] \\ \text{Cov}[Y,X] & \text{Var}[Y]\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{11}{144} & \frac{1}{144} \\ \frac{1}{144} & \frac{11}{144}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{144}\begin{bmatrix}11 & 1 \\ 1 & 11\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41c2eb1e-faf2-5052-b7d3-11c0c68817f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{x}^{2}-9=0" :db/id 17592186603407} {:answer/id #uuid "5d0d76fc-2ae8-50d0-9ee8-6ed4f69747c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{x}^{2}+36=0" :db/id 17592186603456} {:answer/id #uuid "63fdc9bb-30b0-545b-a4fd-dc00131282d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{x}^{2}+2=0" :db/id 17592186603473} {:answer/id #uuid "853d1b04-8880-54bd-91a9-c9d25fec75ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{x}^{2}+18=0" :db/id 17592186603554} {:answer/id #uuid "c27a72ee-194a-50e5-9d43-acd41089a9b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8{x}^{2}-18=0" :db/id 17592186603690}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603554} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a4ec05f-1baa-5cff-a452-2475061e3b7e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603871}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "90aa62dd-1b0a-50ca-81dd-2689d5b5bcac" :question/math-academy-id "q-83583" :question/problem "A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\frac{3\text{i}}{2}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $8$, find the equation." :question/worked-solution "Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-\frac{3\text{i}}{2}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=\frac{3\text{i}}{2}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{\left(\frac{3\text{i}}{2}\right)}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{9}{4} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{3\text{i}}{2},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $8.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $8.$ This gives

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186604063 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f3accf9-f767-56b0-9743-2e3f57098953" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186603289} {:answer/id #uuid "10432fea-1613-55c3-83b6-d55b0bf17fd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186603292} {:answer/id #uuid "6903fae6-c651-56f3-b776-2b40ff862cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{8}" :db/id 17592186603486} {:answer/id #uuid "8350f9da-9842-5a04-96ed-36d9257132c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{16}" :db/id 17592186603549} {:answer/id #uuid "fa3c393d-a3d1-5ab6-a636-8d456d29b5ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186603803}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603292} :answer-field/id #uuid "144f653a-8d6b-5d65-a5f8-9cffe060819e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603834}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bbdad888-d1ed-5bee-81fe-bd5d7b063822" :question/math-academy-id "q-143616" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following conditional probability density function:

Find $$

$$

$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{8}<Y<\frac{1}{6}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}) & ={\int }_{1/8}^{1/6}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{1}{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1/8}^{1/6}\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1/8}^{1/6}3\,\text{d}y \\  & =[3y]_{1/8}^{1/6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604066 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07e505c1-7b04-5ea4-8a22-42817884eca4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186603279} {:answer/id #uuid "320024ba-7729-5b70-a700-ad30b12ca67c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186603368} {:answer/id #uuid "6e26a1b5-503c-5d57-9e3e-ec3709027d02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186603500} {:answer/id #uuid "88c8c0cf-1756-55d6-a8db-7c3e7f02f173" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186603562} {:answer/id #uuid "b7bc605c-d66c-5863-8bc0-80981b3129a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186603667}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603368} :answer-field/id #uuid "e8fe7eae-0057-5a94-9dc5-fab446ef22bc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603980}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "bdce7dd7-93d4-5440-ad30-de028ae7dc24" :question/math-academy-id "q-146280" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|4}=\frac{1}{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{12}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{4}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=4] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)]-{\mu }_{X|4}^{2} \\  & =[{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}+{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}]-{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =0+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604080 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6c2a4748-f18e-5936-9bf5-1b3a84d865a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186603489}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603489} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b04c552-55e8-5026-ab64-341c84959763" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603846}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e11e0320-ef19-592e-b34a-3e578bf79f09" :question/math-academy-id "q-310127" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)\,{e}^{-4x}-1)=
$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can rewrite the first term as

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)\,{e}^{-4x}=\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)}{{e}^{4x}}.
$$

Both the numerator and denominator approach $\infty$ as $x\to \infty .$ However, since ${e}^{4x}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)$ for large values of $x,$ the denominator is growing much faster than the numerator. Consequently, we conclude that

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)}{{e}^{4x}}=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)\,{e}^{-4x}-1) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(6x)}{{e}^{4x}}-1) \\  & =0-1 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604083 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7ba7769e-9712-5617-85a8-d1c6538679bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(\frac{x}{4}+4)+2" :db/id 17592186603526} {:answer/id #uuid "865e2861-d1fb-58c8-8caa-b0b91daa6e19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(\frac{x}{4}+1)-2" :db/id 17592186603558} {:answer/id #uuid "9284e630-49a0-5c06-996f-03978b1eb666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(4x+16)+2" :db/id 17592186603584} {:answer/id #uuid "dfd4946f-cd2a-54a2-9034-782473941173" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(\frac{x}{4}+1)+2" :db/id 17592186603751} {:answer/id #uuid "e8b78150-526f-58cf-9b89-7a20e9f02602" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=f(\frac{x}{4}-4)-2" :db/id 17592186603773}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603526} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6b021ea-313f-560c-bd23-f1f9bc530b79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186603976}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9ef19ca-f57a-5aec-a936-bee6e7f1ea6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-87470" :question/problem "Given the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

1\. Translate it to the left by $4$ units

2\. Translate it up by $2$ units

3\. Stretch it by a scale factor of $4$ parallel to the $x$-axis

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?" :question/worked-solution "To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

1\. Translating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $4$ units to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ by $(x+4).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=f(x+4).
$$

2\. Translating the graph of $y=f(x+4)$ up by $2$ units is equivalent to adding $2$ to the function expression. Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=f(x+4)+2.
$$

3\. Stretching the graph of $y=f(x+4)+2$ by a scale factor of $4$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{1}{4}x.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
y=f((\frac{1}{4}x)+4)+2=f(\frac{x}{4}+4)+2.
$$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=f(\frac{x}{4}+4)+2.$"} {:db/id 17592186604084 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c2ddd957-3907-59bf-ae04-9da78e6a3191" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\ln(4)-3}{3}" :db/id 17592186603692}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186603692} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a19268c-6e84-5082-ba11-e68fd7eedc44" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186603859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e9f647bf-3ea5-5789-b77b-4dae6f9278b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-351043" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

$$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{3x+1} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{0}^{1}-{\int }_{0}^{1}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)\,(x){|}_{0}^{1}-{\int }_{0}^{1}x\left(\frac{3}{3x+1}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)\,(1)-{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3x}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-\frac{1}{3x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-{[x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-(1-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)) \\  & =\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-3}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer/id #uuid "eadb2d19-1ed5-578b-ae3a-ccb267676aa0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\in (-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})" :db/id 17592186604452} {:db/id 17592186604581 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24248b07-b288-5511-b05f-bba88534e18e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "<" :db/id 17592186604244}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604244} :answer-field/id #uuid "293546ef-da9d-5838-ab3c-fcd58518cc7c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186604485} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "15499c2a-aea5-5c84-ab3a-22e246e7f627" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186604226}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604226} :answer-field/id #uuid "396d0142-37e3-5d7e-a95d-1db082342739" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186604492} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d3a805c3-715d-5049-a7fa-8be3707e485a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186604430}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604430} :answer-field/id #uuid "d491a274-d06e-522c-8bed-e1d66b8bccb6" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186604543}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3b4e52c0-b130-5cf7-b754-aa1b76b8e846" :question/math-academy-id "q-353170" :question/problem "Find the interval of convergence for the series

$$

The interval of convergence is
{{field-1}}

{{field-2}}{{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=(-2x)^{n}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(-2x)^{n+1}}{(-2x)^{n}}| \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }|-2x| \\  & =2|x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $2|x|<1,$ or equivalently $|x|<\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the radius of convergence is $\frac{1}{2},$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=\frac{1}{2},$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=\frac{1}{2}$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=\frac{1}{2}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(-2x)^{n} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(-1)^{n} \\  & =1-1+1-1+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is divergent by the $n$th term test.  So the endpoint $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is not included in our interval.

- When $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(-2x)^{n} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(1)^{n} \\  & =1+1+1+1+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is divergent.  So the endpoint $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is not included in our interval.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{8x+1}+1 & \le 3 \\ \sqrt{8x+1} & \le 2\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(2).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{8x+1})}^{2} & \le {2}^{2} \\ 8x+1 & \le 4 \\ 8x & \le 3 \\ x & \le \frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x+1 & \ge 0 \\ 8x & \ge -1 \\ x & \ge -\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le \frac{3}{8},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{3}{8}].$ The domain of the square root is $x\ge -\frac{1}{8},$ which can be expressed as $[-\frac{1}{8},\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{3}{8}]\cap [-\frac{1}{8},\infty )=[-\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{8}]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [-\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{8}],$ which can also be written as $-\frac{1}{8}\le x\le \frac{3}{8}.$"} {:db/id 17592186604618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "001cc0fc-54d0-57cc-a5aa-b1ddcf07befd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\infty" :db/id 17592186604203} {:answer/id #uuid "15f46fec-3563-570b-b8b5-31ad25f0a411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186604227} {:answer/id #uuid "1fde8c1e-2c42-5404-90b2-27414ca13d02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\text{DNE}" :db/id 17592186604239} {:answer/id #uuid "791d91a3-cf80-5ca5-ae15-4e6c2db26a65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186604349} {:answer/id #uuid "e34f48c9-4b8a-56dd-8aba-d0eb8ff0ff3a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\infty" :db/id 17592186604447}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604227} :answer-field/id #uuid "decf05dc-79bd-5534-a692-c1b2480a764b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186604549}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d8d64dd8-1408-5c35-8e37-ca364a99f3e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-67627" :question/problem "

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨3x-\operatorname{cos}y,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{7}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{5}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/00bceda1bdf4f515646b3a1e8476f1eadde721aa52dbc9be9c7e866bcab99d3b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{5}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & =4\left(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}\right){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186604626 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1bfab534-b326-54c8-8e58-4258d864cdae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}" :db/id 17592186604234} {:answer/id #uuid "51a9909f-6a31-5dca-9af9-5de3f88044a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{{\log }_{2}⁡|x|}" :db/id 17592186604304} {:answer/id #uuid "5addde4b-6175-57cd-a4eb-08ed39da7574" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}" :db/id 17592186604312} {:answer/id #uuid "8ed20646-1e8a-51cf-815a-dbf18cd0a7e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|}{2}" :db/id 17592186604365} {:answer/id #uuid "c60203c6-0636-57a7-949d-50645a319f8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}" :db/id 17592186604420}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604420} :answer-field/id #uuid "9aa7d848-7c7c-5a81-a35d-eda97cc0d91a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186604525}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ff65e0f7-62fc-5c1a-b48e-24f228ff8410" :question/math-academy-id "q-31587" :question/problem "What is the value of $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{\log }_{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $u={\log }_{2}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{\log }_{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\log }_{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{0}^{1}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot (\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605084 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9cb7046e-69af-5a3a-a06b-1ee372a21bff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16.6" :db/id 17592186604894}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604894} :answer-field/id #uuid "8ea9e99d-aa75-5d84-beaa-3936adcb0472" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605043}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "13a3763d-ce88-5709-8ca3-28b3c05a87d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-325133" :question/problem "The net weight of flour in $2\,kg$ bags is normally distributed with an average of $2.0\,kg$ and an unknown standard deviation. {{field-1}}$\%$ of bags weigh less than $1.76\,kg.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the net weight (in $kg$) of a randomly selected bag. Then we have $X∼N(2.0,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X<1.76).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X>2.405)=0.05.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2.4) & =1-P(X>2.405) \\  & =1-0.05 \\  & =0.95\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2.405) & =0.95 \\ P(Z\le \frac{2.405-2.0}{\sigma }) & =0.95 \\ Φ\left(\frac{0.405}{\sigma }\right) & =0.95 \\ \frac{0.405}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.95).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.95)=1.6449.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.405}{\sigma } & =1.6449 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{0.405}{1.6449} \\ \sigma  & ≈0.2462.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(X\le 1.76)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1.76) & =P(Z\le \frac{1.76-2.0}{0.2462}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -0.97) \\  & =Φ(-0.97) \\  & =0.1660 \\  & =16.6\%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $16.6\%$ of bags weigh less than $1.76\,kg.$"} {:db/id 17592186605085 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d7d3e72-5b9f-5193-974f-78e6e9c2a2e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186604748} {:answer/id #uuid "3c62aef9-d368-5ec6-9492-d8de59a333ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186604801} {:answer/id #uuid "75851388-1efc-56bf-b845-562a440f077a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186604855} {:answer/id #uuid "bb05db02-2f78-5c5f-b4bc-19c83cba16ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186604933} {:answer/id #uuid "bbcfd9c2-1294-5298-a3ad-3ec212b4030f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186604935}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604935} :answer-field/id #uuid "cada26a7-3dac-580f-9811-bbf93a0944d0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605065}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "13aff806-1838-5c05-bae9-2137163ed94e" :question/math-academy-id "q-33469" :question/problem "![](images/a8/a86c7ece9e6263f6b4d196df9fddaa121716ea75ebe3892619488fce2c570eae.png)

The diagram above shows the graph of $y=k{\log }_{4}⁡(x-d).$ Find the value of $k\cdot d.$" :question/worked-solution "In the given graph, the vertical asymptote is $x=-3.$ So, the argument of the logarithm function should evaluate to zero at $x=-3.$ Therefore,

$$
-3-d=0\,⇒\,d=-3.
$$

Now, we substitute coordinates of the point $(1,\frac{1}{2})$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}k{\log }_{4}⁡(x-d) & =y \\ k{\log }_{4}⁡(x-(-3)) & =y \\ k{\log }_{4}⁡(x+3) & =y \\ k{\log }_{4}⁡(1+3) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ k{\log }_{4}⁡(4) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ k\cdot 1 & =\frac{1}{2} \\ k & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

Finally,

k\cdot d=\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-3)=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605087 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c9ec836f-40c6-56c3-98e5-c3f22ec13de2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8.32" :db/id 17592186604952}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604952} :answer-field/id #uuid "cbc919f1-84fc-5bb9-9ec3-e20973bba6fd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605067}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1d8e7183-c5fe-51ed-9f4d-8af1c7a588f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-324913" :question/problem "High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels for a certain population are normally distributed with a mean of $55$ mg/dL and an unknown standard deviation $\sigma .$ Screenings show that $20\%$ of adults have HDL less than $48$ mg/dL. Assuming a normal model, find the standard deviation, **rounded to two decimal places.**

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $\,p\,$ | $0.75$ | $0.80$ | $0.85$ | $0.90$ | $0.95$ | $0.97$ | $0.99$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |

$\sigma ≈$
{{field-1}}$\text{mg/dL}$" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent HDL cholesterol (in mg/dL). Then we have $X∼N(55,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X<48)=0.20.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<48) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{48-55}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ Φ\left(-\frac{7}{\sigma }\right) & =0.20 \\ -\frac{7}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.80)=0.8416,
$$

and therefore, by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.20)={Φ}^{-1}(1-0.80)=-0.8416.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{\sigma } & =-0.8416 \\ \frac{7}{\sigma } & =0.8416 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{7}{0.8416} \\ \sigma  & ≈8.32\,\text{mg/dL.}\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "For large negative values of $x,$ we have $|10x+7|=-10x-7.$ Consequently, for $x\to -\infty ,$ we get

$$
\frac{|10x+7|}{2x+1}=\frac{-10x-7}{2x+1}.
$$

First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{1}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-10x-7}{2x+1} & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(-\frac{10x}{x}-\frac{7}{x})}{(\frac{2x}{x}+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(-10-\frac{7}{x})}{(2+\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\frac{-10-0}{2+0} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605100 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "277cf7bf-db97-5c9f-9352-860489643640" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3228" :db/id 17592186604781} {:answer/id #uuid "56c2298b-c552-581e-8fa4-13b5bd247e30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3520" :db/id 17592186604819} {:answer/id #uuid "7dd8371f-38e5-5254-b3e8-79180ca36b47" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3594" :db/id 17592186604866} {:answer/id #uuid "92a3d0fd-30ea-5506-8d46-251efabdb39a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3897" :db/id 17592186604885} {:answer/id #uuid "fe6aaff2-f057-5fa1-8066-26920b67d2c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3156" :db/id 17592186605004}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604866} :answer-field/id #uuid "9b9024eb-1b62-5c9c-b40e-509a7d8be9d3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605048}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "38137cd5-5e87-5894-8664-29f84ed08378" :question/math-academy-id "q-143106" :question/problem "A shop sells spray foam in small, medium, and large cans.
The volume of liquid in a small can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.3$ liters and a variance of $0.003$ liters2.
On the other hand, the volume of liquid in a medium can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.6$ liters and a variance of $0.008$ liters2, while the volume of liquid in a large can is normally distributed with a mean of $0.9$ liters and a variance of $0.014$ liters2. 

The foam from a small can expands $40$ times its liquid volume after being sprayed,  the foam from a medium can expands $60$ times its liquid volume, while the foam from a large can expands $50$ times its liquid volume. 
If one small, one medium, and one large can are randomly selected, what is the probability that their total volume of foam after spraying is less than $90$ liters?

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |

| $\,-0.2\,$ | $\,0.4013\,$ | $\,0.3974\,$ | $\,0.3936\,$ | $\,0.3897\,$ | $\,0.3859\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the volume of liquid in the small, medium, and large cans, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(0.3,0.003),\,{X}_{2}∼N(0.6,0.008),\,{X}_{3}∼N(0.9,0.014).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total volume of foam after spraying. Since the small, medium, and large cans expand by $40$, $60$, and $50$ times their liquid volumes, respectively, we have

$$
Y=40{X}_{1}+60{X}_{2}+50{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(40\cdot 0.3+60\cdot 0.6+50\cdot 0.9) \\  & =93 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =(40)^{2}\cdot 0.003+(60)^{2}\cdot 0.008+(50)^{2}\cdot 0.014 \\  & =1600\cdot 0.003+3600\cdot 0.008+2500\cdot 0.014 \\  & =68.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(93,68.6).
$$

In order to find $P(Y<90),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<90) & =P(Z<\frac{90-93}{\sqrt{68.6}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.36) \\  & =Φ(-0.36)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-0.36)≈0.3594.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<90) & ≈0.3594.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605102 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "297ede6c-6ddb-551f-8eac-334d2fddd0f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186604782} {:answer/id #uuid "59ae491d-7671-51c3-a6b1-9bef53394af6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186604821} {:answer/id #uuid "9060d91b-6f0e-5f56-89c5-fc2acc83c6ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186604880} {:answer/id #uuid "9235734e-dc47-5b1c-a088-18c4f0046db5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186604884} {:answer/id #uuid "b6fc2b85-9fd1-5fd0-9605-de76990db3fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186604925}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604880} :answer-field/id #uuid "4ed87061-2c6c-5e49-b196-cbf4f5b79c55" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605029}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3cfb12fc-4ec0-58d0-84d4-1ac08e88a6bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-149668" :question/problem "Find $\text{E}[\frac{X+1}{6}],$ given that the continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{(x+1)^{3}}, & x\ge 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
r(x)=\frac{x+1}{6}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\frac{X+1}{6}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{x+1}{6}\cdot \frac{18}{(x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{[-\frac{1}{x+1}]}_{2}^{\infty } \\  & =3(-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605107 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18a9c88b-9f29-5189-a9e0-3fa6a9082892" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7262" :db/id 17592186604767} {:answer/id #uuid "66195fab-9baf-583b-b7c1-55ab9ca2f614" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8882" :db/id 17592186604840} {:answer/id #uuid "86c95d94-d657-5bed-885e-94d525befdc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8092" :db/id 17592186604869} {:answer/id #uuid "b1cfb13f-226c-57ec-a04a-77f7c1751e67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.9006" :db/id 17592186604918} {:answer/id #uuid "dc999348-74f2-56cb-84e0-928bbf1a1e14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8944" :db/id 17592186604972}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604840} :answer-field/id #uuid "7db1b01e-3ff4-5fa2-8c62-fd7ffbcb12da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605038}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4f924df4-3a43-566e-bf5d-e9b5f0bf0ca3" :question/math-academy-id "q-143118" :question/problem "Given that the random variables
