</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(5,6),\,{X}_{2}∼N(4,3),\,{X}_{3}∼N(5,7),
$$

and

$$
Y={X}_{1}-5{X}_{2}+5{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =1\cdot 5+(-5)\cdot 4+5\cdot 5 \\  & =10, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 6+(-5)^{2}\cdot 3+{5}^{2}\cdot 7 \\  & =1\cdot 6+25\cdot 3+25\cdot 7 \\  & =256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(10,256).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|Y|<30)=P(-30<Y<30).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-30<Y<30) & =P(\frac{-30-10}{\sqrt{256}}<Z<\frac{30-10}{\sqrt{256}}) \\  & =P(-2.5<Z<1.25) \\  & =P(Z<1.25)-P(Z<-2.5) \\  & =Φ(1.25)-Φ(-2.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-2.5)≈0.0062,\,Φ(1.25)≈0.8944.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|<30) & =Φ(1.25)-Φ(-2.5) \\  & ≈0.8944-0.0062 \\  & =0.8882.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605109 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ff4c428-c703-5f86-b877-c88edfe9d684" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0154" :db/id 17592186604752} {:answer/id #uuid "c4a8cac5-6105-54c0-ac9b-0f888389a872" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0073" :db/id 17592186604945} {:answer/id #uuid "da32ec75-e8a7-57a9-b095-f9d4ec9d5cf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0113" :db/id 17592186604969} {:answer/id #uuid "dcbbd6b8-8361-5325-bd15-9e4acb41318d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0096" :db/id 17592186604973} {:answer/id #uuid "ffa1128b-a1dc-5174-8897-644f200233b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0146" :db/id 17592186605008}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605008} :answer-field/id #uuid "a070ad5c-49a9-5894-98a9-72760e866fd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "56900097-c624-5c58-8e9b-65f1c7173d06" :question/math-academy-id "q-143102" :question/problem "At a cafe, the time waiting for service is normally distributed with a mean value of $3$ minutes and a standard deviation of $1$ minute.

What is the probability that a randomly selected customer will get their order in less than $10$ minutes after entering the cafe? You may assume that the time waiting for service, ordering time, and the time waiting for the order to arrive are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $\,-2.2\,$ | $\,0.0125\,$ | $\,0.0122\,$ | $\,0.0119\,$ | $\,0.0116\,$ | $\,0.0113\,$ | $\,0.0110\,$ |
| $\,-2.1\,$ | $\,0.0162\,$ | $\,0.0158\,$ | $\,0.0154\,$ | $\,0.0150\,$ | $\,0.0146\,$ | $\,0.0143\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the time waiting for service, ordering time, and time waiting for the order, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(3,{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(1,{0.2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(15,{4}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the time before starting to eat. Then, we have

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =3+1+15 \\  & =19, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={1}^{2}+{0.2}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =17.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(19,17.04).
$$

We want to find $P(10<X<14).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10<X<14) & =P(\frac{10-15}{3.5}<Z<\frac{14-15}{3.5}) \\  & =P(-1.43<Z<-0.29)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.43<Z<-0.29) & =P(Z<-0.29)-P(Z\le -1.43) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.29)-P(Z\le -1.43) \\  & =Φ(-0.29)-Φ(-1.43)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.29) & =0.3859 \\ Φ(-1.43) & =0.0764\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.43<Z<-0.29) & =Φ(-0.29)-Φ(-1.43) \\  & =0.3859-0.0764 \\  & =0.3095.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the randomly selected incoming call has a waiting time between $10$ and $14$ minutes is approximately $0.31.$"} {:db/id 17592186605115 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0716ddf6-1022-528e-9736-422b023a5b0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3936" :db/id 17592186604739} {:answer/id #uuid "161452f4-1c05-528b-9a85-b65afde9bbe0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3632" :db/id 17592186604761} {:answer/id #uuid "3388e88f-e104-5470-93ff-3637fd298747" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3859" :db/id 17592186604792} {:answer/id #uuid "7abc5429-9a96-5a11-a430-2903508aa7e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4404" :db/id 17592186604862} {:answer/id #uuid "9f988ca1-61ed-575e-9841-25c8e4db5b35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4286" :db/id 17592186604897}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604792} :answer-field/id #uuid "b84c2967-d609-5f5f-bfe0-a817819abbe3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605062}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "778926ad-8da2-5678-8b6d-aa3a9c6fef38" :question/math-academy-id "q-143238" :question/problem "A store sells wooden boards in two lengths. $$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(5,6),\,{X}_{2}∼N(1,{4}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(-1,3),

and

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =1\cdot 5+1\cdot 1+1\cdot (-1) \\  & =5, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 6+{1}^{2}\cdot {4}^{2}+{1}^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =6+16+3 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(5,25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(Y<7).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<7) & =P(Z<\frac{7-5}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.4) \\  & =Φ(0.4)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.4)≈0.6554.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<7) & =Φ(0.4) \\  & =0.6554.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605125 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14d44cab-1b45-5305-994f-c5625a5796f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0475" :db/id 17592186604758} {:answer/id #uuid "6f9f8cfc-5cff-514a-87a7-e7baec19a593" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4182" :db/id 17592186604849} {:answer/id #uuid "a67c6b72-7513-574c-aabc-8502860c0bb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.726" :db/id 17592186604905} {:answer/id #uuid "dce91241-8774-5652-8b88-b7d56e259b2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.095" :db/id 17592186604975} {:answer/id #uuid "f2f5d211-5e8c-5166-9f5a-75b10515736d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3707" :db/id 17592186604995}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604849} :answer-field/id #uuid "5f161e26-c543-5f3e-98a1-a9a8b6c310cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605032}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a2f1de25-85fe-5538-8ef0-401d3ebd0abe" :question/math-academy-id "q-143119" :question/problem "Given that the random variables

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(1,3),\,{X}_{2}∼N(-1,2),\,{X}_{3}∼N(3,1),
$$

and

$$
Y=3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 1+2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 3 \\  & =4, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3+{2}^{2}\cdot 2+{1}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 3+4\cdot 2+1\cdot 1 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(4,36).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(|Y|>6).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|Y|>6) & =P(Y<-6)+P(Y>6) \\  & =P(Z<\frac{-6-4}{\sqrt{36}})+P(Z>\frac{6-4}{\sqrt{36}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-1.67)+P(Z>0.33) \\  & =P(Z<-1.67)+(1-P(Z<0.33)) \\  & =1+Φ(-1.67)-Φ(0.33).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.67)≈0.0475,\,Φ(0.33)≈0.6293.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ | $\,0.8315\,$ | $\,0.8340\,$ | $\,0.8365\,$ | $\,0.8389\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the weight of the chicken, the duck, and the goose, respectively. Then, we have

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$

$$
f(x)=\frac{3(1+x)}{4},\,-1\le x\le 1.
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ and a function $r(x),$ the rule of the lazy statistician states that 

$$
\text{E}[r(X)]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
r(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[\frac{1}{X+1}] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(x)f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{3(1+x)}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{\cancel{x+1}}\cdot \frac{3\cancel{(1+x)}}{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{3}{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{4}x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(1-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605137 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62deed74-9fed-5195-8a38-1774dc8b9bee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3085" :db/id 17592186604834} {:answer/id #uuid "7adf4055-14c4-5236-8909-bcfabdc63297" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3050" :db/id 17592186604864} {:answer/id #uuid "8fbcfd83-df1d-5406-9f02-030d3699bc6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2743" :db/id 17592186604878} {:answer/id #uuid "c9d8bee5-2446-579b-8c1b-254426f6694d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7257" :db/id 17592186604951} {:answer/id #uuid "efa70c8b-90f1-5193-b35b-3dd911fe81b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6915" :db/id 17592186604994}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604994} :answer-field/id #uuid "164239da-9f6f-5dea-b045-dd8e6b626601" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605015}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c71a26b8-827d-5172-a3cf-b05e6942e27c" :question/math-academy-id "q-143419" :question/problem "Given that the random variables 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(3,{3}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(-1,4),\,{X}_{3}∼N(2,3)

are mutually independent and $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3},$ calculate $P(Y>2).$ 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |

| $\,-0.5\,$ | $\,0.3085\,$ | $\,0.3050\,$ | $\,0.3015\,$ | $\,0.2981\,$ |
| $\,-0.4\,$ | $\,0.3446\,$ | $\,0.3409\,$ | $\,0.3372\,$ | $\,0.3336\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{1}∼N({\mu }_{1},{\sigma }_{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N({\mu }_{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N({\mu }_{3},{\sigma }_{3}^{2}),
$$

and ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(3,{3}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(-1,4),\,{X}_{3}∼N(2,3),
$$

and

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3}.
$$

Since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =1\cdot 3+1\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 2 \\  & =4 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}+{1}^{2}\cdot 4+{1}^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =9+4+3 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y∼N(4,16).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(Y>2).$ Thus, we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>2) & =P(Z>\frac{2-4}{\sqrt{16}}) \\  & =P(Z>-0.5) \\  & =1-P(Z<-0.5) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.5)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-0.5)≈0.3085.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>2) & =1-Φ(-0.5) \\  & =1-0.3085 \\  & =0.6915.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19515152-8bb9-5c11-9b92-09b6d68ddaa2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{1}{8}" :db/id 17592186604768} {:answer/id #uuid "311daad9-c5f5-5f9d-8bfe-16d61c249a56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=8" :db/id 17592186604791} {:answer/id #uuid "61743acd-ce61-5856-a0c1-c43a9e894502" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186604832} {:answer/id #uuid "667020b0-c626-5c77-961e-3f553da035cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No horizontal asymptote" :db/id 17592186604842} {:answer/id #uuid "8f13667f-7cca-51c5-bff5-3d674df17cb3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=0" :db/id 17592186604876}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604876} :answer-field/id #uuid "ddc4bd01-8241-5705-9c7a-148e4e3c072b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605072}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "caec5bae-5176-547a-b0ab-8120eceb2aee" :question/math-academy-id "q-35827" :question/problem "Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{4{x}^{4}+5x}{8{x}^{5}-10}.$" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote is $y=\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{5}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{4{x}^{4}+5x}{8{x}^{5}-10} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{5x}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{8{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{10}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4}{x}+\frac{5}{{x}^{4}})}{(8-\frac{10}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & =\frac{0+0}{8-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186605143 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b1d4c9e7-9966-50a9-89bd-d14dd884c673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\ln 5}" :db/id 17592186604919}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186604919} :answer-field/id #uuid "0967827d-5215-5889-bcdd-7f7a89bd1103" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605011}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e5ddd3dc-e6b3-555b-8238-54ebaafe3035" :question/math-academy-id "q-351509" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. $$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we substitute $u=4-{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty$ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=4-{x}^{2}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $2$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{2}^{\infty }{5}^{4-{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{5}^{u}\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{5}^{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }{5}^{4-{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\lim_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{5}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\lim_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\lim_{a\to -\infty }[{5}^{u}]_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\lim_{a\to -\infty }(1-{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(1-\lim_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={5}^{a},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a}=0$

- $\lim_{a\to \infty }{5}^{a}=\infty$

![](images/df/dfacdebf754f239c4b5feebed75b49d1d9061594593286b7b837799372076cae.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }{5}^{4-{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot (1-\lim_{a\to -\infty }{5}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605833 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "897b4ce9-081c-5c27-8b97-2c9527be496d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2025" :db/id 17592186605496}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605496} :answer-field/id #uuid "1374d5e8-96ec-5729-9d69-061a8952e860" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605724} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "313e1e50-7d6b-5b8e-8beb-3ccf87c6a12b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186605343}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605343} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8dcc5e9-741a-51ee-afeb-00390a5f9d56" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605825}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0d2ca2d7-91f3-5609-bff1-8a03e9cb5b8e" :question/math-academy-id "q-349992" :question/problem "The total amount of money $M(t)$ in a charity’s fundraising account $t$ days after the first day of a campaign is given by the function

$$

$$

where $M$ is measured in dollars, and $t\ge 0$ is the time (in days) since the first day of the campaign.

Find the time when the total amount is minimum, and how much money was in the account at that time.

The minimum amount is

{{field-2}} days." :question/worked-solution "To find when the total amount is a minimum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2100+6{\int }_{0}^{t}(x-5)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2100)+6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\int }_{0}^{t}(x-5)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(x-5)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6(t-5)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
6(t-5)=0\,⇒\,t=5
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=5.$ To find out how much money is in the account when $t=5,$ we figure out $M(5)$:

$$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 1\}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0\le x\le 1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}6xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{[\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1} \\  & =3{[x{y}^{2}]}_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1} \\  & =3[x\cdot {1}^{2}-x\cdot {({x}^{2})}^{2}] \\  & =3[x-{x}^{5}] \\  & =3x-3{x}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186605847 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "084d6296-4e0e-5291-a90f-82b7617ff7a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186605264} {:answer/id #uuid "2341f810-fcdd-5f61-be44-39e52dde1228" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/id 17592186605311} {:answer/id #uuid "320634f0-cac2-5787-bb32-88a333793829" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186605344} {:answer/id #uuid "86afb790-2d4b-5953-a77a-737ee084b7a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186605490} {:answer/id #uuid "a9fbf28e-c6bd-5a97-8692-75b54a26c81b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}" :db/id 17592186605562}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605311} :answer-field/id #uuid "d01f36ee-521c-54fe-9274-182cb22b18d4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605813}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3d11b8d3-3d89-559d-9bb2-2df9905b80bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-13544" :question/problem "$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /18}}^{\sqrt{\pi /9}}2x{\sec }^{2}⁡(3{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\sqrt{\pi /18}}^{\sqrt{\pi /9}}2{\sec }^{2}⁡(3{x}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}2{\sec }^{2}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\sec }^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)-\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}\end{aligned}

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{6n-2}{3n}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $3n,$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by $n$ and get

$$

If the sequence converges, what is its limit?" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for large values of $n,$ we have

$$
n!≫{e}^{n}≫{n}^{m}≫\operatorname{ln}⁡(n),
$$

where $≫$ means "much greater than," and $m>0.$

We calculate the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\lim_{n\to \infty }(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(14n)}{n}-3)=-3+\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(14n)}{n}
$$

Both the numerator and denominator approach infinity as $n\to \infty .$ However, the denominator is growing much faster than the numerator, and we conclude that

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(14n)}{n}=0.
$$

Hence, 

$$
-3+\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(14n)}{n}=-3+0=-3.
$$

At what time is the volume of the pond a minimum, and, to the nearest integer, what is the volume at this time?" :question/worked-solution "To find when the volume is at minimum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(50-{\int }_{0}^{t}3(4-{2}^{x/3})\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(50)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\int }_{0}^{t}3(4-{2}^{x/3})\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(4-{2}^{x/3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3(4-{2}^{t/3})\end{aligned}

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3(4-{2}^{t/3}) & =0 \\ {2}^{t/3} & ={2}^{2} \\ \frac{t}{3} & =2 \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=6.$ To find the volume when $t=6,$ we figure out $V(6):$

$$

$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $0\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

For the given probability density function, we have

$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186605890 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d3db550-ee1e-555b-bc06-390b655b9f88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡z{\csc }^{2}⁡z)+C" :db/id 17592186605303} {:answer/id #uuid "8f72f014-9e7c-59fb-98ca-5331183256fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡z{\csc }^{2}⁡z)+C" :db/id 17592186605506} {:answer/id #uuid "93f3445d-8a85-5c2f-8baa-633dd26d1b5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(5+{\cot }^{2}⁡z)+C" :db/id 17592186605516} {:answer/id #uuid "c36518f3-9d8f-570c-bc9d-9d52b3886265" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(5+{\cot }^{2}⁡z)+C" :db/id 17592186605603} {:answer/id #uuid "f9e87827-2dcf-5ee9-ae1c-1a99767181e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5+{\cot }^{2}⁡z)+C" :db/id 17592186605704}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605603} :answer-field/id #uuid "b32f6229-f7ef-5aeb-8794-e2748decb297" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605801}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9da80b7e-7d28-5432-bd06-d6318df2aa62" :question/math-academy-id "q-73679" :question/problem "Calculate the integral $$

What is the function $g(y)?$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) &={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[xy]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[2y-0] \\  & =\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $Y$ for $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{f}_{Y}(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{u}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{2}}{4}]}_{0}^{y} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[{y}^{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${F}_{Y}(y)$ is

$$
{F}_{Y}(y)=\left\{\begin{aligned}0, & y<0 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}, & 0\le y\le 2 \\ 1 & y>2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Finally, $g(y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}.$"} {:db/id 17592186605904 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "069c3ecb-d129-572d-8d8c-8a1e1ff62762" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186605259} {:answer/id #uuid "dff76f53-e14d-5746-b8ac-2e534f326cec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186605657} {:answer/id #uuid "e5b66112-a5d4-5e41-9d35-e572cd64a24f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The sequence diverges" :db/id 17592186605668} {:answer/id #uuid "f62d622f-10b6-55e1-a790-ebcad2d023f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186605697} {:answer/id #uuid "f980e1e9-f4f7-5892-bd7c-69932796fd6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186605703}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605259} :answer-field/id #uuid "8cfec23c-13fa-58f1-9245-1d1f88b1855b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605779}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c6a9b443-780a-50a7-ae26-de2f76322aed" :question/math-academy-id "q-123306" :question/problem "What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{7-2{n}^{6}}{3{n}^{6}+5{n}^{3}}$ for $n\ge 1?$" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether the sequence converges or diverges, we need to determine the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

Find the expression for the marginal PDF ${f}_{X}(x).$" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) &={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's sketch the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le x\le 1\}.$

![](images/e6/e63b557f30a1a54e5fbaea8999dd420deec67f4a0ed770dc1ada48affb7c9be7.png)

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0\le x\le 1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{0}^{x}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{x}(x+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{[xy+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x} \\  & ={[2xy+{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x} \\  & =(2x\cdot x+{x}^{2})-(2x\cdot 0+{0}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186605906 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6030d762-dc86-599a-97b7-3808568c4075" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186605427} {:answer/id #uuid "ab35d913-bb6a-55ee-bbcc-7e1db2866cf7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None" :db/id 17592186605566} {:answer/id #uuid "cec8366c-d7ac-52d6-9ff4-213822f4913e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186605623} {:answer/id #uuid "d7c37ff2-391d-5233-bd96-2a16b91ef2b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186605637} {:answer/id #uuid "f595af35-db72-5cc6-b9c9-9d172ed09b7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186605694}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605637} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dfe3234-3568-5526-a75d-e908e818f14e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605759}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cd3d623a-8365-59f7-8177-4be42fef6aa6" :question/math-academy-id "q-123317" :question/problem "Which of the following sequences diverge?

I. ${a}_{n}=\frac{7}{{n}^{7}}$ for $n\ge 1$

II. ${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}+1}$ for $n\ge 1$

III. ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}+4n}$ for $n\ge 1$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches infinity.

- In sequence I, the limit is

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{7}{{n}^{7}}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence II, the dominant term in the denominator is $3{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{2{n}^{2}}{3{n}^{2}+1} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\left(\frac{2{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}\right)}{(\frac{3{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{2}{(3+\frac{1}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3+0} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence III, the dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{\left(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}}\right)}{(\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{(1+\frac{4}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{1+0} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

In conclusion, sequence III diverges."} {:db/id 17592186605908 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c17c29d-5cfb-5737-8e38-ec91a1bc0d7b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186605271} {:answer/id #uuid "81cf3979-0118-5efb-91a1-cca6386197d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186605485} {:answer/id #uuid "afdd7dc9-3049-5c17-9f60-e853e1b8c2ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186605576} {:answer/id #uuid "b6b3033d-7600-5924-ba1a-b179be7629e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The sequence diverges" :db/id 17592186605587} {:answer/id #uuid "f929ca39-1b38-5fab-bcf1-063954bf43c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186605702}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605702} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a65d06c-cc44-5340-8c70-d5fb63396c73" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186605735}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cf5f5311-bd11-542e-822c-120ab1904db3" :question/math-academy-id "q-123310" :question/problem "What is the limit of the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}+3n}{n-{n}^{5}}$ for $n>1?$" :question/worked-solution "To determine whether the sequence converges or diverges, we need to determine the limit of the sequence as $n$ approaches infinity:

$$
\lim_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}+3n}{n-{n}^{5}}.
$$

The dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{5},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{5}$ and get

Since the limit exists, the sequence converges, and its limit is $0.$"} {:db/id 17592186605910 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "eb5d7649-0a8b-5247-9774-7eecb5abd534" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{6x}}{2}" :db/id 17592186605674}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186605674} :answer-field/id #uuid "a0f4a8de-1e15-5a40-8e35-86d69e5ddebf" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186605792}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d5ee1fb9-a255-54a9-b5da-b2c0be72c283" :question/math-academy-id "q-210764" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=3{e}^{-|6x|},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}h(x),\, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-6x}}{2},\, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}3{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{-6t}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}3{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{6t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{6x}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{6t}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{6x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{-6t}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-6x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{-6t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{-6t}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-6x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-6x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

\displaystyle z=\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right))
$$ in the form $z=x+\text{i}y.$" :question/worked-solution "To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

First, we find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right)$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the values and expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{11\pi }{6}\right)) \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606801 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10d36410-ab43-56ed-a284-3498f30c9cf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2+{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186606168} {:answer/id #uuid "297baf28-f6d4-5333-8cbe-de20f1b81660" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y(1-{y}^{2})" :db/id 17592186606231} {:answer/id #uuid "8ea788a6-c3e6-54d1-8d17-fe51be4cd191" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-2{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186606440} {:answer/id #uuid "a7a1cefc-f3c2-587b-950b-6d1d5ec26c83" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2y(1+{y}^{2})" :db/id 17592186606495} {:answer/id #uuid "ef0fced5-5052-574c-9483-db931099aa43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+2{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186606635}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606495} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebce920f-decc-5f96-99af-c68975b09269" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606785}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "18618779-ab66-5688-87c9-96ba590b199b" :question/math-academy-id "q-161078" :question/problem "$$
⟨\,(1+{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\text{_______}\,,\,(1+{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

  

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=1+{y}^{2}$ by $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-1,1]$ is given above. What is the $2$nd component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x=1+{y}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r &=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ and 

$$
D=\{(y,\theta )\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y},\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=1+{y}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2y.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} &=⟨(1+{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-2y(1+{y}^{2}),\,(1+{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606810 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "98a6dab8-eac0-5586-b56c-b080838910dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/id 17592186606467} {:answer/id #uuid "bddedb9b-8de9-5006-8fd9-7a5bc0efda01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36\operatorname{cos}⁡t" :db/id 17592186606532} {:answer/id #uuid "c166cd3a-b85e-542f-9686-9d2e279e6872" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36t" :db/id 17592186606539} {:answer/id #uuid "d91b1969-e75d-548c-b721-d1c569a93d0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "36\operatorname{sec}⁡t" :db/id 17592186606596} {:answer/id #uuid "fed796f3-1aab-5ff3-b564-922d825a5f95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\operatorname{sec}⁡t" :db/id 17592186606663}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606663} :answer-field/id #uuid "8296ef51-9a0d-536f-af90-7d10f69b8dd7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606741}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2546cccc-d039-5cb9-a144-ca3b62213170" :question/math-academy-id "q-164444" :question/problem "$$
\mathbf{f}(t,z)=⟨\operatorname{tan}t,\hspace{0.167em}\text{_____},\hspace{0.167em}z⟩,\hspace{2em}t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,z)$ above parametrizes one sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\frac{{y}^{2}}{36}-{x}^{2}=1$ for $y\ge 6.$ What is the second component of $\mathbf{f}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the hyperbola $\frac{{y}^{2}}{36}-{x}^{2}=1$ for $y\ge 6$ in $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
⟨x,y⟩=⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{36}-{x}^{2} & =\frac{(6\operatorname{sec}⁡t)^{2}}{36}-(\operatorname{tan}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =\frac{36{\sec }^{2}⁡t}{36}-{\tan }^{2}⁡t \\  & ={\sec }^{2}⁡t-{\tan }^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Therefore, the second component of $f$ is $6\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$"} {:db/id 17592186606811 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18629bc5-d102-515c-91ef-1b58195a9c3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3788" :db/id 17592186606186} {:answer/id #uuid "37f789e5-1ec2-5806-8b77-45c0908b0f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3825" :db/id 17592186606257} {:answer/id #uuid "86b244fa-3431-509a-a577-b69abae5bb9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3942" :db/id 17592186606427} {:answer/id #uuid "a370731f-fea4-5205-96dc-b3c1b34f2d1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4005" :db/id 17592186606486} {:answer/id #uuid "f3a540d7-451e-5562-af70-a77f7b93e8da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3970" :db/id 17592186606642}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606642} :answer-field/id #uuid "a0dfc0e0-0f2c-5d17-adee-6a0fb6d8e508" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606754}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "25adca44-2993-5707-ac4b-3d0654363758" :question/math-academy-id "q-110504" :question/problem "In a certain shop, eggs are sold in cartons by the ten. The weight of an egg, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $55\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $6\,\text{g},$ while the weight of a carton, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $20\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $3\,\text{g}.$ If one carton filled with eggs is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs more than $560\,\text{g}$ and less than $580\,\text{g}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ |
| $\,0.4\,$ | $\,0.6554\,$ | $\,0.6591\,$ | $\,0.6628\,$ | $\,0.6664\,$ |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.6915\,$ | $\,0.6950\,$ | $\,0.6985\,$ | $\,0.7019\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th egg, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a carton. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(55,{6}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 10,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(20,{3}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected carton filled with eggs. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{10}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =10\cdot 55+20 \\  & =570, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =10\cdot {6}^{2}+{3}^{2} \\  & =369.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(570,369).
$$

In order to find $P(560<W<580),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(560<W<580) & =P(\frac{560-570}{\sqrt{369}}<Z<\frac{580-570}{\sqrt{369}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.52<Z<0.52) \\  & =Φ(0.52)-Φ(-0.52) \\  & =Φ(0.52)-(1-Φ(0.52)) \\  & =2Φ(0.52)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.52)≈0.6985.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(560<W<580) & ≈2Φ(0.52)-1 \\  & ≈0.3970.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606816 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1463575a-3a83-57fb-83aa-5898366b38a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne 0" :db/id 17592186606171} {:answer/id #uuid "3e1d2fd1-bf06-57dd-8130-13d9820d3f88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2})" :db/id 17592186606271} {:answer/id #uuid "570e6f41-bdef-5998-b197-b68cba260f49" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186606325} {:answer/id #uuid "abf8c9ab-2c1e-52d8-b9d5-d7575c74c3d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in [0,\pi ],\,t\ne \frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186606503} {:answer/id #uuid "c5a119ca-739a-52cd-b4f8-4e9d6ea6abca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "t\in [-\pi ,-\frac{\pi }{2})\cup (\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]" :db/id 17592186606549}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606271} :answer-field/id #uuid "5bf23437-448e-5f9b-a35e-548daccdcff9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606715}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2e0ef19a-7838-5667-961a-0fb7594e779b" :question/math-academy-id "q-91390" :question/problem "![](images/14/1474fb8efcada2aec61c1aa2b2ed16615e0ba968ec4e53a8fbfe05b1107c085f.png)

$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the upper branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the upper branch are

$$
x=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606825 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18a94d21-3adb-5a68-9ae9-3f5d7302301c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7422" :db/id 17592186606187} {:answer/id #uuid "37fd6478-948b-5942-821e-2b75f70cfd10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7123" :db/id 17592186606258} {:answer/id #uuid "5b1fdc57-1d2c-5330-9aac-ad1a4e6cb1f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7704" :db/id 17592186606330} {:answer/id #uuid "8509138a-3f63-5584-a644-06f9273dc336" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2546" :db/id 17592186606420} {:answer/id #uuid "ec834be2-53ff-5ed9-9a85-e3682e7461b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2296" :db/id 17592186606633}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606330} :answer-field/id #uuid "fec713ad-bc6a-531b-aff9-02400b70dc79" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606793}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4339876c-db06-5900-b9ce-d8d5eb6f3106" :question/math-academy-id "q-110502" :question/problem "A seller delivers bricks on pallets. | $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th brick, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a pallet. Then, we have

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$

\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{1}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx=
$$ 

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{1}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt[3]{y}\le z\le 1\}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type I region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
E=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/bf/bf06c344661079ef45437a6afd98be4e485ad300ba62eae91299a3773ca20cdb.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $\sqrt[3]{y}\le z\le 1.$

![](images/9e/9ec0cfb27cf6b7ea47ccb010f2fd2238bbd0426b9dbd0035c8b78422ac32e4a4.png)

 

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/fc/fcf5ded147f2937165c2f7a1a7d1f030103d64f6cb277fb09fb9049a21cf4b8c.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
z=\sqrt[3]{y}\,⟹\,y={z}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le {z}^{3}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/2d/2dfeb845363b5721b936af1aadbffb47e55902fbe4db2c99894632e85405c0cf.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane with the bottom curve given by $z=\sqrt[3]{0}=0.$

![](images/90/90c6f2912371b5a2951a19bc4ae1fba827b98fdff6bbf73c18c2f8c139f53950.png)

Hence,

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt[3]{y}}^{1}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{3}}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{3}}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}[y]_{0}^{{z}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4{z}^{3}\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}4{z}^{3}\sqrt{{z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2}}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{2}{3}{({z}^{4}+\frac{x}{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{(1+\frac{x}{2})}^{3/2}-{\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{3/2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{4}{5}{(1+\frac{x}{2})}^{5/2}-\frac{4}{5}{\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}{[{(1+\frac{x}{2})}^{5/2}-{\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}[({2}^{5/2}-1)-(1-0)] \\  & =\frac{8}{15}[4\sqrt{2}-2] \\  & =\frac{16(2\sqrt{2}-1)}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606852 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "39a73f47-b3f0-58ce-b137-6bad0738aeb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2483" :db/id 17592186606262} {:answer/id #uuid "3a6812f7-8aee-5bc1-8aa2-795b018e81ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2843" :db/id 17592186606265} {:answer/id #uuid "6a47a23c-85e8-5a4f-8299-089c74b02305" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2578" :db/id 17592186606364} {:answer/id #uuid "738b3356-5bea-5f49-b79e-8270aa090bb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2206" :db/id 17592186606387} {:answer/id #uuid "e2d689f7-c5e0-5e2d-9c06-a696a2a85007" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2190" :db/id 17592186606615}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606387} :answer-field/id #uuid "fce26851-6d54-5363-8f4f-4f7f3e80d063" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606791}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7efe4f7a-82e9-522f-9311-d716b8e328f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-143457" :question/problem "The weight of a chestnut, in grams, is normally distributed with a mean of $5\,\text{g}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{g}.$
A machine fills packages with $42$ chestnuts each.
What is the probability that a randomly chosen package weighs less than $200\,\text{g}?$
You may assume that the weights of the chestnuts are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ | $\,0.7123\,$ | $\,0.7157\,$ | $\,0.7190\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ | $\,0.7454\,$ | $\,0.7486\,$ | $\,0.7517\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ | $\,0.7764\,$ | $\,0.7794\,$ | $\,0.7823\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th chestnut put into the package. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(5,{2}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 42.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected package filled with $42$ chestnuts. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{42},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =42\cdot 5 \\  & =210, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =42\cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =168.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(210,168).
$$

In order to find $P(W<200),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<200) & =P(Z<\frac{200-210}{\sqrt{168}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.77) \\  & =Φ(-0.77) \\  & =1-Φ(0.77)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.77)≈0.7794.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<200) & ≈1-Φ(0.77) \\  & ≈0.2206.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606858 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62950012-7d7f-5fdc-9942-0f80b3ea543e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7910" :db/id 17592186606346} {:answer/id #uuid "68e0d4f0-73e8-5059-aa28-355ae059aadc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3628" :db/id 17592186606360} {:answer/id #uuid "6a723b51-81f8-5b7b-abce-83d57502372e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8186" :db/id 17592186606366} {:answer/id #uuid "8d4cbff4-4bed-538f-b906-f071cfd9323e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6372" :db/id 17592186606438} {:answer/id #uuid "e64c3be5-4116-5fe4-82b2-edf308d9e77a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1814" :db/id 17592186606620}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606438} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a5f2bcb-455e-5dd5-a83b-ececc2a75f60" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606704}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "8871f9fa-71e6-5894-a3d5-c56ea88e48ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-143341" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ are I.I.D random variables, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(-1,{1}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 30,
$$

calculate $P(-35\le Y\le -25),$ where  $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{30}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{30}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{30} & ∼N(30\cdot (-1),\,30\cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(30\cdot (-1),\,30\cdot 1) \\  & =N(-30,30).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(-35\le Y\le -25).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-35\le Y\le -25) & =P(\frac{-35-(-30)}{\sqrt{30}}\le Z\le \frac{-25-(-30)}{\sqrt{30}}) \\  & =P(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}\le Z\le \frac{5}{\sqrt{30}}) \\  & =P(-0.91\le Z\le 0.91) \\  & =1-2P(Z\ge 0.91) \\  & =1-2(1-P(Z\le 0.91)) \\  & =2P(Z\le 0.91))-1 \\  & =2Φ(0.91)-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.91)=0.8186.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(-35\le Y\le -25)=2Φ(0.91)-1=0.6372.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606860 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "240bdc45-1153-59ee-be05-4f760b844003" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "63.6\%" :db/id 17592186606213} {:answer/id #uuid "a45a0aec-59ef-5ac0-93b6-071570d52fad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "72.5\%" :db/id 17592186606489} {:answer/id #uuid "a8d529f8-50ef-5c86-bc3a-76d64000bf3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "67.4\%" :db/id 17592186606498} {:answer/id #uuid "d4c48ffe-781d-533a-b574-c418a3db114e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "69.3\%" :db/id 17592186606585} {:answer/id #uuid "e10966af-746f-55fa-adcc-1af0b5d3599f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "61.8\%" :db/id 17592186606611}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606498} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d512896-d27c-5600-8c7b-e855ff37a8cd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606697}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8d67cbfd-0220-5994-aff5-cb754fd34cdc" :question/math-academy-id "q-95152" :question/problem "The duration of canine pregnancies is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu$ days and a standard deviation of $12$ days. | ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |

| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3669\,$ | $\,0.3632\,$ | $\,0.3594\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the length of a randomly selected pregnancy. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{12}^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>260).$ But first, we need to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(X<250)=0.10.$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<250) & =0.10 \\ P(Z<\frac{250-\mu }{12}) & =0.10 \\ Φ\left(\frac{250-\mu }{12}\right) & =0.10 \\ \frac{250-\mu }{12} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10)\end{aligned}

From the table, 

$$

$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(260<X)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>260) & =P(Z>\frac{260-265.3792}{12}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-0.45) \\  & =1-Φ(-0.45) \\  & =1-0.3264 \\  & ≈67.4\%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $67.4\%$ of the pregnancies have a duration greater than $260$ days."} {:db/id 17592186606865 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "215ae1ae-76d4-59de-a227-558b73ed8b55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6578" :db/id 17592186606208} {:answer/id #uuid "2b13c023-3eda-5498-a1f2-8fa814ca5df3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8289" :db/id 17592186606235} {:answer/id #uuid "4bb037fc-3187-546d-b181-aa73306f295d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.8729" :db/id 17592186606306} {:answer/id #uuid "527b5c6e-3b4d-5343-aa1a-82796dcf15ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.7458" :db/id 17592186606316} {:answer/id #uuid "f0d60070-41cf-55d2-9dfc-3b60c8f7b8e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3422" :db/id 17592186606638}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606208} :answer-field/id #uuid "b2353c29-2ea0-54a5-abf9-2286e61d9ed9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606763}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "91de87a8-9f00-58cc-be2c-509d4262c0ae" :question/math-academy-id "q-143410" :question/problem "The time Annie takes to complete a level of her favorite videogame, in minutes, is normally distributed with a mean of $6\,\text{min}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{min}.$ If she completes $10$ levels of the game, what is the probability that she will take more than $57\,\text{min}$ and less than $63\,min?$ You may assume that the games are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.* 

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8264\,$ | $\,0.8289\,$ | $\,0.8315\,$ | $\,0.8340\,$ |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ | $\,0.8554\,$ | $\,0.8577\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ | $\,0.8770\,$ | $\,0.8790\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the time Annie takes to complete the $i$th level. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(6,{1}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 10.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the time Annie takes to complete $10$ randomly selected levels. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{10},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =10\cdot 6 \\  & =60, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =10\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(60,10).
$$

In order to find $P(57<W<63),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(57<W<63) & =P(\frac{57-60}{\sqrt{10}}<Z<\frac{63-60}{\sqrt{10}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.95<Z<0.95) \\  & =Φ(0.95)-Φ(-0.95) \\  & =Φ(0.95)-(1-Φ(0.95)) \\  & =2Φ(0.95)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.95)≈0.8289.
$$

Therefore,

$$
k(x)=\frac{{y}^{″}(x)}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}},\,{y}^{″}(x)=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(x) & =\frac{\left(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\right)}{{[1+{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}{(1+\frac{1}{x})}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}k(1) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{1}^{3}}{(1+\frac{1}{1})}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\cdot {2}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,dy\,dx\,dz.
$$ The region of integration is shown above.

*Hint: Change the order of integration to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.$*" :question/worked-solution "We cannot integrate the given integral because we cannot find a simple antiderivative of the integrand. So, we change the order of integration.

We wish to find the limits of integration ${u}_{1}(y,z),$ ${u}_{2}(y,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,dy\,dx\,dz={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{x}\le y\le 1\}
$$

The region $R$ is shown below.

![](images/3c/3c7ca5c1ee5257c197248ef75e29ed0df58566563cc54cc2ee605a997ee06570.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type II region and its projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $x$-axis and in the direction of increasing $x,$ as shown below.

![](images/f4/f4961b2856545cccdc66869b2f2da8c7cceb38a2112ddbd5a9f699ee175ca5cf.png)

The arrow enters the region through the back boundary and leaves through the front boundary:

- The back boundary of the region is

$$
x=0.
$$

- The front boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y,z),$ is

$$
y=\sqrt{x}\,⟹\,x={y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e4/e4696825851b2a2ad692e27269859d80e7216d7c9f1d331337ad759103ade6b2.png)

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I plane region in the $yz$-plane with the left curve given by $y=\sqrt{0}=0.$

![](images/e4/e499db1d6da06ddeb7979c57ff7524633edf532473ab703d3af5b8c9f891742d.png)

Hence,

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,dx\,dy\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\sqrt{1+{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{2}{9}{(1+{y}^{3})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{9}({2}^{3/2}-1)\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2(2\sqrt{2}-1)}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{2(2\sqrt{2}-1)}{9}[z]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2(2\sqrt{2}-1)}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186606896 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4477310a-f45c-5c0d-8859-078598309ced" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y∼N(-20,60)" :db/id 17592186606292} {:answer/id #uuid "64021ae8-fe77-52b9-bb25-02a536cd98be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y∼N(-20,30)" :db/id 17592186606349} {:answer/id #uuid "c2524edd-878b-5684-a672-183bc974e860" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y∼N(-12,60)" :db/id 17592186606540} {:answer/id #uuid "d358f268-8533-5a3b-9c9a-15b32f08384f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y∼N(20,30)" :db/id 17592186606578} {:answer/id #uuid "e99995ba-e806-5be9-ae1d-6ac295e893fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Y∼N(12,15)" :db/id 17592186606626}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186606292} :answer-field/id #uuid "25d6879c-068f-5bbc-8557-f5792168661f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186606684}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d6c8e04c-f435-5624-a6dd-4b93b30508c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-143290" :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{15}$ are I.I.D random variables, where

what is the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{15}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{15}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the distance traveled by the car with a gallon of gas. Then we have $X∼N(26,{6}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(25\le X<30).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(25\le X<30) & =P(\frac{25-26}{6}\le Z<\frac{30-26}{6}) \\  & =P(-0.17\le Z<0.67)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.17<Z<0.67) & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-0.17) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z\le -0.17) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-0.17)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67) & =0.7486 \\ Φ(-0.17) & =0.4325\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.17<Z<0.67) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-0.17) \\  & =0.7486-0.4325 \\  & =0.3161.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the car travels a distance greater or equal than $25\,\text{mi}$ but less than $30\,\text{mi}$ with a gallon of gas is approximately $0.32.$"} {:answer/id #uuid "d12ff3e9-ffc5-5ec8-aa2d-5b8df43b2d12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},\infty )" :db/id 17592186607361} {:db/id 17592186607587 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f98734f2-ead6-506f-9592-aab1a73b8bc7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\le" :db/id 17592186607426}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607426} :answer-field/id #uuid "09cb8856-371b-5dfb-b464-08311c3dd795" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186607435} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "296f3ee1-93dd-5668-8f75-477f31cce0ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186607104}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607104} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c82430d-0d9e-5868-bdb0-1c00c4118b3e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186607477} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7996a30e-6892-5819-830b-138bd7c82e6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi}{4}" :db/id 17592186607226}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607226} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3cfc86b-a00d-5ec2-a595-505c97f02e5f" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186607535}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "6d812880-789c-52fc-8b28-ef8d5436b5bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-329167" :question/problem "Solve the inequality

{{field-3}}" :question/worked-solution "Since $-\frac{\pi }{4}<x<\frac{\pi }{4},$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\pi }{4} & <x<\frac{\pi }{4} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(-\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & <\operatorname{tan}⁡x<\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\ -1 & <\operatorname{tan}⁡x<1 \\ 1-1 & <1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x<1+1 \\ 0 & <1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x<2.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is positive for all the values of $x$ that we are considering $(-\frac{\pi }{4}<x<\frac{\pi }{4}).$ So, we can multiply both sides by $1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ and solve the resulting inequality as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4x-1}{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x} & \ge 0 \\ (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\cdot \frac{4x-1}{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x} & \ge (1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\cdot 0 \\ 4x-1 & \ge 0 \\ 4x & \ge 1 \\ x & \ge \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality will be the numbers that satisfy both $-\frac{\pi }{4}<x<\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x\ge \frac{1}{4}.$ So, the solution to our inequality is

$$
\frac{1}{4}\le x<\frac{\pi }{4}.

*Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.*" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $v,$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =0,\,v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\left(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}t+\frac{1}{3} \\ 3t\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ${x}_{E}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since ${x}_{E}^{′}(t)=0.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=3x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

$$

- When ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ we get the following curve:

\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=t+\frac{4}{3} \\ y &=3t+3\end{aligned}\right.

Let's add it to the phase space:
