The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/7b/7b8050c83207f47d52de00273a24eaba6ed361b049124cba50a498e98a4239f4.png)"} {:db/id 17592186607605 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5457eb34-6518-5417-adad-1b0b4dd6cd73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186607160} {:answer/id #uuid "6b8bb4e0-e60a-5439-9257-556d45f1170c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186607196} {:answer/id #uuid "6be617da-4fa3-58bd-b67f-ac46cabebbe1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186607198} {:answer/id #uuid "7a2e58ad-28a9-5988-8f4d-fbe1fb5b18c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186607228} {:answer/id #uuid "be5a7c3a-cad4-5d81-a2a7-a131d86e4588" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186607328}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607228} :answer-field/id #uuid "2e1645e0-faae-5c67-b4d9-d5c7b75d22d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186607449}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98b0ba23-fec6-5c8f-b838-63c988917078" :question/math-academy-id "q-123637" :question/problem "$\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)=$" :question/worked-solution "Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](images/db/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{3\pi }{4}$ corresponds to the point $$
\displaystyle (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using the fact that $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },
$$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)}=\frac{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}=-1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186607627 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "052db62b-cd3b-5a9d-89c2-43b05cc51bf6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "∅" :db/id 17592186607054} {:answer/id #uuid "6ff05c2e-bf43-5ba1-8f24-93f5418c455c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{3}]" :db/id 17592186607208} {:answer/id #uuid "74803734-9f20-5df8-a4db-c31ac9bc894b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "R" :db/id 17592186607218} {:answer/id #uuid "cbf30e32-e106-5b40-852a-ab2d8d98539f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,\frac{1}{3}]" :db/id 17592186607353} {:answer/id #uuid "d12ff3e9-ffc5-5ec8-aa2d-5b8df43b2d12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{4},\infty )" :db/id 17592186607361}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607218} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebc7c4b5-6a46-5543-8ec4-1cd788a12c27" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186607538}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d48322d8-1865-5ae9-94d3-0ec3f3c2434b" :question/math-academy-id "q-177453" :question/problem "Find the truth set of $P(x)∨Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $R:$

- $P(x):$ $3x-1\le 0$

- $Q(x):$ $4x>1$" :question/worked-solution "The truth set of $P(x)∨Q(x)$ represents the *union* of the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x):$

$$
{T}_{P∨Q}={T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q}
$$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x):$

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & \le 0 \\ 3x & \le 1 \\ x & \le \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is
${T}_{P}=(-\infty ,\frac{1}{3}].$

- To find the the truth set of $Q(x),$ we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & >1 \\ x & >\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $Q(x)$ is
${T}_{P}=(\frac{1}{4},\infty ).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∨Q} & ={T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =(-\infty ,\frac{1}{3}]\cup (\frac{1}{4},\infty ) \\  & =R.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608164 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1eb2f314-6218-5d20-846d-b1f62c244921" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186607839} {:answer/id #uuid "1f4d7f16-9e28-5cde-9ed7-301d3003cbf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186607841} {:answer/id #uuid "4b379efb-0a72-500a-8ebf-e235cb2af673" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186607901} {:answer/id #uuid "bafabf47-e243-501e-acbd-67f3d795684d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186608015} {:answer/id #uuid "fdc1e9c9-25e8-5c9a-a2fb-c81db3158f1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/id 17592186608088}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608015} :answer-field/id #uuid "f92ab846-6ecb-5402-adcb-73ad9f5b7d61" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608163}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "08c4a96f-48cd-5998-9cd6-61ef07570afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-49536" :question/problem "Find the value of $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1/10}\frac{15}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/10}\frac{15}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=15{\int }_{0}^{1/10}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{10}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/10}\frac{15}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =15{\int }_{0}^{1/10}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =15{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608172 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "920c4839-691b-5f0b-ae39-75303095e34f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{t}-e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186607975}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607975} :answer-field/id #uuid "ae81f2c0-ad34-527e-ab91-cd62521a7ae4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608138} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dce162a-22ec-55fb-8796-baa2c199db37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e^{t}-e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186607992}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607992} :answer-field/id #uuid "b618b247-16d5-5424-af09-f5944151ccd3" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608140}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2b3f41d9-87bd-58d9-a922-b51acf791e52" :question/math-academy-id "q-334585" :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $2.$*

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${e}^{At}=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="120px">$-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="120px">$-2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="120px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}))t \\  & =-({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608176 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "490e1b31-93d0-5418-8639-62de3385c547" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\cos\left(t-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)" :db/id 17592186607899}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607899} :answer-field/id #uuid "394b31ff-8e68-502b-93c9-78b6aeff1699" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608102}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3217b1a2-56a2-5db1-9377-bac79d4bf040" :question/math-academy-id "q-345270" :question/problem "Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)+y(t)={u}_{\pi /2}(t),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1,
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+1+Y(s)=\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s}.
$$

The solution is $y(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})\,\cdot \,($

$)-\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).$" :question/worked-solution "Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+1+Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+1)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-\pi s/2}}{s}-1 \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-\pi s/2}\cdot \frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}-\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{Bs+C}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=1$, $B=-1$, and $C=0$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+1)}=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-\pi s/2}(\frac{1}{s}-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1})\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{\pi /2}(t)(1-\cos \,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ y(t) & =u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{2})(1-\cos \,(t-\frac{\pi }{2}))-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608179 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ef8d047d-df7d-5c8c-b0fe-49a0ce8ba769" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e^{t}+3e^{6t}" :db/id 17592186608070}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608070} :answer-field/id #uuid "29352027-8aad-5321-9384-194d5af7cd6b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608096} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d7aeb964-4404-5e25-a395-63dde2f6215c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3e^{t}+2e^{6t}" :db/id 17592186608043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608043} :answer-field/id #uuid "32824489-d69c-5c83-b512-6bf3a0a07d87" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608101}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "37e4011e-9f24-5fc3-848f-0f90f756ba01" :question/math-academy-id "q-333922" :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $6.$*

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${e}^{At}=\,\,\frac{1}{5}$</td>

<tr>

<td align="center">$2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="120px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(6t) &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-5t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $6$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
5{\alpha }_{0}=6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-3{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t})+(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3{e}^{t}+2{e}^{6t}) \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4(-\frac{1}{5t}({e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}))t+\frac{1}{5}(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}((-4{e}^{t}+4{e}^{6t})+(6{e}^{t}-{e}^{6t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{t}+2{e}^{6t} & 3{e}^{t}-3{e}^{6t} \\ 2{e}^{t}-2{e}^{6t} & 2{e}^{t}+3{e}^{6t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608180 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "377c1b2b-d039-55c9-bd85-be4cfc875a6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}-5" :db/id 17592186607868} {:answer/id #uuid "c5fb55e1-eb1c-56ad-b93a-54d262e07f7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{25}{x}^{2}-3" :db/id 17592186608024} {:answer/id #uuid "deed88f8-b75f-5762-bc86-c4596acfa1e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{25}(x-3)^{2}" :db/id 17592186608051} {:answer/id #uuid "eda3dacf-53bb-521a-8c87-c87f1365d35d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}+5" :db/id 17592186608065} {:answer/id #uuid "edd316d3-35d1-5e04-be4e-221e5a03938e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{9}(x-5)^{2}" :db/id 17592186608067}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607868} :answer-field/id #uuid "d6213a92-efd9-5b02-a808-2fa866c2ea06" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608156}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3a233cce-a262-55ee-b4e5-8722e1adba98" :question/math-academy-id "q-148495" :question/problem "Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=3\sqrt{x+5}.$" :question/worked-solution "To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=3\sqrt{x+5}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=3\sqrt{y+5}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\sqrt{y+5} \\ \sqrt{y+5} & =\frac{1}{3}x \\ {(\sqrt{y+5})}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{3}x)}^{2} \\ y+5 & =\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2} \\ y & =\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{9}{x}^{2}-5.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\ge -5,\,f(x)\ge 0.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x\ge 0,\,{f}^{-1}(x)\ge -5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608184 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4509901e-f9a9-51bd-9843-b72e2a5ea1a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186607893} {:answer/id #uuid "5718c096-0547-5c20-b5b5-e3ffff431e40" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "160" :db/id 17592186607916} {:answer/id #uuid "7dbadb83-9110-548f-a0c8-d349a3b35f24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "80" :db/id 17592186607956} {:answer/id #uuid "995fe3be-5ba6-5c96-b9e5-2b6ee89bced3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "120" :db/id 17592186607987} {:answer/id #uuid "f6657d71-5e2e-5c0f-96e0-670bfc63ca39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "140" :db/id 17592186608076}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607956} :answer-field/id #uuid "b0b50335-1f15-5732-ae6d-39d62e0ce446" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608139}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "46fc820e-4197-5e9b-9901-eb94f384763a" :question/math-academy-id "q-124589" :question/problem "Evaluate the series $$
\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }25{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{n}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{2},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & =25{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{2}=16 \\ {a}_{3} & =25{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{3}=\frac{64}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{\left(\frac{64}{5}\right)}{16}=\frac{4}{5}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }25{\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{16}{(1-\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =\frac{16}{\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)} \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608189 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4ade5a23-8cac-5f6c-9e1e-d06a283f53a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.57" :db/id 17592186607900} {:answer/id #uuid "7a0637a1-7bf3-500d-add8-4dd7574465f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.35" :db/id 17592186607953} {:answer/id #uuid "a0baf4f6-8b9b-52dd-a085-9abbc2c09e6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.23" :db/id 17592186607995} {:answer/id #uuid "b0c4cb53-e0d1-53e9-aca5-e9a8a57be477" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.49" :db/id 17592186608011} {:answer/id #uuid "e342688f-bbba-56ff-8771-4fccd900294a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.68" :db/id 17592186608053}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608011} :answer-field/id #uuid "28e23342-5157-52c1-a103-d2f8cade008c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608095}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5842a4d5-df96-50bb-ae16-8e81cc3dcbfe" :question/math-academy-id "q-345150" :question/problem "![](images/b5/b5603a9a67072aad7aa18715715a0899bf47add1f165a02831db9f2282e5021a.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{24}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/24)}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}=4\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=4\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
10\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=20\,\frac{dq}{dt}+24q+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+6q=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+5\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+6{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+5(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\, &  \\ +\,6(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (2\alpha +10\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-10\alpha +2\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\alpha +10\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -10\alpha +2\beta &=\frac{5}{2}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{25}{104},$ $\beta =\frac{5}{104}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{25}{104}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{104}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-3t}-\frac{25}{104}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{104}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-3t}-\frac{25}{104}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{104}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-2A{e}^{-2t}-3B{e}^{-3t}+\frac{25}{52}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{52}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-2A{e}^{-2t}-3B{e}^{-3t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=\frac{25}{52}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{52}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{25}{52}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{5}{52}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{25}{52}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{5}{52}\right)}^{2}}≈0.49,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186608201 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74fa4ef0-bc4a-5b9f-95d5-8fc6692068df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5e^{-8t}+2e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186607947}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607947} :answer-field/id #uuid "2e0c10bb-d8d4-5466-8822-4b22e56926d8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608100} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9572cba2-7628-5c63-ba7c-0723db7863d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e^{-8t}-2e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186607980}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607980} :answer-field/id #uuid "5a1a999c-17ad-5049-9539-0a68ca73be4c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "81b181d8-d80f-5719-a61c-0648ba2eb3f4" :question/math-academy-id "q-333919" :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$ 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-8$ and $-1.$*

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${e}^{At}=\,\,\frac{1}{7}$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>

</tr>
<tr>

<td align="center" width="160px">$2{e}^{-8t}+5{e}^{-t}$</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -5 \\ -2 & -3\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & -3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-8t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-8t) &={e}^{-8t} \\ r(-t) &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-8t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-8t} \\ -t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-7t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}).
$$

- Multiplying the second equation by $-8$ and adding to the first one, we get

$$
-7{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=-\frac{1}{7}({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-6(-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}))t-\frac{1}{7}({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}((6{e}^{-8t}-6{e}^{-t})-({e}^{-8t}-8{e}^{-t})) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(5{e}^{-8t}+2{e}^{-t}) \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2(-\frac{1}{7t}({e}^{-8t}-{e}^{-t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{7}(2{e}^{-8t}-2{e}^{-t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{7}\begin{bmatrix}5{e}^{-8t}+2{e}^{-t} & 5{e}^{-8t}-5{e}^{-t} \\ 2{e}^{-8t}-2{e}^{-t} & 2{e}^{-8t}+5{e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608218 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "41a97fc2-b57f-57e4-86a7-649fe6cb09ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}e^{-2(t-1)}" :db/id 17592186607888}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607888} :answer-field/id #uuid "04113e93-4f7d-5601-abb5-be6feb3b2cd6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608090}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b636fb55-1e06-50d6-89a3-a47bf68ea2cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-345298" :question/problem "Find the solution $y(t)$ given that the Laplace transform of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}(t)+3{y}^{′}(t)+2y(t)={u}_{1}(t),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,
$$

is given by

$$
{s}^{2}Y(s)+3sY(s)+2Y(s)=\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s}.
$$

The solution is $y(t)=u(t-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-(t-1)}\,+\,$
{{field-1}}
$).$" :question/worked-solution "Using the transformed equation, we solve for $Y(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}Y(s)+3sY(s)+2Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s} \\ ({s}^{2}+3s+2)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s} \\ (s+1)(s+2)Y(s) & ={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\ Y(s) & ={e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{1}{s(s+1)(s+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the inverse transform, we first use partial fraction decomposition on the algebraic part:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+3s+2)}=\frac{A}{s}+\frac{B}{s+1}+\frac{C}{s+2}
$$

Solving for the constants, we find $A=\frac{1}{2}$, $B=-1$, and $C=\frac{1}{2}$, giving:

$$
\frac{1}{s({s}^{2}+3s+2)}=\frac{1}{2s}-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{2(s+2)}
$$

Now, we apply the inverse Laplace transform. Let 

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{2s}-\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{2(s+2)},
$$

then, we have 

$$
f(t)=\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t}.
$$

According to the second shifting theorem, 

$$
{L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-as}F(s)\}={u}_{a}(t)f(t-a).
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{e}^{-s}F(s)\} \\ y(t) & ={u}_{1}(t)\,f(t-1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y(t)=u(t-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-{e}^{-(t-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2(t-1)}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608223 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06b5ebe5-c210-5b35-835d-d9deeeabec7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C" :db/id 17592186607812} {:answer/id #uuid "093177fd-5db2-57d5-9b5c-850e7b01fb2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C" :db/id 17592186607813} {:answer/id #uuid "41629820-71e3-5199-b636-aa0a0102d247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C" :db/id 17592186607887} {:answer/id #uuid "e4e0cba8-3339-5415-84a0-92836507db7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C" :db/id 17592186608056} {:answer/id #uuid "e5ccf36b-4d0e-5552-bc07-10a01cad864b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C" :db/id 17592186608057}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186607812} :answer-field/id #uuid "c1f2b0b4-ffb2-5d8c-aa82-efd5909fb1b8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608149}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c5cec407-ac09-52aa-af07-f10036319399" :question/math-academy-id "q-13738" :question/problem "$$
\displaystyle \int 2{x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}\,\text{d}x=
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's introduce the new variable $u=-{x}^{3}-5.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-{x}^{3}-5}+C.\end{aligned}

If the cormorant is directly above the tuna's position, how far apart are the two animals?" :question/worked-solution "To determine how far apart the two animals are, we must calculate the difference between the locations of the cormorant and the tuna. So, we wish to compute

$$
6\,\frac{1}{2}-(-5\,\frac{2}{3}).
$$

First, we convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions. This gives,

$$
\frac{6\cdot 2+1}{2}-\left(-\frac{5\cdot 3+2}{3}\right)\,\,
$$

and simplifying further, we get

$$
\frac{13}{2}-\left(-\frac{17}{3}\right).
$$

We now subtract the two numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{13}{2}-\left(-\frac{17}{3}\right) & =\frac{13}{2}+\frac{17}{3} \\  & =\frac{39}{6}+\frac{34}{6} \\  & =\frac{39+34}{6} \\  & =\frac{73}{6}\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
73÷6=12\text{R}1=12\frac{1}{6}
$$

Therefore, the cormorant and the tuna are $12\frac{1}{6}$ meters apart."} {:db/id 17592186608981 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23cf7645-8d5c-59e0-b05b-e2a87e9f91ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\times {9}^{7}" :db/id 17592186608479} {:answer/id #uuid "3338c949-ce10-51e9-b1d8-c101c487f23d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{7}\times 9" :db/id 17592186608498} {:answer/id #uuid "3b2c45c8-3c71-533a-8d62-5364063acf10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{7}\times {9}^{7}" :db/id 17592186608515} {:answer/id #uuid "431e51e5-b98c-5a56-a743-a0f0b4ddc5c9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}\times {9}^{7}" :db/id 17592186608531} {:answer/id #uuid "528741c0-10ab-59bc-b60c-59569dedbfb5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{4}^{7}\times {9}^{7}" :db/id 17592186608554}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608515} :answer-field/id #uuid "1f84660a-bfa5-501e-8058-746b4ba78abc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186608852}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "83f995a1-d740-552f-b803-40ce9fb2ee79" :question/math-academy-id "q-68623" :question/problem "${(-\frac{1}{4}\times 9)}^{7}=$" :question/worked-solution "To raise the product of two numbers to the power of $7$, we can raise each number to the power of $7,$ and then multiply:

If the particle has position $x=0$ and velocity $v=\frac{1}{2}$ when $t=0,$ the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$x(t)=$
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C \\ \frac{1}{2} & =0+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $$
\displaystyle v(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{2}\int \,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0+K \\ 0 & =-\frac{1}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{1}{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186608999 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a296a3d7-7e7e-5ed9-ae20-9f21711ab9c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186608678}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608678} :answer-field/id #uuid "71f10ab4-e8ff-5f85-827a-768c109e0f77" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608878} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d4315fae-3c4f-52bd-b60e-9954fa51cde4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186608771}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608771} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf585b2a-11dd-5841-9c3c-7d0bf42219f5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608916}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6834fc7-5fc8-5d54-aa35-2e6beb3558f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-181995" :question/problem "What are the minimum and maximum of the set $A=[\frac{3}{2},8]?$

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right)+{f}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right)(x-\frac{\pi }{8})+\frac{{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right)}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{8})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{8})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡4x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡4x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right)=-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=-16.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{8})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}\left(\frac{\pi }{8}\right)}{2} & =\frac{(-16)}{2}=-8\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186609007 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6dd37a2f-cf28-5664-bc7f-9a6246ea1179" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186608598}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186608598} :answer-field/id #uuid "def42209-9bfc-59c5-a6f5-8abd1609b27a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186608925}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "cbe3d838-3218-5372-9503-9ceabd4e4a92" :question/math-academy-id "q-341804" :question/problem "$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=2\sqrt{x} & \,⟹\,v=\int 2\sqrt{x}\,dx=\frac{4{x}^{3/2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{4}}2\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{4}}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{4}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{4}}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x\left(\frac{4{x}^{3/2}}{3}\right){|}_{1}^{{e}^{4}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{4}}\left(\frac{4{x}^{3/2}}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\frac{4({e}^{4})^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{4})}{3}-\frac{4(1)^{3/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)}{3}]-\frac{4}{3}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{4}}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{4})}{3}-\frac{8{x}^{3/2}}{9}{|}_{1}^{{e}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{16{e}^{6}}{3}-(\frac{8{e}^{6}}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(48{e}^{6}-8{e}^{6}+8) \\  & =\frac{8}{9}(5{e}^{6}+1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186609835 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "461990c9-5b71-5a2d-9b48-683988719005" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4050" :db/id 17592186609349} {:answer/id #uuid "4c54cf39-68ad-5170-912f-e0467901c455" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4198" :db/id 17592186609356} {:answer/id #uuid "55887b91-d205-53bc-986b-cde4200fc7a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3987" :db/id 17592186609378} {:answer/id #uuid "b644bd5b-9693-537e-a333-436a4c384b48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4108" :db/id 17592186609550} {:answer/id #uuid "dd549e00-64a7-5b96-9c1e-0e2e175c66b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4234" :db/id 17592186609619}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186609550} :answer-field/id #uuid "c046db41-7e2a-5d53-a5bc-587b3f78b908" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186609782}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "29b23a99-2fbb-5aa2-b17f-1e3898160ce3" :question/math-academy-id "q-94336" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Given a normal random variable $Y∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 33.05) & =P(Z\ge \frac{33.05-14}{15}) \\  & =P\,(Z\ge \frac{19.05}{15}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 1.27)\end{aligned}

\displaystyle {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\left(\frac{n+2}{4}\right).
$$ Does it converge or diverge? If it converges, what is the sum of the series?" :question/worked-solution "The given series is an arithmetic series. Its first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{1+2}{4}=\frac{3}{4},
$$

Its $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{n+2}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we get the following formula for the $n$th partial sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{n} & =\frac{n}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{n}) \\  & =\frac{n}{2}(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{n+2}{4}) \\  & =\frac{n(5+n)}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the limit of the partial sums, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{n\to \infty }{s}_{n} & =\lim_{n\to \infty }\frac{n(5+n)}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\lim_{n\to \infty }{n}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the limit of the sequence of partial sums is infinite, the series is divergent."} {:db/id 17592186609890 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5436d1a7-8d3b-59f8-80a6-5d878246e66f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186609373} {:answer/id #uuid "b306d3b7-bbb4-51a6-b8da-4d2ce46a9b7f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2}+2)" :db/id 17592186609546} {:answer/id #uuid "d6e7d6f6-2a20-5138-aefe-342aada3d0ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}(2{e}^{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186609606} {:answer/id #uuid "d72879fa-59ee-5aec-8f24-d0f465deae42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4(1-{e}^{2})" :db/id 17592186609608} {:answer/id #uuid "fe3d4796-e888-5944-a6fb-6cb2089e0eac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}+1" :db/id 17592186609685}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186609373} :answer-field/id #uuid "2bde457d-7956-5580-91ca-213eed8d75c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186609705}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "cd2cb8b6-4dd3-5139-9be0-ca32f293a728" :question/math-academy-id "q-49738" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=x & \,⟹\,v=\int x\,dx=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}

$${{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({\log }_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{\log }_{2}⁡(2x)}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=24{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 24{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=8{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 24{x}^{2}({\log }_{2}⁡(2x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({\log }_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}(8{x}^{3})-\int (8{x}^{3})\left(\frac{2{\log }_{2}⁡(2x)}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\right)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{3}{({\log }_{2}⁡(2x))}^{2}-\frac{16}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {x}^{2}{\log }_{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $$
\displaystyle \int {x}^{2}{\log }_{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={\log }_{2}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi ,2\pi )$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval. 

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

- We differentiate $f(t)$ to find ${f}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({\sin }^{2}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${f}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we conclude that $f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$ to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\sqrt{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{t},\,-2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of  ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined for all  $t\in (\pi ,2\pi )$, we have that $g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

- Finally, we differentiate $h(t)$ to find ${h}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,2,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the answer is: 

$\,$ All the functions are differentiable on $(\pi ,2\pi ).$

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,3)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,3⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ ({1}^{2}+3)-({0}^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =⟨2{c}_{1},1⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 3 & =2{c}_{1}+2 \\ 1 & =2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

If $F$ and $G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for curl:

- $∇\times (kF)=k∇\times F$

- $∇\times (F+G)=∇\times F+∇\times G$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-3G) & =∇\times F+∇\times (-3G) \\  & =∇\times F-3∇\times G.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to calculate $∇\times F.$ In doing so, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times F & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 2\sqrt{z}+x & xy & {y}^{2}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2\sqrt{z}+x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{z}+x)]k \\  & =(2y-0)i-(0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}})j+(y-0)k \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the linearity properties, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (F-3G) & =∇\times F-3∇\times G \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k-3[3{x}^{2}y\,k] \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y\,k-9{x}^{2}y\,k \\  & =2y\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,j+y(1-9{x}^{2})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating at the point $(1,0,9),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\times (F-3G))(1,0,9) & =2(0)\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{9}}\,j+0(1-9(1)^{2})\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =x{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2})y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}(x-1)^{2}y+{y}^{3}-4{y}^{2}+4y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}(x-1)^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}+2{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{9}{2}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{9}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}(x-1)^{3}+\frac{9}{4}x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{9}{2}-(-\frac{3}{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}

When a polar curve is differentiable at a point ${\theta }_{0}$, there is a horizontal tangent at ${\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}=0
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a horizontal tangent at this point if

$$
\lim_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right){\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-3) \\  & =1\cdot 0\cdot (5\cdot 0-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to \frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{{\cos }^{3}⁡\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -4)}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\cancel{cos}}^{2}\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{{cos}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -4)}\right) \\  & =\lim_{\theta \to \pi /2}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -3)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,(5{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta -4)}\right) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (5\cdot 0-3)}{0\cdot (5\cdot 0-4)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{0} \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the limit in part II does *not* equal to $0,$ there curve does *not* have a horizontal tangent at $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}.$ In fact, it is a vertical tangent.

![](images/d7/d7881ba860bcc32301a162eb200ea9075b06b63c780be74c14aedbcb1654eaaa.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

We are given the units $\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}},$ and we want to convert this into $\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.$ We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}
$$

One of the conversion factors should change $\text{m}$ to $\text{km}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}\cdot \,\frac{?}{?}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}
$$

The other conversion factor should change $\text{min}$ into $\text{hour}.$

$$
\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{hour}}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}
$$

So, our conversion formula is

$$
\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}}\cdot \frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}}=\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.
$$

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use, and apply it.

- The rate given in the problem statement is $1\,000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}.$

- There are $1\,000$ meters per kilometer, therefore, there are $\frac{1}{1\,000}$ kilometers per meter.

- There are $60$ minutes in one hour.

Applying our conversion formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}} & =1000\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{m}}\cdot 60\,\frac{\text{min}}{\text{hour}} \\  & =1000\cdot \frac{1}{1\,000}\cdot 60(\frac{\cancel{\text{m}}}{\cancel{\text{min}}}\cdot \frac{\text{km}}{\cancel{\text{m}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{min}}}{\text{hour}}) \\  & =60\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{hour}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, a speed of $1\,000$ meters per minute is equivalent to $60$ kilometers per hour. Thus, the car will travel $60$ kilometers in one hour.

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2 \\ z &=4y-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

$$

However,

$$

$$

and, hence, $-f(x)\notin B.$

- Statement II is false. For example, consider the functions $f(x)={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2},$ $g(x)=\frac{1}{2},$ and $h(x)=2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2},$ from $B.$ Then:

$$
\begin{aligned}[f(x)-g(x)]+h(x) & =[{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}]+2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ f(x)-[g(x)+h(x)] & ={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}-[\frac{1}{2}+2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}] \\  & ={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}-[2{x}^{2}+1] \\  & ={x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}-2{x}^{2}-1 \\  & =-{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{x+1}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{k}{x+1}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int \left(-\frac{k}{x+1}\right)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=8-k\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).

$$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-1+2}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-1+2}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{1}{2}$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4(x+1)(x-2) \\  & =-4\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}-2\right) \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $\left(\frac{1}{2},9\right),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,9].$

$$

$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$ and $t\ge 0.$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & ⇒ & v=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t| \\  & =|\,-\frac{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\,| \\  & =|\,-\frac{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}\,| \\  & =|\,-\frac{\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2}+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,| \\  & =|\,\frac{\pi }{4}\,| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=90$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =90\cdot 0.5 \\  & =45 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =90\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =45 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(90)(0.5)=45
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(90)(0.5)(1-0.5)=22.5.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(45,22.5).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=35).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=35)≈P(34.5\le Y\le 35.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(34.5\le Y\le 35.5) & =P(\frac{34.5-45}{\sqrt{22.5}}\le Z\le \frac{35.5-45}{\sqrt{22.5}}) \\  & ≈P(-2.21\le Z\le -2.00) \\  & =P(Z\le -2.00)-P(Z<-2.21) \\  & =P(Z\le -2.00)-P(Z\le -2.21) \\  & =Φ(-2.00)-Φ(-2.21) \\  & =0.0228-0.0136 \\  & =0.0092\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=35)≈0.009.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0092.$

Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=300$ and $p=0.55.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =300\cdot 0.55 \\  & =165 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =300\cdot (1-0.55) \\  & =135 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(300)(0.55)=165
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(300)(0.55)(1-0.55)=74.25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(165,74.25).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=180).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=180)≈P(179.5\le Y\le 180.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(179.5\le Y\le 180.5) & =P(\frac{179.5-165}{\sqrt{74.25}}\le Z\le \frac{180.5-165}{\sqrt{74.25}}) \\  & ≈P(1.68\le Z\le 1.80) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.80)-P(Z<1.68) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.80)-P(Z\le 1.68) \\  & =Φ(1.80)-Φ(1.68) \\  & =0.9641-0.9535 \\  & =0.0106\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=180)≈0.011.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$

The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,4)-f(1,2) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,4⟩-⟨1,2⟩) \\ ({2}^{2}+2(2)(4))-({1}^{2}+2(1)(2)) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x+2y,2x⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2},2{c}_{1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2},2{c}_{1}⟩\cdot ⟨1,2⟩ \\ 15 & =2{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}+4{c}_{1} \\ 15 & =6{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-2}{4-2} & =\frac{x-1}{2-1} \\ \frac{y-2}{2} & =x-1 \\ y-2 & =2x-2 \\ y & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =2{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $6{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=15,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{c}_{1}+2(2{c}_{1}) & =15 \\ 6{c}_{1}+4{c}_{1} & =15 \\ 10{c}_{1} & =15 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=2{c}_{1}=3.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{3}{2},3).$

First, we factor the quadratic denominator, giving us the equation

$$
\frac{2}{v-7}+\frac{5}{v-1}=\frac{12}{(v-1)(v-7)}.
$$

We now make the following observations:

- The least common denominator of our equation is given by

$$
\text{LCM}(v-1,\,v-7,\,(v-1)(v-7))=(v-1)(v-7).
$$

- The values $v=1$ and $v=7$ cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{v-7}+\frac{5}{v-1} & =\frac{12}{(v-1)(v-7)} \\ (v-1)(v-7)\cdot (\frac{2}{v-7}+\frac{5}{v-1}) & =(v-1)(v-7)\cdot \frac{12}{(v-1)(v-7)} \\ \frac{2(v-1)(v-7)}{v-7}+\frac{5(v-1)(v-7)}{v-1} & =\frac{12(v-1)(v-7)}{(v-1)(v-7)} \\ \frac{2(v-1)\cdot \cancel{(v-7)}}{\cancel{v-7}}+\frac{5\cdot \cancel{(v-1)}\cdot (v-7)}{\cancel{v-1}} & =\frac{12\cdot \cancel{(v-1)(v-7)}}{\cancel{(v-1)(v-7)}} \\ 2(v-1)+5(v-7) & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $v,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(v-1)+5(v-7) & =12 \\ 2v-2+5v-35 & =12 \\ 7v & =49 \\ v & =7\end{aligned}
$$

However, since $v=7$ is not a valid solution, our equation has no solutions.

$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/4}}{8}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/4}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/4}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/4}}{8}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/4}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/4}}{8}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/4}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/4}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/4}}{8}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/4}}{8}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/4}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/4}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/4}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/4}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

First, we compute $\text{E}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{2}^{6}x\cdot (\frac{x}{8}-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{3}}{24}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8})|}_{2}^{6} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x}{8}-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{32}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{12})|}_{2}^{6} \\  & =\frac{68}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{68}{3}-{\left(\frac{14}{3}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/db/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{5\pi }{4}$ corresponds to the point $$
\displaystyle (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using the fact that $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },
$$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{4}\right)}=\frac{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}=1.
$$

First, let $r$ be the radius and $h$ be the height of the cylinder.

We wish to maximize the volume

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

We know that the surface area is fixed at $12\pi \,{cm}^{2},$ so we also have the constraint equation

$$
2\pi rh+\pi {r}^{2}=12\pi .
$$

Now, by making $h$ the subject of the constraint equation, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =12\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{6}{r}-\frac{r}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}(\frac{6}{r}-\frac{r}{2}) \\ V(r) & =(6r-\frac{{r}^{3}}{2})\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=(6-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2})\pi .
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ (6-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2})\pi  & =0 \\ 6 & =\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =4 \\ r & =2\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=2$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(2)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=2$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=2\,\text{cm}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume ${V}_{\text{max}},$ we substitute $r=2\,\text{cm}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{max}}=V(2) & =(6(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{3})\pi  \\  & =(12-4)\pi  \\  & =8\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot (1-x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{10(x-1)}{{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{10x-10}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}){|}_{0}^{1}+(-\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{10}{3{x}^{3}}){|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{1}{12}+0+5-\frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}-{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}2\pi rh & =108\pi -\pi {r}^{2} \\ h & =\frac{54}{r}-\frac{r}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging the above into our expression for $V,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}V(r) & =\pi {r}^{2}\left(\frac{54}{r}-\frac{r}{2}\right) \\ V(r) & =\left(54r-\frac{{r}^{3}}{2}\right)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We want to maximize $V,$ so we need to differentiate $V$ and set the derivative equal to zero. The derivative is 

$$
{V}^{′}(r)=\left(54-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2}\right)\pi .
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $r$ gives a stationary point, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =0 \\ \left(54-\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2}\right)\pi  & =0 \\ 54 & =\frac{3{r}^{2}}{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =36 \\ r & =6\,\text{in}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that, in the last step, we only considered the positive root because the radius $r$ must be positive.

Finally, we confirm that $r=6$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative ${V}^{″}(r)$ is

$$
{V}^{″}(r)=\frac{-6\pi r}{2}=-3\pi r,
$$

and we can see that ${V}^{″}(6)<0.$ So, the stationary point $r=6$ is indeed a maximum of $V(r).$

So the cylinder with the largest volume has a radius of $r=6\,\text{in}.$

Finally, to find the largest volume ${V}_{\text{max}},$ we substitute $r=6\,\text{in}$ into the equation for the volume $V:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{max}}=V(6) & =\left(54(6)-\frac{1}{2}(6)^{3}\right)\pi  \\  & =\left(324-\frac{216}{2}\right)\pi  \\  & =(324-108)\pi  \\  & =216\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

\displaystyle I=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4({e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+4I) \\ I & =-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-16I \\ 17I & =-{e}^{-4x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\left(-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\right){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\left(-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{17}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))\right) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}(-1+0)+\frac{1}{17}(1+0) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{17}+\frac{1}{17} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}(1+{e}^{-4\pi }).\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $\lim_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{x\pi }{4}\right)+3x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}(2\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{x\pi }{4}\right)+3x) \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4}\right)+3(1) \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+3 \\  & =2\cdot 1+3 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=4\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{x\pi }{4}\right)+kx.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}(4\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{x\pi }{4}\right)+kx) \\  & =4\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4}\right)+k(1) \\  & =4\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+k \\  & =4\cdot 1+k \\  & =4+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & =\lim_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ 4+k & =5 \\ k & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Let the random variable $X$ be the number of players winning an apple.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=15$ players in the game

- the probability of choosing a door that hides an apple is $p=\frac{3}{4}$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(15,\frac{3}{4}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{x}{(1-\frac{3}{4})}^{15-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{x}){\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{x}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{15-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that at least $14$ players will win an apple. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 14) & =P(X=14)+P(X=15) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{14}){\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{14}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{15-14}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{15}{15}){\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{15}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{15-15} \\  & =15{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{14}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{1}+1{\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{15}{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{0} \\  & ≈0.0802\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.
